| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What must an assistance plan specify? | Task allocation, trained personnel, coverage, escalation, backup and supervision | Each element closes a gap where therapy could be missed or done unsafely. |  |
| 2 | Which team verifies pediatric prescriptions and infection protocols? | The pediatric nephrology and PD team, using age-appropriate standards | Adult defaults can harm a child. The pediatric team decides. |  |
| 3 | According to the 2020 ISPD acute PD guideline for adults, PD is: | A suitable modality for AKI in all settings (1B) | The guideline supports PD for AKI everywhere, with minimum-standard options for limited resources. |  |
| 4 | Which acute PD recommendation carries GRADE 1A? | A closed delivery system with a Y connection | The closed Y system is 1A (optimal) for adults and children. |  |
| 5 | Bicarbonate-containing solutions are recommended in acute PD particularly for: | Critically ill patients with significant liver dysfunction and marked lactate elevation (1B) | A damaged liver handles lactate poorly, so bicarbonate solutions are preferred. |  |
| 6 | Why is automated PD not suitable for newborns in the 2020 pediatric guideline? | Fill volumes are too small for current machines | The recommendation is graded 1D; it reflects machine limits, not unsuitability of PD itself. |  |
| 7 | How should the pediatric automated PD benefit be discussed with a family? | Verify current status with PhilHealth first, because the reviewed extension ended 31 July 2026 | Coverage after that date was not verified. Never promise a benefit you have not confirmed. |  |
| 8 | What does the 2024 ISPD position paper say about offering PD? | PD should be offered to every eligible person considering maintenance dialysis | Assistance is the tool for widening that access. |  |
| 9 | Observational studies comparing assisted and self-care PD in older patients found: | Broadly similar adjusted survival and peritonitis-free survival | They support feasibility but cannot prove equivalence. |  |
| 10 | Bea, 7, visiting from Manila, has a hazy bag and a stomachache. What is the adult PD nurse’s role? | Screen for instability, keep the bag, and call her pediatric PD team at once | Recognize urgently, hand over quickly. Pediatric protocols govern sampling and treatment. |  |
| 11 | Why is acute PD monitoring more intense than chronic PD? | Fluid, potassium, glucose, acid–base balance and blood pressure can change within hours | Unstable patients need hourly attention, not monthly review. |  |
| 12 | A stroke patient can explain PD but cannot manage the connections. First step? | With consent, assess his remaining abilities and the available caregivers, and coordinate evaluation for assisted PD | He keeps the tasks he can do safely; the rest are reassigned and verified. |  |
| 13 | Lola Felicidad skipped therapy every Sunday because her caregiver was off. What was missing from the plan? | Coverage for every day, with a named backup | Read the plan against the calendar. Every absence needs a name. |  |
| 14 | Catheter insertion by trained nephrologists in acute PD is: | Safe, with results equivalent to surgical insertion in patients without contraindications (1B) | This is one reason acute PD can be started where surgical teams are scarce. |  |
| 15 | Which statement fits this module’s level? | It provides orientation; independent practice needs additional training and authorization | Recognize, keep safe, hand over. Independent practice needs more. |  |

| 4 | Which source governs when a vendor help page conflicts with a PhilHealth advisory? | The advisory | A vendor page explains steps; it cannot override an issuance. |  |
| 5 | What is the risk of a hold note without a due date? | No one owns the clock, so a filing period can lapse unnoticed | Holds need an owner and a date. |  |
| 6 | Who releases a refund to a patient? | Finance, through the approved process | Claims staff document the variance and route it. |  |

| 9 | A supervisor asks you to relabel an acute kidney injury discharge as stage 5 to fit a batch. What do you do? | Hold the claim, preserve the source, route the diagnosis question, and escalate the request | A request to misrepresent the record is escalated, not argued. |  |

| 9 | What happened to the late-filing flexibility under Circular 2025-0006? | It ran from March 21 to September 21, 2025 and is closed | History, not a remedy. |  |
| 10 | What must the statement of account be under eClaims 3.0? | XML | PDF statements are returned. |  |
| 11 | Why set an internal target before the deadline? | To leave time to fix problems before the legal clock ends | Problems take time to fix. |  |
| 12 | Do calendar-day filing periods skip weekends and holidays? | No, unless an issuance says otherwise | Count every day. |  |
| 13 | Status shows “still unsure” after a timeout. What do you do? | Hold, escalate, and do not resend | Uncertainty is not permission to resend. |  |
| 14 | What does a transmission acknowledgment prove? | Receipt at that stage | Track adjudication separately. |  |
| 15 | What should you use to log in to eClaims? | Your own individual authorized account | Accounts make the audit trail. |  |

## Module 7: Returned Claims, Denials, and Escalation

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Do you reuse the ordinary filing clock for every denial? | No; verify the remedy-specific period against the notice and issuance | Each remedy has its own clock. |  |
| 2 | What should a useful PRO request include? | Authorized claim reference, dates, notice reason, facts, one precise question, and a secure channel | Short and specific. |  |
| 3 | A return arrived October 10 with a verified October 22 deadline. What is a sensible internal target? | Several working days earlier, for example October 17 | Leave time for review. |  |
| 4 | Is a denial for “duplicate” automatically correct? | No; compare claim references and treatment evidence first | Two distinct sessions can be mistaken for one. |  |
| 5 | Who signs a motion for reconsideration or an appeal? | The authorized signatory named in the facility adoption record | Authority is assigned in writing. |  |
| 6 | What must never be overwritten during a correction? | The original record and notice | Add corrections with an audit trail. |  |
| 7 | A returned claim is: | A deficiency to fix and refile through the linked process | A denial is the decision. |  |
| 8 | Twelve claims are returned for the same missing signature. What is this? | A process defect to fix at the step that let them out | Returns are a quality signal. |  |
| 9 | Which entry do you correct when a claim shows “received” and “draft”? | Match the notice’s claim reference to the received record and correct through the linked workflow | Never turn a draft into a new claim. |  |
| 10 | A claim is paid, but less than expected. Who owns the first look? | Claims and finance together | Document the variance and review the remedy. |  |
| 11 | Where do you confirm the remedy and deadline when the notice is unclear? | Written guidance from the PRO and the applicable issuance | Keep the written reply. |  |
| 12 | What is the first entry in a case chronology? | The service date or dates | Service comes first. |  |
| 13 | The same session was really sent twice after a timeout. What next? | Refer for authorized disposition; do not refile | This is why Module 6 says check before resending. |  |
| 14 | Which identifiers go in a message to the PRO? | Only those the question needs | Minimum necessary data. |  |
| 15 | Why keep one chronology per case? | So anyone can understand the case quickly and the trail survives staff changes | It protects the claim and the facility. |  |

| 6 | Which cases are excluded from performance rates? | Unsubmitted cases, tracked separately | Rates describe adjudicated claims. |  |
| 7 | Two allowed sessions and one 6,350-peso posting found. How is the rest classified? | Unexplained until confirmed, with an owner | Never assume. |  |

| 15 | Why does reconciliation matter to patients? | Payments fund the unit that keeps them on dialysis, and unmatched deposits hide problems | Finance sustains care. |  |

| 15 | Which document decides which benefit a session belongs to? | The clinician-documented diagnosis and modality | Never route by convenience. |  |

## Module 12: HMOs, Accreditation, and the Payer Profile

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which government agency now regulates and supervises HMOs in the Philippines? | The Insurance Commission | Executive Order No. 192 (2015) moved HMO regulation to the Insurance Commission. |  |
| 2 | How do you confirm that an HMO is licensed to operate? | Check the Insurance Commission’s list of HMOs with certificates of authority | The Commission publishes and updates the list. |  |
| 3 | Under Circular Letter 2024-01, which is an unsound business act? | Denying a claim without reasonable investigation of the available documents | Denials must rest on a reasonable investigation. |  |
| 4 | Circular Letter 2024-01 requires an HMO to act on a letter of authorization within what period? | A reasonable time after all required documents are submitted | The circular says reasonable time; your contract gives the number of days. |  |
| 5 | Where does the number of days an HMO has to pay your unit usually come from? | The payment term in the accreditation agreement | The signed agreement governs. |  |
| 6 | A patient shows a valid HMO card. What does it prove? | Membership in a plan, not dialysis coverage or your unit’s accreditation | Coverage and accreditation are separate checks. |  |
| 7 | Why do many HMO plans limit maintenance dialysis? | It is lifelong, predictable, and costly, unlike the episodic illness plans are priced for | Plans are priced for illness that comes and goes. |  |
| 8 | The agreement does not say whether professional fees go through the unit. What do you do? | Ask provider relations in writing and file the answer in the payer profile | Never fill a contract gap with a guess. |  |
| 9 | A covered session within the 156, package items only. What does the HMO pay? | Nothing for items the PhilHealth package already paid | Each peso is billed once. |  |
| 10 | A patient has used all 156 sessions in October. Who may become the first payer for later sessions that year? | The HMO, if the plan covers dialysis | After the allocation, PhilHealth pays no more sessions that year. |  |
| 11 | PhilHealth registration is pending. Can you bill PhilHealth’s share to the HMO to save time? | Not unless the contract allows it; ask the claims lead | The HMO will deduct a share that belongs to PhilHealth. |  |
| 12 | What did the October 1, 2026 PhilHealth memorandum with HMOs and insurers establish? | PhilHealth as the first payer for primary care under YAKAP, with HMOs paying beyond its limits | It covers primary care; dialysis units already follow the same order. |  |
| 13 | The HMO has not approved coverage yet and the patient is due on the chair. What happens? | Treatment goes ahead under unit policy while coverage is worked out | Coverage never delays treatment. |  |
| 14 | What did the cohort studies on missed hemodialysis sessions show? | An association between missed sessions and more hospitalization and death | Observational studies show association, not proof of cause. |  |
| 15 | A statement line has two payers listed. What does that mean? | The statement is not ready; each line needs one payer | One line, one payer. |  |

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which three checks make up HMO verification? | Active membership, plan coverage for the service, and your unit’s accreditation | Each answer needs its own reference. |  |

| 4 | PhilHealth package 6,350, hemodiafiltration difference 1,500 (covered and approved), uncovered blanket 250. What is the split? | 6,350 PhilHealth, 1,500 HMO, 250 patient | Each line has one payer. |  |

| 6 | What should a transmittal end with? | A control total: the number of claims and the batch amount | Control totals let both sides check the batch. |  |
| 7 | Why keep proof of receipt for each batch? | It proves timely filing and starts the aging clock | No receipt, no start point. |  |
| 8 | You are not sure a batch reached the HMO. What do you do first? | Ask the HMO for its status before any resend | Duplicates are slow to unwind. |  |

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A deposit is smaller than the approved amount by exactly the tax on the certificate. What is the difference? | Tax withheld on the unit’s behalf, not a short payment | Keep approved, withheld, and paid in separate columns. |  |

| 3 | Billed 260,000 pesos, approved 212,000. What is the disallowance? | 48,000 pesos | Only the gap between billed and approved. |  |
| 4 | A disallowance says “LOA expired,” and your file shows a valid LOA for that date. What do you do? | Appeal in writing with the valid LOA, within the contract window | Evidence plus the clause, on time. |  |
| 5 | A disallowance came from the unit’s own split error. Who pays the excess? | Not the patient by default; correct the source and follow unit policy | Unit errors are not moved onto patients. |  |
| 6 | From what point do you age an unpaid HMO claim? | The proof of receipt of the batch | Proof of receipt starts the clock. |  |
| 7 | A claim is 35 days old. When is it late? | When it is past that HMO’s own contract term | Compare each HMO with its own term. |  |
| 8 | What does a written collection ladder add? | Dated, recorded steps that management and the Insurance Commission can follow | A follow-up nobody wrote down did not happen. |  |
| 9 | Under Circular Letter 2018-14, where is a complaint against an HMO that belongs to an industry association first sent? | To that association’s grievance machinery for mediation | Mediation must conclude within 30 days of endorsement. |  |
| 10 | How long does the association have to conclude mediation of an endorsed complaint? | 30 days from receipt of the endorsement | Failed cases go to the Commission’s mediation division. |  |
| 11 | Who decides whether to file a complaint or suspend an HMO accreditation? | Management, following the agreement’s notice clause | The desk prepares the file and the facts. |  |
| 12 | Which is a warning sign of payer risk? | Lengthening time to pay and more partial payments | Watch the pattern, not only the balance. |  |
| 13 | The unit suspends an HMO. What happens to sessions for patients carrying that card? | They continue; patients are told in advance and routed to social service if costs change | A debt is never settled at the chair. |  |

| 15 | What did the Insurance Commission’s 2024 liquidity relief require of HMOs below the full requirement? | A monthly schedule of claims payable and proof of payment of valid claims on request | A sign of sector strain worth watching payer by payer. |  |

# Dialysis Unit Operations Manager

## Module 1: Who Runs the Dialysis Unit

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Who assigns nurses to patients for a shift? | The authorized nursing lead | Nursing assignment requires delegated nursing authority. The manager supports it with the roster but does not make it unless also appointed to a nursing role. |  |
| 2 | A physician phones you, the manager, with a change in a patient's dialysate potassium. What do you do? | Transfer the call to the nurse or POD who can receive and document the order | Orders go to a licensed clinician who can read back, document and execute them. A manager relaying orders adds an error-prone step. |  |
| 3 | Which power does a well-written policy usually give the operations manager? | Authority to place a safety hold, with release reserved for technical and clinical owners | Stopping is reversible and low-risk. Releasing requires expertise, so it stays with the designated technical and clinical authorities. |  |
| 4 | What closes an escalation? | A named person accepts it and records the next action and time | Closure needs receipt and ownership. Without them, the issue is still open, however many people know about it. |  |
| 5 | In the I-PASS study, what happened to preventable adverse events after a structured handoff program? | They fell by about 30% | Preventable adverse events fell from 4.7 to 3.3 per 100 admissions, and handoff duration did not change. |  |
| 6 | One person is both head nurse and unit manager. What protects the unit? | A written appointment covering both roles and stating which role applies to each decision | Dual roles are legitimate when written. The appointment defines scope and prevents disputes later. |  |
| 7 | Under DOH AO 2012-0001, which role leads QAPI, infection surveillance and water safety oversight? | The Medical Director | The order places technical and medical oversight, including QAPI, infection surveillance and water safety, with the Medical Director. |  |
| 8 | The owner tells you to seat all booked patients even though one nurse is absent. The best first step is to: | Ask the head nurse how many stations can be safely staffed now | Coverage decides capacity. The nursing lead determines what is safe, and you build the opening plan around her answer. |  |
| 9 | Which item belongs on a decision-rights map? | Owner, backup, escalation trigger and deadline for each decision | A decision map works only if it names who decides, who covers, when to escalate and by when. |  |
| 10 | RA 9173 §29 is relevant to a unit manager because it: | Sets minimum qualifications for supervisory nursing positions, if the role is one | HR must determine whether the specific position falls under §29 and document the decision. |  |
| 11 | A patient's relative asks you for a copy of the treatment record. You should: | Route the request through the facility's data privacy process | RA 10173 treats health data as sensitive personal information. Release follows the authorized process. |  |
| 12 | What makes an opening huddle closed-loop? | The receiver repeats the action, the owner and the check time | Read-back confirms the message was received as intended. |  |
| 13 | Which statement about governance evidence is most accurate? | Comparable regulators separate governing body, medical director and nurse manager roles, but outcome trials of these structures are lacking | These are policy designs, not trial results. We use them as informed models. |  |
| 14 | Who is responsible for releasing a machine back to service after repair? | The designated biomedical technician, according to the approved procedure | Technical release requires a trained person following a documented checklist. |  |
| 15 | The primary POD is unreachable 20 minutes before opening. What is the correct sequence? | Call the listed backup, record times, hold stations without coverage and notify the Medical Director | A coverage list exists for this moment. You document, hold what is not covered and escalate. |  |

## Module 2: Licensure, Accreditation, and Survey Readiness

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which body issues the license to operate a hemodialysis facility? | DOH through the Center for Health Development | The LTO is a DOH permission. PhilHealth and PSN carry separate processes. |  |
| 2 | What does PhilHealth accreditation primarily allow? | Filing claims for covered benefit packages | Accreditation concerns payment. Operation requires the LTO. |  |
| 3 | The unit installs three new machines in an unapproved room and starts using them. The main problem is: | Operating beyond the approved scope of the LTO | Station count and location form part of the approved scope. Expansion needs prior approval. |  |
| 4 | What is the most useful single checklist for preparing a DOH inspection? | The current DOH assessment tool for your facility type | The assessment tool is the inspector's own form. |  |
| 5 | In a tracer, what does the surveyor follow? | One patient or one item through every step of care | Tracers expose handoff gaps between people and departments. |  |
| 6 | A water log lacks a signature from last month. What is the correct fix? | Add a dated late entry with explanation and open a CAPA | Late entries with the current date are honest. Back-dating is falsification. |  |
| 7 | Which part of a CAPA proves the system fix worked? | The effectiveness check with a target, owner and due date | Effectiveness checks show the problem did not recur. |  |
| 8 | When must PDD registration be completed for outpatient package claims? | Before the sessions are claimed, following PhilHealth rules | Registration establishes eligibility for the package. |  |
| 9 | In the CDC collaborative, what was associated with lower bloodstream infections? | A bundle that included routine audits with feedback | Scheduled audits and feedback were core elements of the bundle. |  |
| 10 | An evidence index row should include: | Requirement, source, evidence, location, owner and expiry | Each field answers a question an inspector will ask. |  |
| 11 | An amber row in the evidence index means: | Due within 60 days or incomplete | Amber flags work that must happen soon. Red means expired or missing. |  |
| 12 | Who reviews the Dialysis Clinical Head appointment as part of professional attestation? | PSN | PSN's attestation process reviews the appointment and related documents. |  |
| 13 | During a tracer, a nurse says, "I just know the dialyzer was tested." This is: | A finding, because the evidence is not documented | If it is not written, it cannot be verified. |  |
| 14 | What is the root cause in this finding: "Afternoon logs unsigned because the reviewer works only mornings"? | No reviewer was assigned to afternoon logs | Root causes describe the system gap, not individual blame. |  |
| 15 | Which statement about readiness is most accurate? | Readiness is a daily filing discipline, not a pre-inspection project | Units that keep evidence current handle unannounced visits calmly. |  |

## Module 3: Staffing, Rostering, and Competency

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The DOH nurse-to-station figure of 1:4 is best understood as: | A ceiling that must be tightened for acuity, isolation and breaks | The figure sets the minimum cover. Real conditions often require more. |  |
| 2 | Fifteen stations are in use. How many POD positions does the 1:15 ceiling require at minimum? | One | ceiling(15 ÷ 15) = 1. A POD must be present during operating hours. |  |
| 3 | What does a relief factor account for? | Leave, holidays, training and sick time that reduce productive hours | Relief converts positions into the number of people needed to fill them reliably. |  |
| 4 | Non-productive time is 20%. What is the relief factor? | 1.25 | 1 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = 1.25. |  |
| 5 | In the 2024 US cohort study, the highest quartile of patient-to-technician ratio was associated with: | About 7% higher mortality and 5% higher hospitalization | incidence rate ratio (IRR) 1.07 for mortality and 1.05 for hospitalization, observational data. |  |
| 6 | Why can't the staffing study prove that adding staff improves survival? | It is observational, so other facility differences may explain the association | Association is not causation. Confounding cannot be fully excluded. |  |
| 7 | A new nurse's cannulation competency is marked "supervised only." On the roster you must: | Assign a named qualified supervisor on the same shift | Restrictions must be visible and supervised. |  |
| 8 | Who approves a reallocated nursing roster? | The nursing lead | Nursing assignment requires nursing authority. |  |
| 9 | Which patients need your strongest available staff after an absence? | Isolation patients and new starts | These groups carry the highest procedural and clinical risk. |  |
| 10 | A tired nurse offers to work a second shift. The best decision is usually to: | Decline and reduce stations or reschedule safely | Fatigue impairs performance in ways the person may not notice. |  |
| 11 | Under Labor Code Art. 83, health personnel in large cities or large facilities normally work: | 40 hours a week | HR must confirm which workers and facilities are covered. |  |
| 12 | A meta-analysis of 85 studies associated nurse burnout with: | More infections, falls and medication errors, and lower patient satisfaction | Burnout is consistently associated with worse safety and quality. |  |
| 13 | Fourteen non-isolation stations at 1:4 need how many nurse positions? | Four | ceiling(14 ÷ 4) = 4. |  |
| 14 | When a competency counts on the matrix, it must be: | Signed and dated by a qualified assessor | Observed and signed skills are the proof. |  |
| 15 | If the ratio cannot be met even after calling replacements, you should: | Reduce stations for that shift and reschedule within the treatment window | Capacity follows safe staffing, never the other way around. |  |

| 13 | High-value inventory such as ESAs should be counted: | At least monthly, more often after a variance | Frequent counts detect problems early. |  |
| 14 | A variance report explains: | Material differences between actual and budget | Explanations drive corrective action. |  |
| 15 | Following a session forward through the ledger allows you to: | Prove every delivered session became a claim, cash or a documented denial | Reconciliation closes the loop from care to cash. |  |

## Module 19: Integrated Readiness and Improvement Capstone

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A typhoon is forecast in 72 hours. Who decides on early dialysis? | The Medical Director and clinical team | Early dialysis is a clinical decision supported by operations. |  |
| 2 | A loop culture is 70 CFU/mL with action level 50 and maximum 100. The correct response is: | Action-level response: disinfect, retest and inform the Medical Director | Action levels exist to prevent reaching the maximum. |  |
| 3 | The owner proposes closing two days before the storm. The best reply is: | Propose schedule compression with staffing and cost implications | Closure creates dangerous gaps; compression protects patients. |  |
| 4 | Which calculator tells you whether water or fuel limits operations during an outage? | CALC-12 | Outage autonomy compares generator runtime and water storage. |  |
| 5 | A patient has used 152 of 156 sessions in late November. The right action is to: | Use CALC-07, counsel the patient early and inform the attending | Financial limits must not silently change treatment. |  |
| 6 | Which is a safety-critical failure that stops the capstone? | Bypassing water release | Clearance bypass is a stop item. |  |
| 7 | Two nurses resign effective Friday. The first quantitative step is: | Run CALC-01 for the revised schedule | Numbers define the gap and the options. |  |
| 8 | Returned claims during a crisis week should be: | Assigned with a correction deadline after immediate safety work | Prioritize safety, but do not lose the revenue. |  |
| 9 | Holiday and overtime pay for extra shifts should be computed with: | CALC-10 | Premium pay rules depend on day type and hours. |  |
| 10 | What makes a decision log useful afterward? | Times, decisions, owners and outcomes recorded as they happen | Contemporaneous records support review and accountability. |  |
| 11 | Which patients are on the high-risk list before a storm? | Long-gap, high potassium, catheter-dependent and new-start patients | Prioritize by physiologic risk. |  |
| 12 | Portfolio artifacts must use: | Fictional or de-identified data | Privacy rules apply to training materials. |  |
| 13 | A float nurse without signed dialysis competencies is offered. You should: | Use her only for tasks within her competencies | Competency limits hold in emergencies too. |  |
| 14 | After the storm, treatment resumes only when: | Power, water quality and staffing are confirmed and released | Phased reopening follows release. |  |
| 15 | The central skill the capstone tests is: | Prioritizing by patient risk and routing each decision to its authorized owner with evidence | Integration, routing and evidence define effective management. |  |

# Attending Nephrologist

## Module 1: Taking attending responsibility

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What should be settled before the first shift? | Written primary, backup and transfer arrangements | An order set cannot assign responsibility when a clinician is unavailable or a patient needs transfer. |  |
| 2 | Which document defines whether the facility may operate an HD service? | The facility’s applicable DOH License to Operate | A facility license, physician credentials and payer accreditation are separate authorities. |  |
| 3 | Under the PSN 2024 HD guidelines, how often should the AN review a maintenance HD patient? | At least monthly, preferably face to face, with telemedicine when necessary | Section 1.2 sets a minimum monthly consultation. A documented review supports continuity and the claim you sign. |  |
| 4 | A clinic’s night POD cannot reach you during an emergency. What design element was missing? | A time-limited escalation rule to a named backup and an emergency transfer pathway | Escalation must not depend on one person answering. A time trigger turns an unanswered call into an action. |  |
| 5 | One physician serves as both the AN and the unit’s Medical Director. What should the record show? | Which role is acting for each decision | Patient care and facility oversight carry different duties; naming the acting role keeps accountability clear. |  |

## Module 2: The renal consultation and diagnostic dataset

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which finding most strengthens a glomerular explanation? | Dysmorphic erythrocytes and red-cell casts | Sediment morphology places the injury at the glomerular capillary wall in a way creatinine cannot. |  |
| 2 | Which data clarify whether a creatinine change is acute? | A dated baseline and a serial trajectory | Change over time classifies acuity and gauges progression. Ask for the results the patient keeps at home. |  |
| 3 | Why does a single creatinine underestimate injury early in AKI? | Creatinine takes 24–72 hours to reach a new steady state after GFR falls | Production continues while filtration falls, so the serum level rises gradually toward the new equilibrium. |  |
| 4 | In which patient is cystatin C most useful for estimating GFR? | A bilateral above-knee amputee with low muscle mass | Cystatin C depends less on muscle mass, so it corrects the overestimate of GFR from creatinine when muscle is low. KDIGO 2024 recommends the combined estimate when the creatinine estimate is less accurate and GFR affects a decision (1C). |  |
| 5 | Muddy-brown granular casts most strongly suggest: | Acute tubular injury | Sloughed tubular epithelial cells form granular casts; prerenal states typically show a bland sediment. |  |

## Module 3: Consultant communication and coverage

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which detail closes the communication loop? | Read-back by the person assigned to act | Read-back by the person who will act confirms who acts and on what instruction. A “seen” mark only shows the message was opened. |  |
| 2 | What should a POD communicate during an HD emergency? | Vital trends, timing, circuit and access findings, interventions and response | The attending needs trend and action data to advise what happens next. |  |
| 3 | An attending at home says ‘monitor closely.’ What is missing? | A specific action, owner, reassessment time and fallback | A vague instruction passes on worry, not responsibility. |  |
| 4 | What does the Data Privacy Act require when you share data for a transfer? | Sending only the clinical data the receiver needs, via an approved channel | Share what the purpose needs, through channels the institution controls. |  |
| 5 | A patient with presyncope insists on leaving. What must happen before discharge against advice? | A documented assessment of decision-making capacity for that decision | Capacity is decision-specific; if present, an informed refusal is documented with a safety plan. |  |

## Module 4: Consent, prescribing and medication reconciliation

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which medication instruction supports safe follow-up? | A defined review date, trigger and owner | KDIGO 2024 asks for a clear restart plan whenever medicines are stopped during an acute illness (practice point). |  |
| 2 | How should the physician check consent comprehension? | Ask the patient to explain the options and agreed plan in their own words | Teach-back reveals misunderstandings while there is time to address them. |  |
| 3 | Two weeks after starting an SGLT2 inhibitor, creatinine rises 18% with stable potassium. Best action? | Continue and recheck; this is the expected hemodynamic effect | Lower intraglomerular pressure produces an early, reversible eGFR dip. KDIGO 2024 states it is generally not a reason to stop (practice point). |  |
| 4 | Which drug property most predicts substantial removal by high-flux hemodialysis (HD)? | Low protein binding with a small volume of distribution | Unbound drug in plasma water crosses the membrane; drug held in tissue is not reached. |  |
| 5 | Under the KDIGO 2022 diabetes guideline, metformin should be stopped when eGFR falls below: | 30 mL/min/1.73 m² | The guideline recommends metformin at eGFR 30 or more (1B), halves the dose at 30 to 44, and stops it below 30. |  |

## Module 5: Acute kidney injury and post-AKI care

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What should determine the next step after initial stabilization? | Serial perfusion, urine output, chemistry and complications | The trend in physiology and complications sets the urgency while the cause is worked up. |  |
| 2 | What belongs in the post-AKI discharge plan? | Residual dysfunction, medication changes and named lab follow-up | The next clinician needs a defined action, a time frame and a name. KDIGO advises review at about 3 months. |  |
| 3 | Which electrolyte pattern is characteristic of early leptospirosis-associated AKI? | Non-oliguric AKI with hypokalemia from tubular potassium wasting | Leptospiral injury to the proximal tubule and thick ascending limb wastes sodium and potassium. |  |
| 4 | What did BICARICU-2 show in severe metabolic acidemia with moderate to severe AKI? | No difference in 90-day mortality; less frequent KRT in the bicarbonate group as a secondary finding | The primary outcome was neutral (62.1% vs 61.7%). The KRT finding was one of 18 secondary outcomes. |  |
| 5 | Why does venous congestion worsen AKI? | It lowers the transrenal perfusion gradient and raises pressure inside the encapsulated kidney | Perfusion depends on arterial minus venous pressure; a tense, encapsulated kidney compounds the drop. |  |

## Module 6: Potassium, sodium and acid-base emergencies

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which disposition is appropriate for potassium 7.1 mmol/L with a broad QRS in an HD patient? | Emergency monitored management and same-day dialysis | ECG toxicity signals immediate arrhythmia risk. The UKKA guideline recommends urgent dialysis for HD patients with potassium ≥6.5 mmol/L. |  |
| 2 | What must be anticipated when correcting chronic severe hyponatremia? | Overcorrection risk and a serial monitoring plan with a rescue strategy | Duration, risk factors and an evolving water diuresis determine safety. |  |
| 3 | Why is a 10% glucose infusion added after insulin-glucose when baseline glucose is below 7 mmol/L? | To prevent delayed hypoglycemia, which can occur hours after insulin | Insulin’s effect outlasts the 25 g glucose, especially in chronic kidney disease (CKD) with reduced insulin clearance. UKKA suggests 10% glucose at 50 mL/h for 5 hours (2B). |  |
| 4 | Which treatment actually removes potassium from the body? | Hemodialysis | Calcium protects the membrane, insulin and salbutamol shift potassium; only the gut, the kidney or dialysis remove it. |  |
| 5 | HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L with pCO₂ 38 mm Hg indicates: | Metabolic acidosis with a concomitant respiratory acidosis | Winter’s formula predicts pCO₂ of 26 ± 2; a value of 38 means ventilation is inadequate. |  |

## Module 7: Acute kidney replacement and ICU consultation

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What most strengthens the acute KRT indication? | Worsening refractory organ-threatening fluid overload | Indications depend on the complication and its response to treatment. |  |
| 2 | What belongs in the acute KRT order review? | An indication, a feasible modality, reassessment and stopping criteria | The prescription must address the indication and change with illness and recovery. |  |
| 3 | What did STARRT-AKI show? | No 90-day mortality benefit from accelerated initiation, with more dialysis dependence among survivors | Mortality was 43.9% versus 43.7%; dialysis dependence among survivors was 10.4% versus 6.0%. |  |
| 4 | Which patient most clearly favors CRRT over intermittent HD? | Traumatic brain injury with raised intracranial pressure | Gradual solute removal avoids rapid osmotic shifts that can worsen cerebral edema; KDIGO 2012 suggests CRRT here (2B). |  |
| 5 | Which sign during KRT most suggests renal recovery? | Rising spontaneous urine output with falling interdialytic creatinine | Returning native filtration shows up as urine and as creatinine that no longer climbs between sessions. |  |

## Module 8: CRRT delivery, special indications and stopping

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which measure best reveals a delivery gap? | Actual run time and delivered effluent dose | Interruptions can greatly reduce delivered treatment despite a correct order; KDIGO recommends frequent assessment of the delivered dose (1B). |  |
| 2 | Which team should review drug exposure after an unexpected CRRT interruption? | The treating team with pharmacy input | Delivered therapy affects drug clearance and can change exposure. |  |
| 3 | A 70-kg patient receives 2,100 mL/h effluent for 12 of 24 hours. What is the delivered dose? | About 15 mL/kg/h | 2,100 × 12 / 24 / 70 = 15 mL/kg/h, below the 20–25 mL/kg/h target. |  |
| 4 | During regional citrate anticoagulation, a total-to-ionized calcium ratio of 2.8 with worsening acidosis suggests: | Citrate accumulation from impaired metabolism | Unmetabolized citrate binds ionized calcium while total calcium rises, widening the ratio above 2.5. |  |
| 5 | What did the RENAL and ATN trials show about CRRT intensity? | Higher intensity did not improve survival compared with standard intensity | RENAL: 44.7% mortality in both arms. ATN: 53.6% versus 51.5%. Both support a delivered 20–25 mL/kg/h without escalation. |  |

## Module 9: CKD staging, progression and risk reduction

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which measure adds important prognostic information to eGFR? | Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio | Albuminuria carries prognostic information independent of eGFR and changes which treatments apply. |  |
| 2 | Which finding helps establish CKD chronicity? | Persistent abnormalities documented over more than 3 months | Serial results more than 3 months apart separate chronic disease from an acute change. Old results the patient brings often settle it. |  |
| 3 | How do SGLT2 inhibitors lower intraglomerular pressure? | By restoring macula densa sodium delivery, activating tubuloglomerular feedback and constricting the afferent arteriole | Feedback-mediated afferent constriction complements the efferent dilation from RAS blockade. |  |
| 4 | What did CONFIDENCE demonstrate? | Greater UACR reduction with combined finerenone and empagliflozin than either alone (a surrogate outcome) | The trial measured albuminuria change at 180 days. It does not show fewer dialysis starts or deaths. |  |
| 5 | In KDIGO 2024, a KFRE 2-year risk above 40% can be used to: | Time education about kidney replacement therapy options, with access and transplant planning | Practice Point 2.2.3 uses a 2-year risk above 40% to time modality education. It is a practice point, not a graded recommendation. |  |

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why review transferrin saturation with ferritin? | Inflammation can raise ferritin despite restricted iron availability | Ferritin rises as an acute-phase protein; TSAT shows how much iron is actually available to the marrow. |  |
| 2 | How should CKD-MBD labs guide reassessment? | Interpret calcium, phosphate and PTH trends together | Trends in related measures support one coordinated plan. |  |
| 3 | Per KDIGO 2026, what is first-line therapy for renal anemia once correctable causes are addressed? | An ESA, with HIF-PHIs as alternatives in selected situations | The guideline suggests an ESA rather than a HIF-PHI because long-term cardiovascular and thrombotic safety of HIF-PHIs is uncertain. |  |
| 4 | In which patient should a HIF-PHI be avoided? | A patient with active malignancy or a recent thrombotic event | KDIGO 2026 advises against HIF-PHI use with active malignancy or a recent cardiovascular or thrombotic event. |  |
| 5 | What did TREAT show when darbepoetin targeted a hemoglobin of about 13 g/dL? | No reduction in death or cardiovascular events, and about twice the stroke rate | Stroke occurred in 5.0% versus 2.6%, with no benefit on the primary outcomes; this is why ESAs are not used to normalize hemoglobin. |  |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2 | What makes kidney biopsy most useful? | A reasonable chance of changing management at an acceptable procedural risk | Clinical impact and safety guide biopsy selection. |  |
| 3 | What did PEXIVAS show? | Plasma exchange did not reduce death or kidney failure overall; reduced-dose steroids were noninferior with fewer infections | Death or kidney failure was 28.4% versus 31.0% (hazard ratio 0.86, not significant); reduced-dose glucocorticoids met noninferiority with fewer serious infections. |  |
| 4 | Which screening is essential before rituximab? | Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody | Rituximab can reactivate occult hepatitis B, sometimes fatally; core-antibody-positive patients need monitoring or prophylaxis. |  |
| 5 | Why are nephrotic patients prone to thrombosis? | Urinary loss of antithrombin with increased hepatic clotting-factor synthesis | The coagulation balance tips toward clotting as anticoagulant proteins leak and procoagulants rise. |  |

## Module 20: Conservative kidney management and serious illness

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which element makes a dialysis trial time limited? | Agreed outcomes and a review date | Explicit measures and timing support an honest review of benefit and burden. |  |
| 2 | What is part of comprehensive conservative care? | Active symptom treatment and planned follow-up | Conservative management remains an active clinical pathway; KDIGO 2024 supports it as an option (practice point). |  |
| 3 | The family asks the physician to decide privately before speaking to the patient. Best response? | Assess the patient’s capacity and involve him in the decision | A patient with capacity holds the decision; family support is welcome but not a substitute. |  |
| 4 | What does observational evidence suggest for very elderly patients with high comorbidity? | Dialysis may confer little survival advantage over conservative care | These are nonrandomized data with selection bias; they inform the conversation, they do not decide it. |  |
| 5 | Capacity assessment is best described as: | Decision-specific: understanding, retaining, weighing and communicating a choice | Capacity is assessed for the particular decision at the particular time. |  |

## Module 21: PhilHealth documentation and ethical claims

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What should the attending do first when records conflict? | Hold attestation and reconcile source records | A truthful attestation depends on a traceable reconciliation of delivered services. |  |
| 2 | Which records support verification of an actual dialysis session? | The treatment record and corresponding claim documentation | Claims attest to services delivered on verifiable dates. |  |
| 3 | How many HD sessions per year does PhilHealth cover under Circular 2023-0009? | Up to 156 | The circular expanded the benefit from 90 to 156 sessions, three a week for 52 weeks. Confirm the current rule on the date of service. |  |
| 4 | What is the correct way to fix a duplicated claim entry? | Correct it through the approved workflow with an audit trail | A traceable correction preserves integrity and protects staff. |  |
| 5 | Which principle governs sharing claims data? | Minimum necessary disclosure through approved channels under the Data Privacy Act | Proportional, secure processing protects patients and the facility. |  |

## Module 22: Disasters, outbreaks and service continuity

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What determines disposition during an outage? | Clinical urgency and confirmed receiving capability | Safe continuity depends on risk-based triage and a verified handoff. |  |
| 2 | When can the unit close an outage tracker entry? | When treatment has resumed or disposition and acceptance are confirmed | Confirmed disposition closes the continuity gap. |  |
| 3 | Which patient is at highest risk after missed sessions? | An anuric patient with prior hyperkalemia who missed two sessions | No urine output and a history of high potassium predict rapid, dangerous accumulation. |  |
| 4 | What does the Hurricane Katrina study of 386 New Orleans patients show? | Missing 3 or more sessions was associated with higher odds of hospitalization | The adjusted odds ratio was 2.16. The design was observational, so it shows association, not cause. |  |
| 5 | Why include serologies on the emergency card? | Receiving units need hepatitis B status to place patients safely | Hepatitis B segregation is an infection-prevention requirement in every unit. |  |

## Module 23: Supervision, evidence appraisal and quality improvement

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which comparison supports assessment of the apparent improvement? | Rates based on comparable catheter exposure | The exposure denominator accounts for a changing population at risk. |  |
| 2 | What is an example of a balancing measure in a catheter-reduction project? | Missed or delayed treatments associated with the change | Balancing measures detect new harms introduced by an improvement. |  |
| 3 | A trial shows event rates of 20% vs 15%. What is the NNT? | 20 | ARR = 5 percentage points; NNT = 1 / 0.05 = 20. |  |
| 4 | Why does the same relative risk reduction yield more benefit in high-risk patients? | Absolute risk reduction scales with baseline risk | A constant relative effect applied to a larger baseline risk removes more events. |  |
| 5 | Which feedback is most useful to a learner? | ‘Next time, read back the potassium order before ending the call’ | Specific, behavior-focused feedback gives a repeatable action. |  |

## Module 24: Integrated attending capstone

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which follow-through is required after the acute transfer? | Confirm receipt, reconcile the erroneous claim and reassign longitudinal follow-up | Continuity includes confirmed acceptance, documentation integrity and a named next clinician. |  |
| 2 | What outcome would make the capstone QI claim credible? | An explicitly defined measure compared with baseline at a planned review | A baseline, a denominator and a planned review make improvement observable. |  |
| 3 | After stabilization from catheter sepsis, what should happen to his home-therapy preference? | Reopen PD planning and refer for transplant evaluation | An urgent start does not cancel an informed modality choice. |  |
| 4 | Which is a critical action in the capstone claims task? | Stopping release of a knowingly inaccurate claim | Integrity takes precedence over deadlines. |  |
| 5 | A missed critical action at a station results in: | Feedback and repeat assessment with a different case | Critical actions are non-compensable. |  |

# Attending Pediatric Nephrologist

## Module 1: Taking attending responsibility for children

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A hospital tells you that your PNSP certification means you may perform any pediatric kidney procedure there. What actually grants that permission? | The hospital’s delineated privileges, granted through its credentials committee | Certification shows training; the facility grants privileges for specific procedures, modalities and patient sizes. PhilHealth accreditation and Academy completion are neither. |  |
| 2 | A PhilHealth pediatric PD annex lists a solution bag volume. How should it be used in a child’s PD order? | Not as an order at all; it is a supply item, and the order comes from the child and the unit protocol | Coverage is not a prescription. Bag volumes are supply units; the fill volume is set from the child’s size, tolerance and the unit’s pediatric protocol. |  |
| 3 | What is the status of the pediatric automated PD pilot after July 31, 2026, as of this module? | Unresolved; confirm with the PhilHealth liaison before advising a family | Advisory 2026-0013 extended the pilot to July 31, 2026. No later issuance was found, so the status is shown as unresolved. |  |
| 4 | A referral note says only “pedia nephro to follow.” What is the attending’s first task? | Write down who owns each decision and who is called, day and night | Ownership must be explicit. Until a written co-management note exists, the person facing the decision owns it. |  |
| 5 | A 13-year-old disagrees with a treatment her parents have accepted. What does the AAP describe as the right approach? | Engage her in an active process of assent, giving her view more weight as she matures, while parents give permission | Parental permission and the child’s assent are both part of an active process, with the adolescent’s voice carrying increasing weight. |  |

## Module 2: The growing kidney and the pediatric renal assessment

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A 12-year-old athlete taking creatine has a creatinine above the pediatric range. What is the best next step? | Repeat after rest and stopping supplements, with a cystatin C | Muscle mass, supplements and recent exercise raise creatinine without changing GFR. A cystatin C estimate is less dependent on muscle. |  |
| 2 | In which child is a creatinine-based eGFR most likely to be falsely high? | A 10-year-old with spastic cerebral palsy and low muscle mass | Low muscle mass means little creatinine is produced, so the estimate overstates GFR. KDIGO 2024 suggests a cystatin C-based equation in such children. |  |
| 3 | By AAP 2017, how is a blood pressure of 132/84 mm Hg classified in a 14-year-old? | Stage 1 hypertension | From age 13, AAP 2017 uses adult-style cut points: 130/80 to 139/89 mm Hg is stage 1 hypertension. |  |
| 4 | Which sample best quantifies proteinuria in a school-age child while excluding orthostatic protein? | A first-morning spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio | A first-morning UPCR avoids the protein that appears when a child is upright and active. IPNA defines nephrotic range as UPCR ≥200 mg/mmol (2 mg/mg). |  |
| 5 | What did the CKiD U25 equations change compared with the bedside Schwartz formula? | They use sex-specific and age-dependent constants across ages 1 to 25 | CKiD U25 uses K × height / creatinine with sex-specific or age- and sex-dependent K, and parallel cystatin C equations, developed in 928 participants aged 1 to 25. |  |

## Module 3: Fluids, sodium and acid-base in children

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why do hypotonic maintenance fluids cause hyponatremia in hospitalized children? | Illness switches on ADH, so the kidney retains the free water infused | Non-osmotic ADH release from vomiting, pain, volume depletion and lung or brain disease means infused free water is kept. |  |
| 2 | Which statement matches the AAP 2018 maintenance fluid guideline? | Isotonic solutions are recommended for ages 28 days to 18 years, with evidence quality A and a strong recommendation | The guideline excludes neonates under 28 days, renal dysfunction and other groups, where fluids must be individualized. |  |
| 3 | What did the PIMS trial show? | Hyponatremia in 4% with sodium 140 mmol/L versus 11% with sodium 77 mmol/L | PIMS, a double-blind RCT, found 12 of 319 versus 35 of 322 children developed hyponatremia; no cerebral edema occurred in either group. |  |
| 4 | A child is seizing with acute hyponatremia. What is the correct immediate principle? | Hypertonic saline per the unit protocol to raise sodium promptly, with frequent checks | Hyponatremic encephalopathy is an emergency; hypertonic saline reverses brain swelling. Restriction alone does not. |  |
| 5 | In which dengue phase is fluid overload most likely to appear? | The recovery phase, when leaked fluid returns to the circulation | WHO describes reabsorption of leaked fluid in recovery; children given generous fluid during the leak can become overloaded. |  |

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What does intravenous calcium do in hyperkalemia? | Stabilizes the cardiac membrane by restoring the firing threshold, without lowering potassium | Calcium protects the heart while shifting and removal take effect; it does not change the potassium concentration. |  |
| 2 | A well 5-day-old has a potassium of 7.2 mmol/L on a squeezed heel-prick sample and a normal ECG. What is the best next step? | Repeat by free-flowing venous sample while monitoring the infant | Pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis and tissue squeezing is common in small children. Treat the ECG and confirm the number. |  |
| 3 | Which set fulfills laboratory tumor lysis syndrome by Cairo–Bishop in a child? | Potassium 6.4 mmol/L and phosphate 2.5 mmol/L on day 2 of chemotherapy | Two or more of potassium ≥6.0, phosphate ≥2.1 (children), uric acid ≥476 µmol/L or calcium ≤1.75 mmol/L, within 3 days before to 7 days after therapy. |  |
| 4 | What did the pediatric randomized trial of rasburicase versus allopurinol show? | Faster and greater lowering of plasma uric acid, a surrogate outcome | In 52 high-risk children, uric acid fell 86% versus 12% four hours after the first dose. The trial was not powered for dialysis or death. |  |
| 5 | A child on amphotericin B has hypokalemia that does not correct despite repeated potassium. What should you check? | Serum magnesium | Hypomagnesemia causes refractory hypokalemia and hypocalcemia; amphotericin B and aminoglycosides are common culprits. |  |

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A 15-year-old has repeated office readings of 134/82 mm Hg, confirmed by auscultation. How does AAP 2017 classify this? | Stage 1 hypertension | From age 13, AAP 2017 uses adult-style cut points: 130/80 to 139/89 mm Hg is stage 1. |  |
| 2 | How fast should acute severe hypertension with encephalopathy be lowered, according to AAP 2017? | By no more than 25% of the planned reduction over the first 8 hours | Expert opinion (grade D, weak): a shifted autoregulatory range makes fast falls dangerous. |  |
| 3 | What did ESCAPE show? | Intensified control to a 24-hour MAP below the 50th percentile reduced the 5-year primary end point from 41.7% to 29.9% | HR 0.65; about 12 fewer children per 100 reached a 50% GFR fall or kidney failure over 5 years. Withdrawals did not differ. |  |
| 4 | Which child most needs an extensive search for a secondary cause of hypertension? | A 4-year-old with stage 2 hypertension and an asymmetric kidney on ultrasound | Renal and renovascular causes are more common in younger children; stage 2 pressure with abnormal kidneys needs a full workup. |  |
| 5 | KDIGO 2021 suggests which blood pressure target for children with CKD? | 24-hour MAP by ABPM at or below the 50th percentile for age, sex and height (2C) | Recommendation 5.1 (2C), based largely on ESCAPE. When ABPM is unavailable, office targets are ungraded practice points. |  |

A boy with a distended bladder still needs action now. |  |

| 5 | A 6-month-old with valves and a low nadir creatinine is polyuric and falling across weight percentiles. ## Module 7: Urinary tract infection, reflux and bladder-bowel dysfunction

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A 10-month-old with fever has a bag urine culture growing E. coli and Enterococcus. The AAP definition requires pyuria and at least 50,000 colonies per mL of a single uropathogen in an appropriately collected specimen. |  |
| 2 | What did RIVUR show about renal scarring? | Scarring did not differ significantly: 11.9% with prophylaxis vs 10.2% with placebo | Prophylaxis halved recurrences (39/302 vs 72/305) but did not change scarring, and resistance to TMP-SMX rose (63% vs 19%). |  |
| 3 | In PREDICT, what was the number needed to treat for 2 years to prevent one first UTI in infants with grade III to V reflux? | 7 | First UTI 21.2% vs 35.6%; NNT 7 (95% CI 4 to 29). New scars and eGFR did not differ substantially, and resistant and non-E. coli organisms were more common with prophylaxis. |  |
| 4 | After a first febrile UTI in an 8-month-old, which imaging does the AAP 2011 guideline advise routinely? | Renal and bladder ultrasound; VCUG only if it is abnormal, the course is atypical, or the UTI recurs | VCUG is not recommended routinely after the first febrile UTI. Ultrasound findings, an atypical course or recurrence trigger it. |  |
| 5 | A 6-year-old girl has a fourth cystitis, a normal ultrasound, voids twice a day and has hard stools. What comes first? | Treat constipation and start timed voiding | Bladder and bowel dysfunction drives recurrence. In the RIVUR/CUTIE cohort, BBD carried an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.07 for recurrence. |  |

|---|---|---|---|---|

Gitelman (distal convoluted tubule) typically brings low magnesium and low urine calcium. |  |

What does that point to? | Extrarenal chloride loss, such as vomiting or sweat loss in cystic fibrosis | When chloride is lost outside the kidney, the kidney conserves it. | 3 | What did ILLUMINATE-A demonstrate for lumasiran in primary hyperoxaluria type 1? | A large fall in urinary oxalate over 6 months, a surrogate outcome | Urinary oxalate fell by 53.5 percentage points more than placebo. The trial was small (39 patients) and short, and it did not test kidney failure or stones. |  |
| 4 | What is the strength of evidence for early ACE inhibition in Alport syndrome? | A registry showing later dialysis with earlier treatment, and a small randomized trial with a non-significant hazard ratio of 0.51 and no safety signal | The direction is consistent but the precision is weak: observational registry data plus an underpowered randomized trial. |  |
| 5 | A genetic panel reports one pathogenic variant and one variant of uncertain significance in a recessive tubulopathy gene. What is the best response? | Treat by phenotype, consider parental segregation testing, and plan to re-query the laboratory | Under ACMG/AMP classification only pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants support a diagnosis. A VUS can be reclassified either way. |  |

## Module 9: Steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A nephrotic 4-year-old has tachycardia, capillary refill of 4 seconds, abdominal pain and a FENa of 0.1%. Furosemide is ordered. What do you advise? | Hold the diuretic; give albumin per protocol with monitoring and exclude peritonitis | These are signs of hypovolemia. The IPNA recommends withholding diuretics in hypovolemia (grade X, strong) and using albumin; FENa below 0.2% suggested volume contraction in a small prospective study. |  |
| 2 | By the IPNA 2022 definitions, which course is frequently relapsing? | Two relapses in the first 6 months after remission of the first episode | FRNS is ≥2 relapses in the first 6 months after remission, or ≥3 in any 12 months. Two consecutive relapses on therapy or within 14 days of stopping define steroid dependence. |  |
| 3 | What did PREDNOS show? | 16 weeks did not lengthen time to first relapse compared with 8 weeks (hazard ratio 0.87) | FRNS (50% vs 53%), SDNS (44% vs 42%) and need for other immunosuppression did not differ. KDIGO 2025 recommends 8 or 12 weeks (1B). |  |
| 4 | Which feature in a child with a first episode of nephrotic syndrome calls for kidney biopsy according to the IPNA? | Macroscopic hematuria or a low C3 | Atypical features (macroscopic hematuria, low C3, AKI not from hypovolemia, sustained hypertension, arthritis or rash) call for biopsy (grade A, strong). Typical disease over age 1 does not. |  |
| 5 | A nephrotic child on high-dose glucocorticoids is due for school vaccinations. What is correct? | Give inactivated vaccines on schedule; avoid live vaccines during high-dose immunosuppression; vaccinate the household | The IPNA reports a low risk of vaccine-induced relapse, recommends avoiding live vaccines during high-dose immunosuppression (grade X), and recommends vaccinating the household (grade A). |  |

## Module 10: Frequent relapses, steroid dependence and steroid resistance

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A child relapses twice in a row, once during the taper and once 9 days after stopping glucocorticoids, and always remits. How is the course classified? | Steroid dependent | Two consecutive relapses during therapy or within 14 days of stopping define steroid dependence (IPNA 2022). Remission each time excludes resistance. |  |
| 2 | What did the randomized levamisole trial show in frequently relapsing children? | Hazard ratio for relapse 0.22; 26% vs 6% still in remission at 12 months | Levamisole lengthened remissions; most children still relapsed within the year. Neutropenia occurred in 4 of 50 and reversed. |  |
| 3 | What proportion of children with SRNS have a monogenic cause, according to the IPNA 2020 recommendations? | 10% to 30% | With exome sequencing, 10% to 30% are diagnosed with a monogenic disease, more often with early onset, family history or extrarenal features. |  |
| 4 | A child with confirmed SRNS has two pathogenic NPHS2 variants. What does the IPNA recommend? | Withhold calcineurin inhibitors and stop glucocorticoids; continue supportive care | Monogenic SRNS rarely responds to immunosuppression (grade B, moderate recommendation to withhold CNI and stop glucocorticoids). |  |
| 5 | In the Indian trial of tacrolimus versus intravenous cyclophosphamide for SRNS, what was the complete remission rate? | 52.4% vs 14.8% | Tacrolimus was superior; three children needed tacrolimus for one additional remission, and cyclophosphamide had more withdrawals for infection. |  |

| 3 | What did the ppCRRT anticoagulation analysis show? | Heparin and citrate circuits lasted similarly; circuits without anticoagulation clotted more; life-threatening bleeding occurred only with heparin | Mean circuit life was 42.1 hours with heparin and 44.7 with citrate, against 27.2 with none. The data are observational. |  |
| 4 | Which sign suggests citrate accumulation during CKRT? | Rising total calcium with falling ionized calcium and worsening acidosis | When the liver cannot metabolize citrate, citrate-bound calcium accumulates, ionized calcium falls and acidosis worsens. |  |
| 5 | What did the Kwiatkowski 2017 trial of PD versus furosemide in infants after cardiac surgery show? | No difference in the primary outcome; furosemide was associated with more 10% fluid overload, longer ventilation and inotrope use | The primary outcome (negative balance on day 1) was neutral; secondary outcomes favored PD. PD stopped early in 9 of 41 for pleural–peritoneal communication. |  |

## Module 17: Pediatric CKD: progression, growth, nutrition and development

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What did ESCAPE show? | Intensified blood pressure control (24-h MAP below the 50th percentile) reduced the primary end point from 41.7% to 29.9% over 5 years | Hazard ratio 0.65; the end point was a 50% GFR decline or kidney failure, a partly surrogate composite. |  |
| 2 | According to the KDIGO 2024 pediatric summary, what is the advice on protein intake in children with CKD? | Do not restrict protein; aim at the upper end of the normal range for healthy children | Protein restriction risks growth impairment in children. |  |

| 4 | A short child with CKD stage 4 has acidosis, a protein-restricted diet and salt wasting. What comes first? | Correct nutrition, salt and water, acidosis, mineral and bone disease and anemia, then reassess growth velocity | Growth hormone is considered for persistent growth failure after correctable causes are addressed. |  |
| 5 | What did the CKiD neurocognitive study find? | Average scores overall, but 21–40% scored at least 1 SD below the mean in at least one domain | It was cross-sectional; it supports screening school performance, not a causal claim. |  |

What does the KDIGO 2026 pediatric algorithm indicate first? | Iron therapy, after which other causes are sought and ESA is reconsidered | Ferritin below 100 ng/mL with TSAT below 40% meets the algorithm’s indication for iron. |  |

| 5 | What does the CKiD analysis of bicarbonate and growth show? | An observational association between low bicarbonate and lower height z scores in nonglomerular CKD | The authors call for trials; persistent alkali use was associated with better height z scores. |  |

## Module 19: Choosing kidney replacement therapy with families

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which kidney replacement therapy do European pediatric experts recommend as preferred for infants? | Peritoneal dialysis | PD is preferred in infants (1B): it preserves residual function and veins and runs at home. Most centers postpone transplantation until 8–10 kg. |  |
| 2 | In the ERA Registry, which first transplant was associated with lower mortality and graft failure in childhood-onset KRT? | A preemptive transplant, and separately a living-donor transplant | Preemptive (adjusted hazard ratios 0.66 for death, 0.89 for graft failure) and living-donor transplants were associated with better outcomes; the data are observational. |  |
| 3 | When should withholding KRT in an infant be considered, according to the infant recommendations? | Through consensus decision-making in the child’s best interest, weighing prognosis, comorbidities, resources and quality of life, with the family involved | The recommendations grade consensus decision-making for starting or withholding KRT 1B and advise deciding early. |  |
| 4 | What did the IPPN registry show about mortality on pediatric PD? | About 5% at 3 years, varying by region, with country income explaining about half the variation | Probability of death at 3 years was 5% (2% to 9% by region); income explained 50.1% of between-region variance. |  |
| 5 | A family asks how many HD sessions PhilHealth gives. What is the best approach? | State the clinical recommendation first, then explain that up to 156 sessions a year are covered and that coverage does not set the prescription | Coverage is not a prescription; confirm the benefit on the date of service. |  |

## Module 20: Pediatric PD: access, membrane and prescription

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why are pediatric PD fill volumes scaled to body surface area rather than body weight? | Because the peritoneal surface area relates to BSA, so per-kilogram fills underfill the membrane in small children | Fills prescribed per kilogram are small relative to the membrane in young children, giving fast equilibration and early loss of ultrafiltration. Scaling to BSA removes most of the apparent age difference. |  |
| 2 | A 10-month-old on PD started the day after catheter insertion has glucose-positive fluid at the exit site. What is the best first step? | Reduce or stop fills as the protocol allows, keep the child flat, and review with the surgeon | This is a pericatheter leak. Lowering intraperitoneal pressure and resting the catheter give it the best chance to seal. |  |
| 3 | A 3-year-old on rapid nightly cycling has a high Kt/V, a high phosphate and falling height centiles. What is the most likely explanation? | Short dwells clear urea well but phosphate poorly | Phosphate needs three to four times longer than urea to equilibrate. A long dwell and a dietitian review address the problem the Kt/V hides. |  |
| 4 | Which statement about evidence for pediatric PD catheters is correct? | In the IPPN registry, 60% of revisions were for mechanical malfunction, and a double-cuff catheter with a downward or lateral exit is a 2D suggestion | Pediatric catheter guidance is weak (2D) and largely registry-based; omentectomy is recommended for infants without proven preventive value. |  |
| 5 | A family asks whether the PhilHealth PD package decides how many exchanges their child will do. What is the correct answer? | No; the attending prescribes what the child needs, documents it truthfully, and confirms coverage on the date of service | Coverage is not a prescription. The pediatric APD pilot status after July 31, 2026 is unresolved and must be confirmed with the PhilHealth liaison. |  |

| 1 | What does the evidence on caregiver training for pediatric PD show? | Shorter training was associated with more peritonitis in an IPPN survey, but SCOPE found no association with four training components | The evidence is observational and conflicting; the 2024 pediatric guideline makes weak (2D) suggestions to tailor training and to include a home visit. |  |
| 2 | A child on APD has slow outflow, good inflow and no stool for four days. What is the first step? | Treat constipation and recheck drains | Constipation is the commonest reversible cause of outflow failure; it displaces and compresses the catheter. |  |
| 3 | Which pattern should raise concern for encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis? | New ultrafiltration failure in a child with years on PD and repeated peritonitis | In the European pediatric survey, EPS children had longer PD vintage and most developed ultrafiltration failure a median 2.8 months before obstruction. |  |
| 4 | A child on PD becomes breathless with a right pleural effusion and falling drains. What is the most likely diagnosis? | Hydrothorax from dialysate passing through the diaphragm | Stop PD, image the chest, compare pleural fluid glucose with blood and involve the surgeon. |  |
| 5 | A family asks whether PhilHealth pediatric APD coverage continues after July 31, 2026. What is the correct answer? | Its status after that date is unresolved; confirm with the PhilHealth liaison | Advisory 2026-0013 extended the pilot to July 31, 2026. Never say it ended or continues without a later issuance. |  |

## Module 22: PD peritonitis and exit-site and tunnel infection

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which combination meets the 2024 pediatric criteria for PD peritonitis? | Cloudy effluent with abdominal pain, plus effluent white cells over 100/mm³ with at least 50% neutrophils after a 2-hour dwell | Two of three criteria are needed: clinical features, the effluent cell count and differential after an adequate dwell, and a positive culture. |  |
| 2 | A child on CAPD has cloudy effluent at night. When should empirical antibiotics start? | As soon as effluent specimens are taken | The pediatric guideline states antibiotics should begin as soon as possible after appropriate microbiological specimens are obtained. |  |
| 3 | Fungal elements are seen in the effluent of a child on PD. What does the 2024 pediatric guideline suggest? | Immediate catheter removal and antifungal therapy for at least 2 weeks after removal | Fungal peritonitis threatens the membrane; removal is suggested at once (2D). |  |
| 4 | A program has 6 peritonitis episodes in 14 patient-years. Which statement is correct? | The rate is about 0.43 per patient-year, above the 0.40 benchmark | Episodes divided by patient-years at risk: 6 / 14 = 0.43. |  |
| 5 | In the SCOPE collaborative, which factor was associated with a lower peritonitis rate? | Compliance with a standardized follow-up care bundle | Bundle compliance had a rate ratio of 0.49; upward exit sites and touch contamination were associated with more peritonitis. The data are observational. |  |

## Module 23: Pediatric HD prescription: the circuit, the child and adequacy

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What does the European Pediatric Dialysis Working Group guideline advise about extracorporeal volume? | It should preferably be less than about 10% of the child’s total blood volume | A larger circuit takes more of a small child’s blood volume and returns more fluid at the end. Blood or albumin priming is used in babies and small infants. |  |
| 2 | A very uremic 6-year-old starts HD. Why is a standard adult session at high blood flow unsafe? | Rapid urea removal risks dialysis disequilibrium with cerebral edema | Urea falls faster in blood than in brain; water shifts into brain cells. First sessions are short with low blood flow. |  |
| 3 | A 12-year-old on HD has cramps late in most sessions; she has grown 4 cm since her target weight was set. What is the most likely problem? | Her target weight is too low for her current size | In infants and adolescents dry weight should be reassessed almost monthly; a fixed target in a growing child removes tissue, not fluid. |  |
| 4 | What did the 3H study show? | In a non-randomized comparison, vascular scores stayed static and height rose on HDF, while they worsened or stayed static on HD | The findings are associations with surrogates and growth; the authors call for randomized trials. |  |
| 5 | PhilHealth covers up to 156 HD sessions a year. How should this shape a child’s prescription? | It is coverage, not a prescription; prescribe the dialysis the child needs, document the reason, and confirm coverage on the date of service | Coverage never becomes clinical frequency. Longer or extra sessions need a documented clinical reason and a cost discussion. |  |

## Module 24: Vascular access in children

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A 13-year-old dialyzing through a tunneled catheter develops rigors 15 minutes after connection. What is the most appropriate first step? | Draw blood cultures before antibiotics, then give empirical therapy the same hour | Rigors soon after connection suggest catheter-related bloodstream infection. Cultures first, then empirical therapy covering gram-positive and gram-negative organisms (IDSA A-II), chosen from the unit’s pediatric protocol. |  |
| 2 | Which culture result makes IDSA 2009 recommend removing an infected hemodialysis catheter? | Staphylococcus aureus | IDSA recommends removal for S. aureus, Pseudomonas and Candida (A-II). Other organisms can be treated with the catheter in place if the child responds within 2 to 3 days. |  |
| 3 | What did the IPHN registry show about catheters and fistulas in children? | Infections were reported only with catheters, and catheters had more dysfunction and replacements | Catheter infections ran at 1.3 per 1,000 catheter-days; dysfunction 2.5 vs 1.2 per 1,000 days. The study was observational; catheter use was associated with age and with an expected early transplant. |  |
| 4 | A catheter’s arterial pressure alarm sounds at the start of each session and improves when the child turns the head. What is the most likely cause? | The tip lying against the vein wall or pulled back as the child grew | Positional, early-session inflow problems point to tip position. Growth can pull a tip back into the superior vena cava; a chest radiograph and access review follow if it recurs. |  |
| 5 | Which ESPN 2019 statement applies to a child with a central venous stenosis on the left? | Avoid creating a fistula in the left arm | A fistula drains through the central veins on its side. The ESPN group advises avoiding an AVF on the side of a central venous stenosis (ungraded) and imaging central veins when stenosis is suspected (2D). |  |

## Module 25: HD emergencies, water safety, and children in adult HD units

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A newly started 12-year-old develops headache, vomiting and restlessness in the first hour of his third session; blood pressure is high and pulse slow. What is the most likely diagnosis? | Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome | Early sessions, a very high starting urea and neurologic symptoms with a high pressure and slow pulse point to cerebral edema from the urea gradient. Prevention with limited first sessions matters most. |  |
| 2 | Foam appears in the venous line and the child suddenly becomes breathless. What should the nurse do with the blood in the circuit? | Clamp the venous line, stop the pump, and do not return the blood | Suspected air embolism means stopping the pump and clamping; blood is not returned. Lay the child on the left side, head down, and give oxygen. |  |
| 3 | Under DOH AO 2013-0003, who is responsible for the quality of water in a hemodialysis clinic? | The medical director | The order makes the medical director responsible and requires documentation of that involvement, for example by initialing test results. |  |
| 4 | What did Hothi and colleagues find in children on HD? | A steeper fall in relative blood volume in the first hour and a change in heart rate were associated with complications | In 74 retrospective records, early slope and heart rate change mattered; thresholds at hours 1 to 3 discriminated, but no hour-4 value did. |  |
| 5 | PhilHealth covers a set number of HD sessions under PC 2024-0023. How should that number be used? | As information about coverage, with frequency set by the child’s clinical needs | Coverage is not a prescription. Confirm benefit rules on the date of service and write clinical frequency from the child’s needs. |  |
