| 1 | A 14-year-old with posterior urethral valves has a high-pressure bladder and recurrent febrile urinary tract infections (UTIs). A living donor is ready. What is the best next step? | Settle a bladder management plan with the urologist before setting a date | A high-pressure, poorly emptying bladder transmits pressure and infection to the graft. The bladder plan comes before the date. |  |
| 2 | What does DOH AO 2010-0018 say about non-directed living non-related donation? | It is not permitted | The order, aligned with the anti-trafficking law, the Declaration of Istanbul and WHO principles, does not permit non-directed living non-related donation. |  |
| 3 | Why does genetic testing matter before transplant in a child with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome? | A monogenic podocyte defect and a circulating factor carry different recurrence outlooks | IPNA reports a monogenic cause in 10–30% of SRNS. The donor kidney does not carry the child’s podocyte defect, but a circulating factor can attack it. |  |
| 4 | How did the KDIGO 2017 living-donor guideline change donor evaluation? | It replaced single risk-factor cutoffs with a comprehensive assessment of the donor’s whole risk profile | The guideline favors comprehensive, quantitative risk assessment and shared decision-making; many recommendations are ungraded expert opinion. |  |
| 5 | A family says the transplant date depends on when PhilHealth approves the Z benefit. What is the correct framing? | The benefit pays for the transplant under its conditions; clinical readiness decides the date | Coverage is not a clinical decision. Confirm benefit rules with the Z benefit coordinator on the date of service. |  |

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A 16-year-old’s tacrolimus troughs alternate between high and low, and her creatinine has risen 30%. She admits missing evening doses. What is the best next step? | Work up the creatinine rise and address adherence with her before changing the regimen | Intermittent dosing causes swinging levels; a higher dose adds toxic peaks without covering missed doses. Work up rejection, BK, obstruction and toxicity, and solve the adherence problem. |  |
| 2 | What did the USRDS analysis by Foster and colleagues show? | Graft failure was highest at ages 17 to 24, regardless of age at transplant | Crude rates peaked at 19 (6.6 per 100 person-years); hazard ratio 1.20 at 17–24 vs 25–29. The design was observational. |  |
| 3 | What did the TAKE-IT trial demonstrate? | Better electronically measured adherence with a multicomponent intervention | Odds ratio 1.66 for taking doses and 1.74 for timing. The trial was underpowered for rejection and graft loss. |  |
| 4 | According to the 2024 BK polyomavirus consensus, how long should children be screened with plasma BK viral load? | Monthly until month 9, then every 3 months until 3 years after transplant | The schedule extends to 2 years in adults and 3 years in children. Urine cytology can be used where plasma testing is limited. |  |
| 5 | A transplanted 7-year-old who was EBV-seronegative before transplant has a rising EBV viral load. What does the AST guideline name as the best validated intervention? | Reduction of immunosuppression | Reduction of immunosuppression is the best validated intervention; preemptive strategies rest on low-quality evidence, and tissue biopsy diagnoses PTLD. |  |

| 1 | A family has been giving the same number of milliliters of a liquid medicine after a pharmacy changed its concentration. Which safeguard best prevents this error? | Prescribing in milligrams with the concentration checked by a pharmacist at each formulation change | Same volume at a different concentration delivers a different dose. Milligrams, the weight used, and an independent pharmacist check close the gap. |  |
| 2 | Under the 1993 DOJ rules implementing RA 7610, what must the attending physician do when examining a child who appears to have been abused? | Report to DSWD or the local social welfare office within 48 hours | The head of the institution and the attending physician and nurse must report within 48 hours; good-faith reporting is protected from civil or administrative liability. |  |

| 5 | Why is a run chart preferred to a yearly average for a unit’s peritonitis rate? | It shows data in time order so real change can be distinguished from random variation | Perla and colleagues describe run charts, read with probability-based rules, as more useful than summaries that ignore time order. |  |

# Dialysis Head Nurse

## Module 1: Your Role on the Dialysis Floor

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why can a small process failure harm a dialysis patient faster than a ward patient? | The patient’s blood meets a large volume of prepared fluid, and the patient cannot correct water, potassium, or pressure on their own | The circuit, the fluid, and the missing kidney function remove the body’s own safety margin. |  |
| 2 | Which source sets out the three-month structured renal dialysis training for a head nurse? | The PSN standards for hemodialysis clinics | The PSN standards describe the head nurse’s preparation. DOH and the Nursing Act set other requirements. |  |
| 3 | A nurse holds a renal dialysis training certificate but has not been observed connecting a patient in your unit. How is she counted today? | As supernumerary until site sign-off | A certificate and a site sign-off are different evidence. Only signed-off nurses count toward the rule. |  |
| 4 | Twelve stations are planned. How many nurses with sign-off does the DOH provision require? | 3 | Twelve divided by four is three. |  |
| 5 | Two signed-off nurses are present for twelve planned stations. How many stations may open on nursing grounds alone? | 8 | Each nurse covers four stations under the provision. |  |
| 6 | The only ACLS-certified nurse on the roster has an expired certificate. What is the status of that gate? | Closed until a nurse with a current certificate is on the shift | The licensing order expects a nurse with an updated certificate on each shift. |  |
| 7 | Machine 7 was repaired but its release is unsigned. Who may put it back into use? | The designated technical staff, by signing the release | Technical release belongs to the technical staff. You confirm it exists. |  |
| 8 | Which decision belongs to the attending nephrologist or physician on duty, not the head nurse? | Which waiting patient can safely be delayed | Whether a patient can wait is a medical judgment about that patient. |  |
| 9 | Units where every nurse had two years of dialysis experience met more targets. What kind of evidence is this? | Cross-sectional, showing association only | Better-resourced units may have both experienced nurses and healthier patients. |  |
| 10 | What did the DOPPS analysis find about highly trained staff hours? | A higher share was associated with fewer skipped sessions | Skipping was itself associated with 30% higher mortality in the same cohort. |  |
| 11 | The administrator asks you to start now and fix the paperwork later. What is the best response? | Hold the affected stations, call the owners of each gate, and ask the physician who cannot wait | A hold with an owner protects patients without abandoning them. |  |
| 12 | What is the main purpose of an evidence register? | To show each requirement, the proof, the owner, and the expiry in one place | It turns “show me” into a two-minute answer. |  |
| 13 | How far ahead should the register be reviewed for expiring certificates? | About ninety days | Ninety days leaves time to book renewal courses. |  |
| 14 | Older PhilHealth circulars listed head nurse credentials. What should you do about them? | Ask the regional office in writing and file the answer | Their current status could not be confirmed from public documents. |  |
| 15 | Where a limit is not written in your unit’s protocol, what does this series ask you to do? | Follow the protocol, and ask the attending nephrologist for guidance | Inventing a limit at the chairside is how errors start. |  |

## Module 2: Reading Trends Across Sessions

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | For a Monday-Wednesday-Friday patient, on which day is mortality highest? | Monday, after the two-day gap | In the Foley cohort, deaths were higher on the day after the long interval. |  |
| 2 | Why is breathlessness when lying flat important even when the weight gain looks usual? | It suggests fluid in the lungs, and dry weight may no longer fit the body | A patient who has lost muscle can be overloaded at an unchanged dry weight. |  |
| 3 | A 60-kg patient needs 3,400 mL removed in 4 hours. What is the UF rate? | About 14 mL/kg/h | 3,400 ÷ 4 ÷ 60 = 14.2. |  |
| 4 | The same patient wants to leave after 3 hours with the same goal. What happens to the rate? | It rises to about 19 mL/kg/h | Less time for the same fluid means faster removal. |  |
| 5 | What did Flythe and colleagues find for UF rates above 13 mL/kg/h? | An association with higher all-cause and cardiovascular mortality | The study was observational. No trial has shown that a cap saves lives. |  |
| 6 | In DOPPS, the four-month risk of missing a session ranged from under 1% to 24% between countries. What does this suggest? | Systems such as transport and scheduling drive much of it | A fiftyfold difference between countries points to systems. |  |
| 7 | Which nadir pressure definition was most strongly associated with death? | A nadir systolic below 90 mm Hg | Definitions built on symptoms or interventions were not associated with death. |  |
| 8 | Why does water removal faster than refilling lower the pressure? | Blood volume falls because the tissues cannot refill the blood fast enough | The machine removes water only from the blood. |  |
| 9 | What did the lung ultrasound outcome trial show? | More lung congestion cleared, but no reduction in death or major cardiac events | The benefit was seen on images, not on outcomes patients feel. |  |
| 10 | A patient missed Friday, has palpitations, and has a critical potassium with no documented call. Which lane? | Now | Each finding alone is urgent. Together they are a Now finding. |  |
| 11 | What closes a critical result loop? | A named recipient acknowledges it, a decision is recorded, and follow-up has an owner | Until someone owns the next step, the loop is open. |  |
| 12 | Hemoglobin has drifted from 10.8 to 9.9 g/dL over three months. Which lane? | This month | It is a trend for the monthly review with the nephrologist. |  |
| 13 | Which question has outcome data behind it as a routine check? | How long does it take you to recover after a session? | Longer recovery was associated with hospitalization and death in DOPPS. |  |
| 14 | A family member asks for an extra hour after a missed session. Who decides? | The prescriber | Time, rate, and dialysis fluid are part of the prescription. |  |
| 15 | Why should a potassium from a hemolyzed sample still be reported? | The physician decides whether to repeat it, with the context given | Report the value with its context. Do not decide alone that it is false. |  |

## Module 3: The Order, the Machine, and the Record

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which process clears urea and potassium mainly? | Diffusion | Small molecules move down their concentration gradient across the membrane. |  |
| 2 | Why does dialysis fluid flow opposite to the blood? | To keep the concentration gradient steep along the whole fiber | Countercurrent flow keeps fresh fluid meeting blood that still carries solute. |  |
| 3 | The signed order says four hours, the machine is set for three, and the handover sheet says three. What governs? | The current signed order | The current order governs when it is clear. Remove the outdated sheet. |  |
| 4 | When should the nurse call the prescriber about a mismatch? | When the order itself is unclear, incomplete, or seems unsafe today | A clear current order is simply followed. An unclear one is clarified. |  |
| 5 | Pre-dialysis urea is 80 and post-dialysis urea is 28 mg/dL. What is the URR? | 65% | (80 − 28) ÷ 80 = 0.65. |  |
| 6 | A patient’s Kt/V jumps from 1.25 to 1.9 with no change in prescription. What do you check first? | The post-dialysis sampling method | A sample taken at full flow or after rinse-back gives a falsely good result. |  |
| 7 | What did the HEMO Study show? | Higher dose and high-flux membranes did not reduce deaths | The relative risk of death with the higher dose was 0.96. |  |
| 8 | What is the KDOQI 2015 minimum delivered single-pool Kt/V for thrice-weekly dialysis? | 1.2 | The target is 1.4, with a minimum delivered dose of 1.2. |  |
| 9 | Why is the TiME trial weak evidence against longer sessions? | The two groups differed by only nine minutes | A trial cannot show the effect of a difference it did not achieve. |  |
| 10 | What did MyTEMP show about cooler dialysis fluid as a center-wide policy? | It did not reduce cardiovascular death or admission | It may still help an individual patient with frequent low pressure. |  |
| 11 | In CONVINCE, death was 17.3% with HDF and 21.9% with hemodialysis. What is the absolute difference? | 4.6 percentage points | 23% is the relative reduction, and 0.77 is the hazard ratio. |  |
| 12 | Which patients were eligible for CONVINCE? | Patients able to reach a convection volume of at least 23 liters | High-volume HDF needs good access flow. |  |
| 13 | One hour is lost from a four-hour session with the same fluid goal. What happens to the UF rate? | It rises by a third | Four hours of work done in three is a third faster. |  |
| 14 | Unit delivered time is 97%. Why is that not enough? | An average can hide individual sessions that lose 30 minutes or more | Look at the sessions, not only the average. |  |
| 15 | What should happen to a laminated card at a station that lists dialysis settings? | Version-control it from the order or remove it | Any paper at the chair that can disagree with the order eventually will. |  |

## Module 4: Protecting the Access

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What does a healthy fistula feel and sound like? | A soft continuous thrill and a low-pitched continuous bruit | Flow continues through the whole heartbeat. |  |
| 2 | A fistula is pulsatile, the bruit is high-pitched and systolic only, and bleeding lasts longer after needle removal. What is likely? | Narrowing on the outflow side | Downstream narrowing raises pressure in the access. |  |
| 3 | The usual thrill is absent before treatment. What do you do? | Do not cannulate and call for urgent review | No thrill suggests clotting. |  |
| 4 | You see shiny, scabbed skin over a fistula bulge. What is correct? | Do not cannulate there, arrange urgent review, and teach direct pressure | Scabbed skin over an aneurysm signals a risk of rupture. |  |
| 5 | Why can the venous pressure alarm stay silent when the needle comes out? | Most of the reading is needle and line resistance, which does not change | The reading may stay inside its alarm window. |  |
| 6 | In the bench simulation, how often did the machine alarm sound after dislodgement? | In 8 of 19 cases | It sounded in 42% of simulations. |  |
| 7 | The pump runs at 300 mL/min and a dislodgement goes unnoticed for 5 minutes. What is the potential loss? | 1,500 mL | 300 × 5 = 1,500 mL. |  |
| 8 | What is the first action when a needle site bleeds heavily? | Stop the blood pump | Stopping the pump stops the loss from the circuit. Clamp, press, and call follow at once. |  |
| 9 | Why is a blanket over the access arm unsafe? | It hides bleeding that the alarm may not detect | Only a visible access protects against silent bleeding. |  |
| 10 | For catheters used for months, where do most bloodstream infections start? | Inside the lumen, from the hub | That is why hub handling matters most. |  |
| 11 | What did the Philippine catheter cohort report? | 6.72 infections per 1,000 catheter-days, mostly gram-negative | Use of the catheter for transfusion or medicines was a risk factor. |  |
| 12 | What should the gram-negative pattern make you audit? | Water, solutions, multidose containers, and non-dialysis use of the catheter | This is an inference from the organisms, not a study finding. |  |
| 13 | What did the systematic review find about buttonhole cannulation? | No consistent pain benefit in randomized trials and more infection | Use it only for selected patients under a strict protocol. |  |
| 14 | What did the KDOQI 2019 guideline change about access planning? | An access plan built around each patient’s life | It replaced fistula first with an individualized life plan. |  |
| 15 | Nine of 95 patients have had a catheter for more than 90 days. What is the catheter dependence? | 9.5% | 9 ÷ 95 = 9.5%. |  |

## Module 5: Making Infection Prevention Visible

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why does hepatitis B need a dedicated room, machine, and staff? | It survives on surfaces for days at high concentrations | Durability on surfaces drives spread through shared equipment. |  |
| 2 | Why is hepatitis C not isolated? | Guidelines rely on strict standard precautions, because it is less hardy | Outbreaks have followed lapses such as shared vials. |  |
| 3 | For catheters used for months, where should prevention effort focus most? | The hub, each time it is opened | Most long-term catheter infections start inside the lumen. |  |
| 4 | Eighteen of 24 hand-hygiene opportunities were met. What should the audit report? | 75% | 18 ÷ 24. The interval is wide because the sample is small. |  |
| 5 | What goes in the denominator of a hand-hygiene audit? | All observed eligible opportunities | Every observed opportunity counts. |  |
| 6 | Why are 10 observations too few? | The 95% confidence interval is too wide to compare months | Eight of ten has an interval from about 49% to 94%. |  |
| 7 | Three bloodstream infections occur among 95 patients in one month. What is the rate? | 3.2 per 100 patient-months | 3 ÷ 95 × 100. |  |
| 8 | What did the United States collaborative report? | A 54% modeled fall in access-related bloodstream infection, without a control group | No control group, and volunteer facilities, so the true effect may be smaller. |  |
| 9 | Two patients develop chills twenty minutes after connection. Which cause is most likely? | A pyrogenic reaction from fluid or a product | Early onset points to the fluid or a product. |  |
| 10 | What is the first priority when symptoms cluster? | Assess and treat the patients, then escalate and contain | Patients first, with the investigation running alongside. |  |
| 11 | Where should medicines be drawn up? | In a clean area away from the stations | Medicine preparation stays inside the clean boundary. |  |
| 12 | The gap between shifts is too short to clean stations properly. What is the fix? | Change the schedule | When the schedule makes the process impossible, the schedule is the hazard. |  |
| 13 | What should you preserve when a new lot may be the source? | The opened containers, lines, and lot numbers | Evidence must still exist when the investigation asks for it. |  |
| 14 | Why should infection results be posted for staff? | Feedback is one of the core interventions | Surveillance with feedback to staff is part of the bundle. |  |
| 15 | Two catheter infections occur among 30 catheter patients over 30 days. What is the rate per 1,000 catheter-days? | 2.2 | 2 ÷ 900 × 1,000 = 2.2. |  |

## Module 6: Water, Machines, and Supplies

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why is drinking water not safe for dialysis? | The blood meets about 120 liters across a thin membrane, without the gut’s protection | Small contaminants pass the membrane freely. |  |
| 2 | Which stage is the only reliable barrier to chloramine? | Carbon tanks | Reverse osmosis does not reliably remove chloramine. |  |
| 3 | Why is total chlorine tested every shift when cultures are monthly? | Carbon can exhaust within hours, and chloramine causes hemolysis | The test is the last line of defense. |  |
| 4 | Three connected patients develop chest pain and dark, cherry-red blood in the venous lines. What is the rule about the blood? | Do not return it. Stop and clamp | Suspected hemolysis means the circuit is the cause. |  |
| 5 | What is the ISO limit for bacteria in dialysis water? | Under 100 CFU/mL | Endotoxin must be under 0.25 EU/mL. |  |
| 6 | Which fluid must be ultrapure? | Fluid for hemodiafiltration | High-volume HDF infuses fluid directly into the blood. |  |
| 7 | What is an action level? | A lower level, usually half the limit, that triggers corrective action | It lets the unit act before the limit is reached. |  |
| 8 | Can yesterday’s normal result clear today’s abnormal one? | No. Today’s verification and the release process do | Each result stands for its own time. |  |
| 9 | How should a missing water result be treated? | As abnormal | If you cannot see it, the gate is closed. |  |
| 10 | What three documents are required before restart? | Corrective action, a repeat test within limit, and a signed release | A verbal assurance is none of them. |  |
| 11 | Feed conductivity is 400 and product is 12 µS/cm. What is the RO rejection? | 97% | (1 − 12 ÷ 400) × 100 = 97%. |  |
| 12 | Why must carbon contact time be recalculated when stations are added? | Higher flow shortens contact time | Contact time is volume divided by flow. |  |
| 13 | What enables a fast, targeted recall of a dialyzer lot? | Recording lot numbers for each patient and session | Lot numbers link the product to the patients. |  |
| 14 | Two patients have chills and fever within the first hour. Which contaminant group comes first to mind? | Bacteria and endotoxin | Endotoxin causes early pyrogenic reactions. |  |
| 15 | Who releases a water system after correction? | The designated technical authority | You confirm that the signed release exists. |  |

## Module 7: Leading the First Minutes of an Emergency

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What is the first question in any dialysis emergency? | Is the circuit the cause or a bystander? | The answer decides whether blood may be returned. |  |
| 2 | In which events is blood not returned? | Air embolism, hemolysis, and severe dialyzer reaction | In these, the circuit is the cause. |  |
| 3 | A defibrillator advises “no shock” during an in-clinic arrest. What next? | Continue compressions per algorithm | Two thirds of in-clinic arrests were nonshockable. |  |
| 4 | What was staff-started CPR associated with? | About three times the odds of leaving hospital alive | The study was observational, but no stronger evidence is likely. |  |
| 5 | Air is seen in the venous line and the patient coughs. What position is taught? | Left side down, head down | It keeps air in the right heart away from the lung outflow. |  |
| 6 | Why does “somebody call the doctor” fail? | No one owns the task, so no one confirms it was done | A name plus a report back closes the loop. |  |
| 7 | Why must one nurse watch the rest of the floor during an emergency? | Other connected patients still need monitoring and alarms continue | An emergency at one chair does not stop the risks at the others. |  |
| 8 | Pressure stays low five minutes after stopping UF, lying flat, and giving fluid. What has changed? | The working diagnosis. Look for a heart, bleeding, infection, or pericardial cause | Failure to recover is a warning sign in itself. |  |
| 9 | Why can some dialysis patients not hold their pressure during fluid removal? | Nerve damage, a stiff heart, and morning blood pressure tablets blunt their defenses | Compensation depends on vessel tightening and the heart’s response. |  |
| 10 | A patient becomes itchy and wheezy ten minutes into a session, and pressure falls. What happens to the blood? | Do not return it. Stop and clamp | Early onset with itching and wheeze suggests a dialyzer reaction. |  |
| 11 | Which dialysis fluid factor was associated with in-clinic arrest in a case-control study? | Low potassium | Low-potassium fluid was among the associated factors. |  |
| 12 | What must the transfer handoff include that is specific to dialysis? | Whether blood was returned, fluid removed, and estimated blood loss | The receiving team needs to know the volume state. |  |
| 13 | Does a defibrillator on site guarantee better survival? | Not by itself. The early cohort found no survival advantage, consistent with mostly nonshockable rhythms | Compressions remain the core intervention. |  |
| 14 | What did the structured handoff program show in hospital residents? | 23% fewer medical errors | Applying this to dialysis transfers is an inference. |  |
| 15 | What should happen after the emergency? | A short debrief, cart restocking, and checking on staff | The station is not ready until the cart is restocked. |  |

## Module 8: Staffing, Delegation, and Coaching

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Under the DOH provision, how many signed-off nurses are needed for 16 stations? | 4 | 16 ÷ 4 = 4. |  |
| 2 | Which staff count toward the staffing rule? | Only nurses with site sign-off to work alone | Orientees are supernumerary. |  |
| 3 | Which tasks are dropped first under overload? | Tasks without an alarm: looking, asking, teaching, checking | Those are the safety layers that catch what alarms miss. |  |
| 4 | What kind of evidence links staffing to outcomes in dialysis? | Mostly observational studies | They show association and a plausible mechanism, not a proven ratio. |  |
| 5 | Among young patients, what was the most stretched nursing quartile associated with? | 14% lower incidence of transplant | Referral work is among the tasks left undone. |  |
| 6 | Two signed-off nurses are present for twelve stations and neither has ACLS. How many stations may open? | None until ACLS cover arrives | ACLS cover is a separate gate from the ratio. |  |
| 7 | Who decides which waiting patients can be deferred? | The physician on duty or attending nephrologist | It is a medical decision about each patient. |  |
| 8 | What is a single point of failure on a shift? | A critical skill held by only one person | Each one needs a backup or a reliever. |  |
| 9 | What must follow delegation? | Supervision matched to the risk and confirmation of the result | You keep the accountability for delegating well. |  |
| 10 | Which of these is one of the five rights of delegation? | Right person, with competency verified for this task | The others are task, circumstance, direction, and supervision. |  |
| 11 | Which feedback is most likely to change a nurse’s technique? | “The hub was open about twenty seconds at station 6. That is when organisms enter. What made it awkward?” | Specific, observed, linked to risk, and asking about conditions. |  |
| 12 | Why ask what made the correct step difficult? | The cause is often the setup, which you can fix | Fixing the setup protects every nurse who comes next. |  |
| 13 | Why is retention a safety intervention? | Turnover lowers the experience mix, which feeds the overload loop | Experience mix is associated with outcomes. |  |
| 14 | What does a competency matrix show? | Each nurse’s signed-off skills with dates | Empty and expired cells become the teaching plan. |  |
| 15 | A reliever arrives and the arithmetic now works. What else do you check? | Close-observation cover, break cover, and whether the ACLS nurse is also a single point of failure | Arithmetic is where staffing starts, not where it ends. |  |

| 15 | Which staffing finding relates to referrals? | The most stretched nursing quartile was associated with lower incidence of transplant | Referral work is among the tasks left undone. |  |

## Module 11: Learning From Incidents and Proving Improvement

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why is blaming the nurse who slipped not enough? | It removes one person and leaves the conditions that caused the slip | Design the work so the slip cannot reach the patient. |  |
| 2 | Which question is best when reconstructing an incident? | What made the safe action hard at that moment? | The answer reveals the conditions. |  |
| 3 | Rank from strongest to weakest: retraining, a forcing function, a checklist. | Forcing function, checklist, retraining | Remove or force, standardize, check, then train. |  |
| 4 | A review produces only a memo and a retraining session. What do you ask? | What stronger fix would stop the same slip on a busy morning? | Weak fixes fade within weeks. |  |
| 5 | Baseline errors were 6 of 60 and after a test 2 of 55. What is the best conclusion? | Promising, but the confidence intervals overlap. Keep measuring | Small samples move a lot by chance. |  |
| 6 | Why keep the denominator beside the rate? | It shows how much the rate could move by chance and whether volume changed | Rates from small denominators are unstable. |  |
| 7 | What is a balancing measure? | A measure that watches for harm caused by the change itself | A new check might delay starts. |  |
| 8 | Six consecutive weekly points fall below the median. What does that indicate? | A shift, a likely real change | Six or more on one side is the shift rule. |  |
| 9 | Five consecutive points each rise above the one before. What is this? | A trend | Five or more rising or falling is a trend. |  |
| 10 | What should happen before testing a change across the whole unit? | A small test on one station group or shift, with a prediction | Test small, learn, then scale. |  |
| 11 | When is a corrective action closed? | When the owner and reviewer have recorded evidence that it worked | Doing it is not the same as showing it worked. |  |
| 12 | What did the structured handoff program show? | 23% fewer medical errors in hospital residents | Before-and-after data in residents. Applying it to dialysis is an inference. |  |
| 13 | Which is a forcing function? | A machine that will not start until the scanned order matches the settings | It makes the wrong action impossible. |  |
| 14 | Which six elements define an indicator? | Numerator, denominator, inclusions, period, data source, owner | Without them, a trend cannot be trusted. |  |
| 15 | What is the median line on a run chart for? | A reference for the shift and run rules | The rules are counted against the median. |  |

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why is a dialysis patient’s deadline in a disaster counted in days? | Potassium and fluid build up each day without treatment | Risk rises fastest after the third day. |  |
| 2 | Why can relief food make things worse? | Canned food is often salty and high in potassium | Salt drives fluid gain and potassium drives arrhythmia. |  |
| 3 | What is a disaster diet? | A short-term, stricter limit on potassium, salt, and fluid to buy days | It is a bridge, not a substitute for dialysis. |  |
| 4 | After Hurricane Sandy, what fraction of surveyed patients carried a detailed medication list? | About 44% | Emergency cards close this gap. |  |
| 5 | What did the Hurricane Katrina study show? | A coordinated response that moved patients quickly prevented excess deaths | The finding is evidence that planning works. |  |
| 6 | Tropical storm exposure was associated with what change in missed sessions? | About 55% higher risk over the following week | Plan for it every rainy season. |  |
| 7 | Who decides which patients are placed first? | The physician, using the facts you provide | It is a medical decision. |  |
| 8 | Which facts help the physician prioritize most? | Days since the last session, last potassium, fluid status, and symptoms | Risk builds with time, potassium, and fluid. |  |
| 9 | Fifteen patients need a session in 48 hours and six slots are confirmed. What is the capacity gap? | 9 | 15 − 6 = 9. Call the next receiving unit now. |  |
| 10 | What closes a patient transfer? | A named acceptor, a handoff, transport, notice to the patient, and a log entry | Acceptance and continuity are verified for each person. |  |
| 11 | What should receiving agreements include? | At least two units in different directions, each with a named contact and backup number | One road may be closed. |  |
| 12 | Which is one of the five restart gates? | Water and machines tested and released | The others are building, staff, supplies and cart, and records. |  |
| 13 | When is a disaster incident closed? | When every patient on the roster has been accounted for | Reconcile who was dialyzed, where, and who was missed. |  |
| 14 | What should be done when a warning is issued? | Ask the nephrologist about moving sessions earlier and call every patient | Dialyzing before landfall buys time. |  |
| 15 | What is a call-down drill? | A test of the patient call list before it is needed | Wrong numbers are found in calm weather, not in a storm. |  |

| 5 | Which is the best escalation statement? | “Beds 13 to 16 have no independent nurse; I have not connected them; I need one nurse or approval to move four patients; I will call back at 6:00.” | Hazard, protection now, help needed, and recheck time. |  |
| 6 | What do the cross-sectional staffing studies in dialysis show? | An association between more patients per nurse and more reported adverse events | They show association, not causation, but the direction is consistent. |  |
| 7 | What does a PhilHealth circular mainly govern? | Reimbursement and covered services | Payer rules answer payer questions; licensing rules come from DOH. |  |
| 8 | The ACLS-trained nurse goes home sick at 9 a.m. What do you do first? | Call for a replacement and tell the physician on duty | The shift no longer meets a licensing condition; get a replacement and keep the physician close. |  |

| 11 | The physician on duty asks you to type a new dry weight on his verbal word. What is the safe response? | Read it back, record it as a verbal order per procedure, and flag it for countersignature | The decision is his; recording it safely is yours. |  |

| 14 | What should you find out before accepting charge for the first time? | Your job description, the escalation ladder, and whether you may pause an unsafe activity | Without the authority to pause, you have responsibility without tools. |  |

## Module 5: Sorting Risk Before Connection

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |

| 1 | For a Monday-Wednesday-Friday patient, mortality was highest on: | The day after the two-day gap | Monday, after the long gap, in the Foley cohort. |  |
| 2 | What is the ultrafiltration rate for 3 liters over 4 hours in a 60-kg patient? | 12.5 | 3,000 ÷ 4 ÷ 60 = 12.5. |  |
| 3 | A rate above 13 mL/kg/h was: | Associated with higher mortality in a cohort | Observational; no trial has proven a cap. |  |
| 4 | Orthopnea before dialysis belongs in which lane? | Now | Call before connection. |  |
| 5 | When is a result loop closed? | When a named person owns the next step | Received, told, decided, recorded, owned. |  |
| 6 | Older patients on hemodialysis fell about how often in the cohort? | 1.6 times per person-year | Nearly half fell at least once. |  |
| 7 | In the glucose monitoring study, glucose during dialysis: | Fell about a third, lowest about two hours in | And 20% of participants had low blood sugar during a session. |  |
| 8 | Who sets the fluid goal? | The attending nephrologist or physician on duty | The nurse presents the numbers; the prescriber decides. |  |
| 9 | The same 3 liters over 4 hours in a 45-kg patient is about: | 17 mL/kg/h | 3,000 ÷ 4 ÷ 45 = 16.7. |  |

| 11 | Which is a Today finding? | Missed medicines | The others are Now. |  |
| 12 | What two questions should a patient on insulin hear before connection? | Did you take your diabetes medicine today, and what did you eat? | Low blood sugar during dialysis is common in this group. |  |
| 13 | A patient lost muscle during a hospital stay but returns at his old dry weight. What may be true? | He may be overloaded, because the same weight now carries more water | Dry weight must fit the body he has now. |  |
| 14 | Why is a long-gap patient who also missed Friday especially risky? | Five days of water and potassium have built up | The longest gap of all. |  |
| 15 | A result arrives with no named owner. Who owns it? | The charge nurse, until someone else does | Unowned results are how loops break. |  |

| 11 | What is moral distress? | Knowing the right thing but being unable to do it | Common in dialysis nursing. |  |
| 12 | Why should the charge nurse take her own break? | Fatigue raises errors, and she models it for the team | A charge nurse who never eats teaches that eating is optional. |  |
| 13 | What does de-escalation start with? | Listening without interrupting | Then state what you can do. |  |
| 14 | Which item is in the capstone portfolio? | An improvement run chart | Evidence from every module. |  |
| 15 | What is the order of priorities in a busy shift? | Patients first, the sicker first, someone always watching the floor | The capstone’s core. |  |

# Dialyzer Reprocessing Technician

## Module 1: The Reuse Room and Your Place in It

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A biomedical technician scores 5 of 5 on the common knowledge module. What may he now do? | Continue to work within his biomedical scope; release requires an observed practical and a facility authorization | A knowledge pass is one of several states. Release authority is granted by the facility after an observed practical. |  |
| 2 | Who decides whether a patient is eligible for dialyzer reuse? | The medical director, through the approved program | Eligibility is a clinical program decision. The technician holds any dialyzer whose eligibility is unknown. |  |
| 3 | A nurse asks for a dialyzer whose record has a missing test result. What is the safest response? | Quarantine it, and give the patient a new dialyzer while the question is answered | An unproven gate is a failed gate until proven otherwise. A new dialyzer protects the patient today. |  |
| 4 | Which task is within a reprocessing operator’s usual scope? | Labeling and storing a processed dialyzer | Labeling and storage are core operator duties. The others belong to nurses, physicians or service staff. |  |
| 5 | Why must two disagreeing staff members not settle the question by using the dialyzer? | Because production pressure cannot resolve a safety question; the owner of the decision must answer in writing | Quarantine first, then a written decision by the person who owns it. |  |
| 6 | What does an observed practical assessment show that a quiz cannot? | That you can perform them correctly on that equipment | A quiz tests knowledge. Only observation shows performance on the unit’s own reprocessor. |  |
| 7 | A job posting lists the title “adding machine technician” but describes dialyzer reprocessing. What should you rely on? | The duties described | Titles vary between employers. The duties tell you what the job is. |  |
| 8 | According to the improvement report from a United States unit, where are most failed dialyzers made? | On the dialysis floor, through heparin and end-of-treatment rinsing | Standardizing heparin and rinsing on the floor raised the average number of uses. It was a single-unit report, not a trial. |  |
| 9 | Which report from the reuse room is most useful to the head nurse? | “Three dialyzers from station 5 failed volume this week, all with clotted headers; quarantined and discarded.” | A useful report gives what, when, where it may come from, and what was done, without blame. |  |
| 10 | What does the DOH licensing order list among dialysis technician duties? | Daily reprocessor calibration, reprocessing, acceptance testing, labeling, records and storage | AO 2012-0001 lists the reuse-room tasks among technician duties. |  |
| 11 | Which statement about this track’s place in the Academy is correct? | It is a technician track; the reuse room works under the medical director and alongside the nursing service | Placement tells learners where to find the track. It confers no nursing or clinical scope. |  |
| 12 | You are asked to photograph a dialyzer label to send to a colleague on a personal phone. What do you do? | Decline; share patient information only through the unit’s approved channels | Labels carry patient identity and sometimes infection status. Use approved channels only. |  |

## Module 2: The Dialyzer and Why Reuse Exists

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why does a clotted fiber reduce the dose of dialysis? | It removes membrane surface the blood can touch | Diffusion depends on surface. Closed fibers remove surface. |  |
| 2 | In the HEMO analysis, how much did urea clearance change with reuse? | It fell about 1% to 2% per 10 reuses | A small, consistent fall regardless of membrane or method. |  |
| 3 | In the same analysis, what happened to beta-2-microglobulin clearance? | It fell, stayed, or rose depending on membrane and method | Middle-molecule clearance depends on the membrane material and the reprocessing technique. |  |
| 4 | What did the 2012 systematic review conclude about reuse and death? | No consistent difference, with very low quality evidence | Fourteen observational studies; very low quality; no consistent difference. |  |
| 5 | What kind of study was the 2011 report of facilities that stopped peracetic acid reuse? | A before-and-after observational comparison | Before-and-after designs cannot exclude changes over time, so the finding is an association. |  |
| 6 | A dialyzer’s volume has gone 92%, 88%, 84%, 81%. What is the best action? | Report the falling trend to the head nurse and the patient’s nurse | The trend is information for the floor and the nephrologist. The baseline is never reset. |  |
| 7 | Where does most fiber clotting begin? | During treatment on the floor | Clotting happens while blood flows. Heparin and rinsing at the end of treatment matter. |  |
| 8 | What did the 2025 study of super high-flux dialyzer reuse show? | Some toxins were removed less well with reuse, in a very small study | Five patients, 15 dialyzers: beta-2-microglobulin kept, other toxins fell. A small study only suggests. |  |
| 9 | Which reason for reuse has largely faded with modern membranes? | Reducing first-use reactions | First-use reactions were mainly a problem of older cellulose membranes. |  |
| 10 | What does total cell volume estimate? | How many fibers remain open | The blood-compartment volume shrinks as fibers close. |  |
| 11 | A colleague says reuse is proven safe. What is the most accurate reply? | The outcome studies are observational and inconsistent; documented harms come from poor execution | The honest summary is uncertainty about outcomes and certainty that execution failures cause harm. |  |
| 12 | Which outcome is a surrogate? | Urea clearance | Clearance is a laboratory measure. It matters, but it is not an outcome the patient feels. |  |

## Module 3: The Rules: Philippine Governance and Other Countries

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A dialyzer has been used for four treatments. Under a five-use ceiling, how many more treatments may it be used for if every gate passes? | One | Five uses total. Four done, one left. |  |
| 2 | “Five uses” under the PhilHealth package means: | The first treatment plus up to four reuses | The count includes the first treatment. |  |
| 3 | A dialyzer failed its first processing cycle and was processed again before passing. What changed? | It had one more processing cycle; the use number is unchanged | A processing cycle is not a treatment. |  |
| 4 | The IFU allows three uses; PhilHealth pays for up to five. How many uses are allowed? | Three | The strictest rule that applies wins. |  |
| 5 | What is PhilHealth Circular 2024-0029’s volume criterion? | TCV of at least 80% | At least 80% of baseline, as one of several criteria. |  |
| 6 | Under PSN 2024 guidance, dialyzer reuse for a patient with HIV is: | Not allowed | The PSN guidance does not allow dialyzer reuse in HIV. |  |
| 7 | Which statement about the United States federal reuse rule is correct? | It excludes patients positive for hepatitis B from reuse | The US rule excludes hepatitis B positive patients. It does not apply to Philippine units. |  |
| 8 | A patient’s hepatitis C result is missing from the transfer folder. What do you do with his dialyzer? | Hold it and report the missing result | Unknown status holds. Eligibility is decided by the clinical team. |  |
| 9 | What does a PhilHealth circular decide? | Payment conditions | A payer rule decides what is paid for, not whether something is safe. |  |
| 10 | You find a 2018 regional standard in a drawer that mentions very high reuse numbers. What should you do? | Check whether it has been replaced; the 2026 edition supersedes it, and it was never a Philippine rule | Always check edition, issuer and applicability. |  |
| 11 | Where does the exact germicide contact time come from? | The germicide IFU and the validated SOP | Chemistry comes from the product instructions and the validated procedure. |  |
| 12 | A dialyzer arrives from another facility with a handwritten label and no processing record. Under most programs it is: | Not accepted for reuse; the patient receives a new dialyzer | Without your unit’s record, nothing about its history is proven. |  |

## Module 4: Infection Prevention and Protecting Yourself

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How long can hepatitis B virus survive on surfaces at room temperature? | At least seven days | The CDC notes survival for at least seven days, which is why surfaces matter. |  |
| 2 | In the Vietnam hepatitis C outbreak, what was the most likely route for most cases? | Indirect contact through a contaminated environment | Investigators judged indirect contact likely for 10 of 11 cases. |  |
| 3 | Which arrangement in the Vietnam unit increased risk? | Medicine preparation next to blood handling and reused dialyzer storage | Clean work beside dirty work invites contamination. |  |
| 4 | Your face shield fogs during header cleaning. What do you do? | Stop, and replace or fix the shield before continuing | A lifted shield protects nothing. Fix the equipment. |  |
| 5 | What is the first action after blood splashes into your eye? | Flush at the eye wash with lids held open | Flush first, report second, record third. |  |
| 6 | Under the academy default, a patient’s hepatitis B surface antigen has turned positive. What happens to his dialyzer? | Stop reprocessing it at once, quarantine it, and tell the head nurse | A change in infection status stops reprocessing. The clinical team decides the plan. |  |
| 7 | Where should a patient’s infection status be confirmed? | In the clinical record, through the nurse | Labels identify; the clinical record holds the diagnosis. |  |
| 8 | Which is the main reason the reuse room needs one-way flow? | So that dirty items never travel back toward clean ones | Layout prevents contamination when people are busy. |  |
| 9 | What does the CDC recommend for susceptible dialysis staff? | Hepatitis B vaccination with a check of response | Vaccination protects staff against hepatitis B. |  |
| 10 | A colleague cleans a cut on her hand with bleach after an injury. Is that correct? | No; let it bleed, wash with soap and water, and report | Bleach damages skin. Washing and prompt reporting are the right steps. |  |
| 11 | Why should an exposure be reported within the hour? | Some preventive treatments work best when started early | Delay can close the window for preventive treatment. |  |
| 12 | Which item should never be in the reuse room? | Food and drink | Eating and drinking where blood and chemicals are handled is a route of exposure. |  |

## Module 5: Water for Reprocessing

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why must reprocessing water meet dialysis water quality? | It fills the blood compartment that the next patient’s blood will flow through | Anything left in the fibers meets the blood. |  |
| 2 | What can cause fever and chills even when bacteria are dead? | Endotoxin | Endotoxin from bacterial walls triggers fever and chills. |  |
| 3 | What happened at Caruaru, Brazil, in 1996? | Untreated reservoir water with algal toxins caused liver failure in 101 patients, 50 of whom died | Water reaches the blood, and anything in it reaches the patient. |  |
| 4 | Under the DOH order, how often is product-water TDS measured? | Weekly | Weekly, with corrective action above 10 mg/L. |  |
| 5 | Under the DOH order, how often at minimum is microbiology tested at the point of use? | Monthly | Before operation, then at least monthly. |  |
| 6 | What is an action level? | A lower value at which you investigate and correct before the limit is broken | It warns while the water still meets the limit. |  |
| 7 | A water sample bottle was opened before it was labeled, and the outlet name was forgotten. What is the result worth? | Little; a result without location and time cannot guide action | Label before opening. |  |
| 8 | Where does persistent bacterial contamination of a water loop usually come from? | Biofilm on pipe walls and in dead legs | Biofilm shelters bacteria and sheds endotoxin. |  |
| 9 | You find an unsigned failed result in the water log at the start of a shift. What do you do? | Do not start; ask the person responsible for water first | An unresolved failure must be addressed before any processing. |  |
| 10 | In the Hanoi report, what were the bacteria found in patients mostly like? | Waterborne organisms | Waterborne organisms point to water or reprocessing. |  |
| 11 | According to a CDC review of dialysis outbreaks, most were: | Preventable with adequate water treatment, disinfection and adherence to reprocessing protocols | Execution, again, is the lesson. |  |
| 12 | Who is accountable for water quality under the DOH order? | The medical director | The medical director is accountable; the technician samples, reads and reports. |  |

## Module 6: Germicides and Chemical Safety

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | In the 1988 CDC investigation, what caused the uneven germicide strength? | Inadequate mixing during dilution | The concentrate layered: weak on top, strong at the bottom. |  |
| 2 | Which check would have caught the weak germicide before storage? | A potency test on the batch and on filled dialyzers | Only a potency or presence test proves strength. |  |
| 3 | To make 10 L at 2.5% from a 50% stock, how much concentrate is needed? | 0.5 L | V1 = (2.5 × 10) ÷ 50 = 0.5 L. |  |
| 4 | What does the dilution formula not tell you? | Whether the batch is mixed evenly and the stock is still at full strength | Arithmetic predicts; testing proves. |  |
| 5 | Where do the germicide concentration and contact time come from? | The product IFU and the validated SOP | No concentration on this page is a working value. |  |
| 6 | Which germicide is a strong sensitizer associated with occupational asthma? | Glutaraldehyde | Glutaraldehyde sensitizes skin and airways. |  |
| 7 | Mixing bleach with an acid germicide releases: | Chlorine gas | Never mix chemicals outside the SOP’s exact sequence. |  |
| 8 | What did the NIOSH studies of hospital staff using peroxide and peracetic acid products find? | More wheeze and eye and airway symptoms, even at low measured levels | Observational, but consistent: these vapors irritate airways. |  |
| 9 | You can smell germicide strongly throughout your shift. What does that suggest? | Ventilation or containment is not working; report it | Persistent odor means exposure. |  |
| 10 | Which SDS section tells you what glove material to wear? | Exposure controls and personal protection | Exposure controls lists protective equipment. |  |
| 11 | An automated reprocessor dilutes germicide in-line. Do you still need potency or presence checks? | Yes; lines kink, containers empty and pumps fail | The same proof is needed whatever the system. |  |
| 12 | Why can a weak germicide cause fever in the next patient? | Bacteria survive and multiply during storage and release endotoxin | Weak disinfection lets bacteria grow; endotoxin causes pyrogenic reactions. |  |

## Module 7: Identity and Chain of Custody

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why is a wrong-patient dialyzer serious even if it was perfectly cleaned? | It exposes the patient to another person’s blood residue and makes every test result meaningless | Identity failure exposes the patient and invalidates the history. |  |
| 2 | A nurse asks for “Santos’s dialyzer.” What do you do? | Ask for the full name and second identifier, then read back | A surname alone is not identification. |  |
| 3 | When should the label be applied? | Before the first use, while the dialyzer is sealed and the patient is present | Labeling before first use anchors the history. |  |
| 4 | A label is smudged and you cannot read the second identifier. What do you do? | Quarantine the dialyzer | Unidentified dialyzers are quarantined. |  |
| 5 | How should a dialyzer be picked from storage? | By label and two identifiers | Position and model are not identity. |  |
| 6 | What should never appear on a label that other patients can read? | The patient’s infection diagnosis | Protect privacy; use a coded marker only if the program requires one. |  |
| 7 | A dialyzer’s use count is unclear after a record error. What is the safest course? | Treat the history as broken: discard under the program and report | A broken history cannot prove eligibility. |  |
| 8 | Why does the record show who received the dialyzer at each step? | So the dialyzer can be traced and accountability is clear | Traceability depends on a named person at every hand-over. |  |
| 9 | Which practice best protects patients with similar names? | A name alert plus separate storage and two identifiers | Several layers together prevent mix-ups. |  |
| 10 | Under the United States federal rule, dialyzer reuse is limited to: | The same patient | Same-patient reuse is required. |  |
| 11 | May a label be moved from a cracked dialyzer to a new one of the same model? | No; a new dialyzer starts a new history with a new label | Labels never move between devices. |  |
| 12 | How should used dialyzers travel to the reuse room? | In a covered, leak-proof tray, separate from clean items | Transport contains blood and keeps clean and dirty apart. |  |

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why does time before processing matter? | Bacteria multiply and protein dries onto the membrane with time and warmth | Residue and bacteria make cleaning less effective and raise endotoxin. |  |
| 2 | Where do the maximum time to processing and the refrigeration rules come from? | Your procedure, following the AAMI standard and the reprocessor maker | No number on this page is a working limit. |  |
| 3 | What does reverse ultrafiltration do? | Pushes water from the dialysate side into the fibers to lift deposits from the inner wall | It cleans the inside of the fibers by backflow. |  |
| 4 | Where does clot often collect in a used dialyzer? | In the headers, at the fiber openings | Blood enters the fibers at the headers. |  |
| 5 | A dialyzer has been in a warm hallway for three hours. Your procedure’s limit is shorter. What do you do? | Follow the procedure, usually discard, and report how it happened | A dialyzer outside the time limit is not processed. |  |
| 6 | What may a different cleaning agent do to a membrane? | Change its pores, so middle-molecule clearance and albumin loss change | The HEMO data showed that technique changes membrane behavior. |  |
| 7 | A colleague suggests adding an extra bleach step to get dialyzers cleaner. What is the correct response? | Decline; only validated agents and sequences approved by the medical director are used | A stronger clean is not a better clean. |  |
| 8 | What may be stored in the used-dialyzer refrigerator? | Used dialyzers only | Mixing food, medicines or clean items invites contamination. |  |
| 9 | According to the FDA, what should happen when reprocessing or required refrigeration is not working? | Dialyzers should not be reused | Without functioning facilities, reuse stops. |  |
| 10 | Which check must be done before starting a processing run? | Procedure, reprocessor checks, water log, products and dialyzer receiving | A run on an unproven system makes every dialyzer in it unproven. |  |
| 11 | When should each cleaning step be recorded? | As it is done | Records made later from memory are not evidence. |  |
| 12 | The IFU for a dialyzer model says the headers must not be removed. What do you do? | Do not remove them; follow the IFU | The IFU sets what is allowed for that model. |  |

## Module 9: Performance Testing and Acceptance

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Baseline 100 mL, measured 85 mL. What is the retained TCV? | 85% | 85 ÷ 100 × 100 = 85%. |  |
| 2 | Baseline 100 mL, measured 79 mL, floor 80%. What is the decision on volume? | Fail | 79% is below the floor. |  |
| 3 | A dialyzer has 90% retained volume but failed its integrity test. What happens? | It fails; volume cannot compensate for a failed integrity test | Each gate is independent. |  |
| 4 | A record has no baseline TCV. What do you do? | Hold the dialyzer until the record is resolved | Without a valid baseline the result means nothing. |  |
| 5 | Measured volume is above the baseline. What is the correct response? | Flag it for review as a possible error | A value above baseline suggests an error. |  |
| 6 | What does a pressure-hold test detect? | A broken fiber or leak in the membrane | A leak lets pressure fall faster than allowed. |  |
| 7 | What did the PhilHealth quality circular set for retained TCV? | At least 80% | At least 80%, as one criterion among several. |  |
| 8 | Your colleague repeats a failed volume test four times and records only the passing result. What is wrong? | It is gaming: every result must be kept, and repeats need a defined reason | Selective recording destroys the evidence. |  |
| 9 | Several dialyzers today gave inconsistent volume readings. What should you suspect and do? | A possible equipment fault; stop and report to the biomedical technician | A pattern across dialyzers points to the machine. |  |
| 10 | Why is a catalog volume not used as the baseline? | Individual dialyzers of the same model differ, so only this dialyzer’s first measurement is valid | Each dialyzer is its own reference. |  |
| 11 | A dialyzer passes volume, integrity and inspection, but its processing record has a blank where the reprocessor run number should be. Is it ready? | No; the processing record gate is not proven | An unlinked record cannot prove the run’s water, germicide and machine checks. |  |
| 12 | A dialyzer at exactly 80% retained TCV means: | It meets the volume floor only; all other gates still apply | Meeting one floor is not release. |  |

## Module 10: Disinfect, Store, Rinse and Hand Off

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why must there be no air pockets after filling with germicide? | Germicide works only where it touches; air pockets shelter bacteria | Contact is required for disinfection. |  |
| 2 | A dialyzer was filled two hours ago. The IFU minimum contact time is longer than that. May it be used now? | No; it is not yet disinfected | The window opens only after the contact time. |  |
| 3 | Filled Monday 14:00, minimum contact 11 h (training values). What is the earliest use? | Tuesday 01:00 | 14:00 + 11 h = 01:00 the next day. |  |
| 4 | A dialyzer’s fill time is missing from its label and log. What do you do? | Hold it; without a fill time it has no proven window | No fill time, no window. |  |
| 5 | The residual strip is read two minutes late. What does the result mean? | Nothing; colors keep changing, so rinse as allowed and retest at the right time | Timing is part of the test. |  |
| 6 | A residual strip shows a faint color. What is the correct interpretation? | Doubtful, treated as failed: rinse again as allowed and retest | Doubt is not a negative. |  |
| 7 | Which strip should be used for a dialyzer disinfected with a peracetic acid mixture? | The strip validated for that germicide | Each germicide needs its own test. |  |
| 8 | What makes a second person a real second check? | Checking independently, reading the label and results themselves | Independent verification catches what one person misses. |  |
| 9 | A stored dialyzer is found with a missing cap and a damp shelf. What do you do? | Treat it as having lost its germicide and proof; reprocess or discard per procedure | Leakage breaks the proof of disinfection. |  |
| 10 | Why are processed dialyzers stored in individual labeled positions? | So they are picked by label, not location, and stay identified | Storage protects identity. |  |
| 11 | What is the purpose of the rinse before treatment? | To remove germicide before blood touches the membrane | Germicide in the blood is a chemical injury. |  |
| 12 | During handoff, the nurse and technician disagree about whether a result is acceptable. What happens? | The dialyzer is not connected; the charge nurse decides, and a new dialyzer is an option | Doubt stops connection. |  |

## Module 11: Machines, Faults and When Things Go Wrong

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A reprocessor’s pressure sensor is found reading high. What does that mean for recent integrity tests? | A leaking dialyzer may have appeared to pass; recent results cannot be trusted | Integrity depends on accurate pressure measurement. |  |
| 2 | After a fault is found, which dialyzers are in question? | Every dialyzer processed since the last proven-good check | The trace-back window starts at the last proof that the equipment was good. |  |
| 3 | Who returns a repaired reprocessor to service? | The biomedical technician, after a documented performance check | Return to service is a service decision. |  |
| 4 | Does returning the reprocessor to service release the dialyzers processed while it was faulty? | No; those dialyzers need their own decision | Repairing the machine does not prove past results. |  |
| 5 | Two patients have chills in the first hour of treatment on the same day, both with reprocessed dialyzers. What does the reuse room do? | Keep the dialyzers and lines, check the run records, hold related stored dialyzers, and report | A possible cluster needs evidence kept and records checked. |  |
| 6 | A daily check written only as “OK” is weak because: | It does not record what was checked or the reading | Evidence needs the reading. |  |
| 7 | Which task is outside the reprocessing operator’s scope? | Replacing a pressure sensor | Internal repair belongs to authorized service staff. |  |
| 8 | What does the FDA advise when reprocessing or required refrigeration is not working? | Do not reuse dialyzers | Reuse stops when the proving system is broken. |  |
| 9 | Power fails in the middle of a reprocessing cycle. What happens to the dialyzers in that cycle? | They are unproven and held | An interrupted cycle proves nothing. |  |
| 10 | During a water treatment failure, patients: | Continue treatment with new dialyzers while reuse stops | Treatment continues; reuse waits for proof. |  |
| 11 | Why does the CDC advise tracking pyrogenic reactions over time? | So a rise can be noticed and investigated | Surveillance finds clusters early. |  |
| 12 | What should a continuity plan for the reuse room say? | Where extra dialyzers come from and who decides when reuse resumes | Planning prevents unsafe improvisation. |  |

## Module 12: Records, Quality and the Capstone

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | When should a processing record be completed? | At the time, by the person who did the step | Records made later from memory are not evidence. |  |
| 2 | How do you correct an error in a paper record? | A single line through it, with the correction, date and initials | The original must stay readable. |  |
| 3 | In a month, 440 treatments used 100 dialyzers. What is the average number of uses? | 4.4 | 440 ÷ 100 = 4.4. |  |
| 4 | 2 pyrogenic reactions in 1,600 treatments is how many per 1,000 treatments? | 1.25 | 2 ÷ 1,600 × 1,000 = 1.25. |  |
| 5 | Why is a rising average use number not a quality target? | Rewarding it can lead staff to pass dialyzers that should fail | A result of good care becomes dangerous as a goal. |  |
| 6 | Average uses rose and volume failures almost disappeared, while reactions appeared. What is the best response? | Audit the records, the tests, the equipment and the reactions before drawing conclusions | Read the numbers together. |  |
| 7 | What did the improvement report from a United States unit show raised average uses safely? | Standardizing heparin and end-of-treatment rinsing on the floor | Upstream care, not looser tests. |  |
| 8 | In the capstone, RU-1104 has baseline 96 mL and measured 77 mL. What is the retained TCV? | 80.2% | 77 ÷ 96 × 100 = 80.2%, meeting the floor only. |  |

| 10 | How should germicide in a discarded dialyzer be handled? | Drained and disposed of as the SDS and waste procedure direct | Follow the SDS and the waste procedure. |  |
| 11 | What did the HEMO secondary analysis suggest about extensive reuse? | The high-flux survival advantage seen with little reuse reversed with extensive reuse | An association that argues against treating more uses as better. |  |
| 12 | You are offered a bonus if the average uses reaches 4.8. What should you do? | Raise the concern with the head nurse or medical director | Incentives tied to uses can make the room unsafe. |  |

Who decides whether he needs dialysis tonight? | The attending nephrologist, in parallel with the surgical plan | Thrombosis is a dialysis-safety problem first. The nephrologist owns the dialysis decision while the surgeon owns salvage. |  |

## Module 3: Examine and preserve the vessels

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which history is especially relevant before choosing an arm for access? | Previous central lines and implanted cardiac devices | Prior central instrumentation and device leads can obstruct outflow and change the plan. |  |
| 2 | A patient has unilateral arm swelling and a large superficial vein on the same side. What should happen? | Assess the possible outflow obstruction before committing to that arm | Superficial appearance does not resolve an outflow warning sign; image the central veins or choose the other side. |  |
| 3 | In the El Ters case-control study, a previous peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) was associated with what? | Lacking a functioning fistula, independent of vessel size and prior central catheters | The adjusted odds ratio was 2.8; the design shows association, not proof of causation in each case. |  |
| 4 | Why record a baseline hand examination before access creation? | So that a new postoperative deficit can be recognized as new | Without a baseline, a later sensory or motor deficit cannot be judged as new or old. |  |
| 5 | UKKA 2025 suggests central vein imaging before access creation in which patients? | Patients with clinical features or a high risk of central venous stenosis | Statement 2.5 (grade 2C) targets imaging to those with signs or risk factors. |  |

## Module 4: Mapping and choosing an access

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What makes a mapping report useful for access selection? | Anatomy interpreted against the planned construction and cannulation segment | The report must answer the clinical question, including whether the access can be needled. |  |
| 2 | Two mapping reports disagree about a vein’s diameter. What is the best next action? | Review images, methods and examination with the mapping team | Method (tourniquet, temperature) changes diameter; resolve consequential uncertainty first. |  |
| 3 | In the Ferring randomized trial, routine preoperative ultrasound most clearly reduced what? | Immediate fistula failure (4% versus 11%) | Immediate failure fell; assisted primary survival at one year also improved, while primary survival did not differ significantly. |  |
| 4 | UKKA 2025 statement 3.3 recommends what when a vessel is under 2.0 mm? | Counsel the patient to expect a poorer outcome | It is a counseling threshold (grade 1C), not an absolute contraindication. |  |
| 5 | Why does UKKA recommend favoring distal sites first? | To keep proximal sites available for later access | Statement 3.2 (grade 1B) preserves future options, accepting a higher primary failure rate distally. |  |

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A patient who missed dialysis arrives for elective access surgery with a high potassium and electrocardiographic changes. What is the best action? | Resolve the immediate risk with nephrology and anesthesia before elective surgery | An elective benefit does not remove an immediate physiologic threat. |  |

| 3 | In the Aitken randomized trial, what did brachial plexus block improve compared with local anesthesia? | Three-month primary patency (84% versus 62%) | The surrogate outcome of three-month primary patency improved; longer-term outcomes were not tested. |  |
| 4 | Why does regional anesthesia plausibly help a new fistula? | Sympathetic blockade dilates the artery and vein, increasing flow | Vasodilation raises early flow, which may reduce early thrombosis. |  |
| 5 | UKKA 2025 statement 3.8 suggests avoiding what during the perioperative and maturation period? | Low blood pressure, with review of medicines and target weight | Low pressure lowers fistula flow; the statement is graded 2C. |  |

# Renal Transplant Coordinator

## Module 1: The Coordinator as Navigator for Two People

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Who decides recipient medical suitability? | The authorized transplant multidisciplinary team | Best: The coordinator assembles evidence and follows through on the team decision. Why not the others: “The insurance officer”: Payment eligibility is a separate decision. “The coordinator alone”: A coordinating role does not confer independent selection authority. “The donor family”: Family preference does not establish medical suitability. |  |
| 2 | A donor asks to withdraw privately. What comes first? | Protect privacy and arrange the donor support pathway | Best: Voluntary donation requires a safe way to withdraw. Why not the others: “Ask the recipient to persuade the donor”: This introduces pressure. “Disclose the reason to the family”: The reason is confidential unless lawful disclosure applies. “Delete the donor file”: The clinical record must remain accurate and retained appropriately. |  |
| 3 | What proves a barrier is closed? | Documented completion confirmed by the responsible service | Best: A referral sent is different from a service completed. Why not the others: “An unanswered email”: Sending does not confirm receipt or action. “A family assumption”: Assumptions cannot replace evidence. “A green dashboard chosen manually”: Status needs auditable supporting evidence. |  |
| 4 | Can the same title automatically confer donor advocate authority? | No; verify the Philippine definition, qualifications and designation | Best: The functions and conflicts of interest require explicit review. Why not the others: “Yes, all coordinators are advocates”: Job titles are insufficient. “Yes, after this quiz”: Self-study does not confer a regulated function. “Yes, if the recipient agrees”: Recipient agreement cannot waive donor safeguards. |  |
| 5 | Which navigation register entry is most useful? | Barrier, owner, due date, next action and closure evidence | Best: These fields support accountable follow-through. Why not the others: “Patient name alone”: Identity is necessary but not a workflow. “A list of completed tests only”: Open decisions and barriers would disappear. “Estimated surgery date only”: An estimate does not show readiness. |  |
| 6 | A cluster randomized trial gave dialysis patients trained transplant-recipient navigators. What did it show? | Navigated patients completed more transplant-process steps (3.5 vs 1.6) | Best: the trial measured process steps, and navigated patients completed about twice as many. Not shown: more transplants or lower mortality; those were not its outcomes. “No difference” is wrong for the primary outcome. |  |
| 7 | A barrier row reads “Cardiology referral sent March 3.” Today is March 20 and no appointment exists. What is its status? | Open and overdue; confirm receipt and escalate to the named owner | Best: a sent referral is not a completed service, and 17 days without an appointment is overdue. Sending, a family promise, or deletion all leave the barrier unresolved and unaudited. |  |
| 8 | The recipient’s sister asks you, “Did my brother pass his donor tests?” The donor has not authorized sharing. You say: | “I can only share his information with his permission. I can tell you what happens next for your sister.” | Best: the donor’s results belong to the donor; you redirect to what you may share. Confirming, hinting, or sending her to read his file all breach his confidentiality. |  |
| 9 | Which SBAR request is most useful to a transplant nephrologist? | “Please decide by Friday whether the expired chest X-ray must be repeated before the case conference.” | Best: a specific decision, an owner, and a time. “FYI” asks for nothing; ordering a test yourself is outside coordination scope; family wishes are context, not a request. |  |
| 10 | In the large US registry study by Wolfe and colleagues, how did death risk after transplant compare with remaining wait-listed? | Higher in the first two weeks, much lower by 18 months | Best: early surgical risk is real (relative risk 2.8 in the first two weeks), then risk falls well below the wait-listed group (0.32 at 18 months). The study was observational, so selection may explain part of it. |  |

## Module 2: Philippine Regulation and Professional Scope

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which source determines a hospital’s current transplant authorization? | Its current DOH authorization and applicable HFSRB requirements | Best: Facility authority must be verified with the regulator. Why not the others: “A course completion page”: Education cannot license a hospital. “A job advertisement”: An advertisement is employer evidence only. “A physician’s social media post”: This is not regulatory authorization. |  |
| 2 | How should the 2015 60-hour criterion be described? | Historical criteria requiring current applicability verification | Best: The later surveyed tools and rules must be reconciled. Why not the others: “Guaranteed current universal minimum”: This was not verified. “Proof that any graduate may prescribe”: Training hours do not confer prescribing authority. “An ABTC requirement”: ABTC has separate experience and examination rules. |  |
| 3 | Does PSN guidance replace PhilHealth package rules? | No; clinical guidance and payment rules serve different purposes | Best: Both may apply to the same case. Why not the others: “Yes, all society guidance overrides payers”: The authorities differ. “Only if the patient requests it”: Patient preference cannot change payer rules. “Only for living donors”: Donor type does not merge the authorities. |  |
| 4 | What should a new revision trigger? | A dated comparison and impact review before workflow changes | Best: Effective dates and transitions affect real cases. Why not the others: “Immediate deletion of all older forms”: Legacy cases may still require them. “Automatic denial of pending cases”: Transition rules must first be applied. “No action until an audit”: Delayed review risks incorrect workflows. |  |
| 5 | A task exceeds the coordinator’s authorized scope. What next? | Escalate to the authorized professional and document the handoff | Best: Navigation includes obtaining the right decision maker. Why not the others: “Do it if staffing is short”: Workload does not create authority. “Ask the family to sign a waiver”: A waiver does not expand scope. “Copy a previous order”: Prior orders do not authorize a new decision. |  |
| 6 | PhilHealth Circular 2026-0019 was published November 21, 2026 and takes effect 15 days after publication. On November 25, 2026 it is best described as: | Published but not yet effective | Best: publication starts the 15-day clock; on November 25 it has not run out. It is not a draft, and nothing limits it to deceased donors. Confirm the formal effective date before applying it. |  |
| 7 | A recipient was pre-authorized and transplanted under PC 2024-0035. Revision 1 takes effect before the claim is filed. Which policy governs the claim? | PC 2024-0035, under the legacy-case rule | Best: Revision 1 states that cases pre-authorized and performed under PC 2024-0035 are claimed under it. Newer is not automatically governing; neither payment size nor hospital preference decides. |  |
| 8 | Each contracted facility must have at least one Z Benefits Coordinator. How many Z packages may one coordinator handle? | At most three | Best: the PhilHealth rule caps each coordinator at three Z Benefits packages. The other numbers are not in the circular. |  |
| 9 | A job posting asks for a registered nurse with three years of experience. This is best understood as: | An employer’s hiring requirement, not a national legal minimum | Best: a posting states what one employer wants. It is not a DOH rule, a PhilHealth condition, or a society credential. |  |
| 10 | A support-path Z Benefits coordinator is asked by a busy resident to “just explain the consent form and get the donor to sign.” You: | Decline; surgical consent is obtained by the surgeon under the living-donor order, and offer to arrange the meeting | Best: under AO 2021-0059 the surgeon obtains donor consent with independent witnessing. Donor agreement does not transfer that duty, and the recipient is never the right witness. |  |

## Module 3: Referral, Intake, and Equitable Access

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What does referral establish? | The need for a transplant evaluation | Best: Selection follows multidisciplinary assessment. Why not the others: “Guaranteed surgery”: No evaluation outcome is guaranteed. “Guaranteed insurance payment”: Payer criteria remain separate. “Donor consent”: Donor consent is a separate process. |  |
| 2 | A missed visit follows a transport failure. What is appropriate? | Identify and address the access barrier | Best: A single event does not establish unwillingness to engage. Why not the others: “Close the file as nonadherent”: This ignores the documented barrier. “Exclude the patient from all future referral”: This is inequitable and outside scope. “Require a donor before rescheduling”: Evaluation does not require such a blanket rule. |  |
