| 3 | What is a closed-loop referral? | Receipt, responsible service and next action are confirmed | Best: Communication must reach an accountable recipient. Why not the others: “A referral fax sent once”: Transmission alone is insufficient. “A patient told to call around”: This transfers the entire navigation burden. “A note with no recipient”: There is no accountable handoff. |  |
| 4 | What should orientation include? | Benefits, risks, alternatives and uncertainty | Best: Balanced information supports informed choices. Why not the others: “Only successful transplant stories”: This hides risks and alternatives. “A promise of a short wait”: Organ availability is uncertain. “A request to recruit strangers online”: Unscreened donor recruitment raises serious ethical issues. |  |
| 5 | A patient reports severe breathlessness during intake. What next? | Activate urgent clinical assessment through the local emergency pathway | Best: Potentially serious symptoms take priority. Why not the others: “Finish the financial form first”: Administrative tasks must not delay care. “Schedule a routine visit next month”: This may be unsafe. “Offer an independent medicine adjustment”: The coordinator must remain within authority. |  |
| 6 | KDIGO 2020 advises referring potential candidates for transplant evaluation: | At least 6 to 12 months before expected dialysis | Best: early referral allows donor evaluation and a possible pre-emptive transplant. Waiting for dialysis, a donor, or a payer approval delays everything. |  |
| 7 | In the House Calls trial, home education that included the family most clearly increased: | Living donor inquiries and evaluations | Best: inquiries (82% vs 61% vs 47%) and evaluations rose. The difference in transplants (15% vs 8% vs 6%) was not statistically significant. Survival was not measured. |  |
| 8 | A referral arrives without a working phone number. The best first step is: | Contact the referring unit the same day to confirm contact details and preferred language | Best: the loop closes through the referrer. Waiting loses people, rejecting is unfair, and social media breaches privacy. |  |
| 9 | Which intake question best uncovers an access barrier? | “What would make it hard for you to come to appointments here?” | Best: open, neutral, and practical. The others are leading or shaming and invite a yes. |  |
| 10 | A referral was faxed on May 2. On May 16 the clinic has no record of it. What happened to the loop? | It was never closed; dispatch is not receipt | Best: a referral closes only when the receiving service acknowledges it. Sending, telling the patient, or time passing confirms nothing. |  |

## Module 4: Recipient Workup and Multidisciplinary Decisions

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A test result has arrived. Is the workup item complete? | Only after the required clinical review and actions are confirmed | Best: Receipt does not establish a clinical decision. Why not the others: “Yes, arrival always means clearance”: An abnormal report may need action. “Yes, if the family has paid”: Payment cannot clear clinical risk. “Yes, if it is uploaded”: Storage is not clinical review. |  |
| 2 | Who defines additional cardiac testing? | The responsible clinical team | Best: The coordinator facilitates the authorized plan. Why not the others: “An automated completion tracker”: A tracker is not a clinician. “The patient’s employer”: Employment does not determine testing. “A generic course list alone”: Testing must be individualized. |  |
| 3 | What does a good deferral plan contain? | Required actions, owners and review timing | Best: Deferral should lead to a navigable plan. Why not the others: “A red label alone”: No next step is defined. “An indefinite silence”: This leaves the patient without guidance. “Automatic permanent exclusion”: Deferral differs from permanent decline. |  |
| 4 | What belongs in an MDT summary? | Dated relevant findings and unresolved questions | Best: The team needs concise traceable evidence. Why not the others: “Every unfiltered duplicated page”: Unstructured volume obscures key issues. “Only favorable results”: Selective reporting risks harm. “A coordinator’s guarantee of suitability”: Suitability is a team decision. |  |
| 5 | Approved evaluation means automatic active listing. True? | No; confirm the separate authorized listing process | Best: National listing and local evaluation are separate gates. Why not the others: “Yes, always”: The processes are distinct. “Yes, when a donor is present”: A donor does not create listing status. “Yes, after insurance enrollment”: Payer enrollment is another distinct process. |  |
| 6 | Why organize the recipient workup by question rather than by test list? | Each question has an owner who must answer it, so nothing is mistaken for clearance | Best: a normal test does not answer a question until its owner reviews it. The method does not cut tests, grant authority, or follow a payer rule. |  |
| 7 | A stress test was done 14 months ago; the program’s protocol accepts 12 months. The case conference is next week. You: | Flag it as expired and ask the transplant physician whether to repeat it | Best: you flag; the physician decides. Presenting it as current misleads, ordering is outside scope, and hiding it removes information. |  |
| 8 | KDIGO 2020 asks programs to assess adherence and its barriers before transplant because: | Medicine-taking problems after transplant are common and linked to graft loss | Best: barriers found early can be addressed. It does not mandate refusal, replace psychosocial assessment, or come from PhilHealth. |  |
| 9 | The team defers a candidate until a dental infection is treated. The most accurate message is: | “The team wants this treated first; here is the next step and when we will review again.” | Best: deferral with a reason, a next step, and a review date. “Rejected” is false, “paperwork” hides a medical reason, and a guarantee is a promise nobody can make. |  |
| 10 | A one-page case-conference summary should open with: | The decision the team is asked to make | Best: a summary is built around the decision. Addresses add privacy risk, raw lists bury the question, and suitability is the team’s call. |  |

## Module 5: Compatibility and Safe Specimen Coordination

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Matching ABO blood groups proves full compatibility. True? | No; immunologic assessment includes other evidence | Best: HLA antibodies and crossmatch may change risk. Why not the others: “Yes, all other tests are optional”: This ignores other immunologic risks. “Yes, if donor and recipient are siblings”: Relationship does not guarantee compatibility. “Yes, if insurance approves”: Payment approval does not establish compatibility. |  |
| 2 | A tube lacks required identifiers. What next? | Follow the laboratory rejection and recollection process | Best: Specimen identity cannot safely be guessed. Why not the others: “Add identifiers from memory”: This may misattribute a sample. “Use a room number alone”: Room numbers are not reliable person identifiers. “Hide the error to avoid delay”: Concealment removes a safety barrier. |  |
| 3 | A transfusion occurred after the last sample. What should the coordinator do? | Notify the team and check specimen requirements | Best: Sensitizing events can affect evaluation requirements. Why not the others: “Assume the old sample remains valid”: The team and laboratory must decide. “Diagnose rejection”: This is not a diagnosis of rejection. “Cancel candidacy permanently”: That is not the coordinator’s decision. |  |
| 4 | A crossmatch report is equivocal. Who resolves its significance? | The authorized transplant and laboratory specialists | Best: The result needs specialist interpretation. Why not the others: “The courier”: Transport staff cannot interpret it. “The insurance liaison”: Payer staff do not resolve clinical meaning. “A color code chosen by the coordinator”: A status color cannot replace interpretation. |  |
| 5 | Which report should guide the final readiness review? | The verified current final report for the correct pair | Best: Version and identity both matter. Why not the others: “The first screenshot found”: It may be preliminary or outdated. “A family recollection”: Memory is not source documentation. “A report from a different donor”: Pair-specific evidence is required. |  |
| 6 | A recipient received two units of blood during a hospital stay last week. Why must the transplant team and HLA laboratory know? | Transfusion can create new HLA antibodies that change compatibility | Best: transfusion, pregnancy, and prior transplant are sensitizing events. Blood group does not change, waiting time is unaffected, and it is a safety matter, not billing. |  |
| 7 | A crossmatch sample is labeled with name only. The courier is waiting. You: | Do not send it; have it re-collected and labeled with two identifiers | Best: an incompletely labeled sample is rejected, not repaired. Adding identifiers after the fact or delegating labeling breaks the chain. |  |
| 8 | The laboratory calls with a “positive crossmatch” result. Your role is to: | Relay it at once, with read-back, to the transplant physician and record the handoff | Best: route a critical result immediately with read-back. Interpreting or announcing decisions is the team’s role; waiting delays a safety-relevant result. |  |
| 9 | What does a high calculated panel reactive antibody (cPRA) mean in plain words? | The person has antibodies against a large share of potential donors | Best: cPRA estimates how many donors a candidate would likely react against. It says nothing about blood group, infection, or age. |  |
| 10 | ABO compatibility follows the same rule as blood transfusion. A group O recipient can usually receive a standard kidney from a donor of group: | O | Best: group O recipients carry anti-A and anti-B antibodies, so a standard transplant uses a group O donor. Other groups need a specialized incompatible program decided by the team. |  |

## Module 6: Living Donor Intake and Protection

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Does relatedness remove the need to assess coercion? | No; family pressure can also compromise choice | Best: Voluntariness must be assessed in every donor. Why not the others: “Yes, relatives are exempt”: The DOH ethical safeguards cover related donors too. “Only siblings are exempt”: No such exemption is established here. “Only if the family signs”: A signature cannot replace a free choice. |  |
| 2 | Which donor age appears in the inspected AO 2021-0059? | 21 years or above | Best: Use the Philippine rule and verify subsequent changes. Why not the others: “18 in every country”: International thresholds are not interchangeable. “Any age with parental permission”: This does not satisfy the cited Philippine living-donor provision. “No age criterion”: The order expressly includes one. |  |
| 3 | Debt cancellation linked to donation should trigger what? | A hold and ethics/safeguarding review | Best: A financial inducement concern must be examined. Why not the others: “Routine scheduling”: The concern is unresolved. “An informal promise to ignore it”: Concealment undermines safeguards. “A larger family payment”: This compounds the concern. |  |
| 4 | Who should answer questions about the donor’s own wishes? | The donor privately with appropriate communication support | Best: Private discussion reduces external influence. Why not the others: “Only the recipient”: The interests are distinct. “Only the employer”: The employer may be a source of pressure. “The oldest family member”: Family hierarchy does not replace donor autonomy. |  |
| 5 | What should the coordinator record about suspected coercion? | Factual statements and actions in the restricted record | Best: Accurate facts support appropriate specialist review. Why not the others: “An unverified criminal label”: Do not replace assessment with accusations. “Nothing until proven in court”: Safety concerns need timely escalation. “A public social-media warning”: This exposes private information and may harm the people involved. |  |
| 6 | Under DOH AO 2021-0059, a potential living donor must be at least: | 21 years old | Best: the order sets 21 or older. Do not import foreign thresholds; verify the current text. |  |
| 7 | Which statement is a red flag for inducement? | “His employer will cancel my debt after the operation.” | Best: a promised benefit tied to donation is a potential reward and must be routed for review. Love, fear, and needing time are normal and deserve support. |  |
| 8 | A donor wants to withdraw but fears the family’s reaction. The safest approach is to: | Agree with the donor and the donor team on neutral wording, such as “the team cannot proceed with this donor,” without inventing a diagnosis | Best: neutral, truthful wording protects privacy. Disclosure breaches confidentiality, a false diagnosis is dishonest and may follow the donor, and persuasion is pressure. |  |
| 9 | Which person should not double as the donor’s designated advocate? | The recipient’s coordinator who is managing the recipient’s case | Best: the recipient’s coordinator has a conflict of interest. The other options describe what an advocate should be. |  |
| 10 | A systematic review of living donor costs found that most donors: | Had some financial loss, with lost income the largest share | Best: about 80% had financial loss in 16 studies. Full reimbursement, earning money, or no travel cost do not match the data. |  |

## Module 7: Donor Medical Evaluation and Long-Term Risk

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Normal creatinine guarantees donor safety. True? | No; suitability requires integrated risk assessment | Best: Kidney function and other risks need specialist evaluation. Why not the others: “Yes, it is the only necessary test”: This ignores multiple risk domains. “Yes, if the donor feels healthy”: Symptoms do not exclude hidden risk. “Yes, if related”: Relatedness does not prove safety. |  |
| 2 | Who explains individualized lifetime risk? | The qualified donor clinical team | Best: The coordinator ensures access and understanding. Why not the others: “The insurance agent alone”: Coverage does not determine medical risk. “The recipient alone”: The donor needs independent clinical information. “An unvalidated web score alone”: A calculator cannot replace full assessment. |  |
| 3 | When should follow-up arrangements be planned? | Before donation | Best: The donor needs a feasible continuity plan. Why not the others: “Only if a complication occurs”: Routine long-term monitoring is also needed. “After insurance ends”: That creates an avoidable gap. “Never if the donor is healthy”: Donation does not remove the need for follow-up. |  |
| 4 | A donor has an incidental abnormal result. What next? | Arrange authorized review and appropriate donor care | Best: The donor’s own health matters regardless of donation. Why not the others: “Hide it from the donor”: This undermines informed care. “Tell the recipient every detail”: Private information requires lawful limits. “Ignore it if surgery is near”: Timing does not negate the finding. |  |
| 5 | Does medical suitability replace HTEC review? | No; separate gates must be completed | Best: Clinical and ethics review answer different questions. Why not the others: “Yes, for relatives”: Relatedness does not remove the safeguards. “Yes, after payment”: Payment cannot establish ethical approval. “Yes, with a normal scan”: Anatomic findings are not ethics clearance. |  |
| 6 | In US national data, surgical mortality after living kidney donation was about: | 3 per 10,000 donors | Best: 3.1 per 10,000 (95% CI 2.0 to 4.6). Rare but not zero; the other numbers are off by orders of magnitude. |  |
| 7 | Muzaale and colleagues estimated 15-year kidney failure risk of 30.8 per 10,000 donors vs 3.9 per 10,000 matched healthy nondonors. The absolute difference is about: | 27 per 10,000 | Best: 30.8 minus 3.9 is about 27 more cases per 10,000 donors over 15 years. “8 times” is the relative ratio, not an absolute difference. |  |
| 8 | The donor kidney failure risk calculator on this site is for: | The clinician to estimate risk; the coordinator collects inputs and routes questions | Best: risk estimation informs a clinical decision made by the team. It does not clear donors or price benefits. |  |
| 9 | In a national US study, how common were perioperative complications after donor nephrectomy? | About 1 in 6 had any complication; about 1 in 40 had a major (grade IV or higher) one | Best: 16.8% any and 2.5% grade IV or higher. The other choices understate, overstate, or misplace the risk. |  |
| 10 | A donor asks, “Am I safe for life?” The most honest answer is: | “Most donors do well; the risk is small but real, and we will check your health every year.” | Best: calibrated, true, and paired with follow-up. Zero risk is false, certain harm is false, and ignorance is false. |  |

## Module 8: Legal Documents and Informed Consent

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What resolves inconsistent identity documents? | The authorized verification or correction process | Best: Source documents must remain authentic and traceable. Why not the others: “Editing the scanned certificate”: This falsifies source evidence. “Using whichever name is shorter”: Convenience does not resolve identity. “Ignoring the mismatch”: An unresolved discrepancy remains a safety and legal concern. |  |
| 2 | Who obtains donor surgical informed consent under the cited DOH order? | The surgeon | Best: The coordinator facilitates and checks the process. Why not the others: “The insurance clerk”: Insurance work does not confer this authority. “The recipient”: The recipient cannot obtain consent on the surgeon’s behalf. “A quiz application”: Educational software cannot conduct the required process. |  |
| 3 | A signed form proves valid informed consent by itself. True? | No; understanding, voluntariness and the required process matter | Best: Documentation records a process rather than replacing it. Why not the others: “Yes, regardless of language”: Unreadable information may not be understood. “Yes, even after withdrawal”: A donor may withdraw before donation. “Yes, if paid for”: Payment does not validate consent. |  |
| 4 | A foreign paired-exchange pathway is offered online. What next? | Obtain current Philippine legal and ethics review before any action | Best: Jurisdiction-specific permission cannot be assumed. Why not the others: “Enroll immediately”: Foreign programs do not override local requirements. “Promise reimbursement”: Coverage is unverified. “Use a different donor identity”: This would be false documentation. |  |
| 5 | What supports an accessible consent discussion? | Qualified interpretation, reflection time and teach-back | Best: Understanding must be assessed in a suitable language. Why not the others: “A hurried signature”: Speed does not establish understanding. “Only an English form”: Language must meet the person’s needs. “The recipient answering every question”: The donor’s own understanding must be heard. |  |
| 6 | A photocopied birth certificate is used to prove a sibling relationship. Before it enters the packet you should: | Verify it against the issuing source or an authenticated copy through the authorized channel | Best: authenticity is verified at the source. Appearance, a family signature, or retyping verify nothing. |  |
| 7 | Under the living-donor order, who obtains the donor’s surgical consent? | The surgeon, with the specified independent witnessing | Best: the surgeon obtains consent, with independent witnessing. Coordinators prepare and support; they do not obtain surgical consent. |  |
| 8 | A donor understands Kapampangan best and reads little English. Consent should be supported by: | A qualified interpreter not related to the recipient, and teach-back | Best: independent interpretation plus teach-back tests understanding. The recipient has a conflict, an unread form is not consent, and shortening removes information. |  |
| 9 | You notice a typo in the donor’s middle name on a notarized affidavit. You: | Route it for a properly executed correction and keep the correction trail | Best: corrections follow the legal route and stay traceable. Altering a notarized document yourself invalidates it; ignoring it may stop the case later. |  |
| 10 | Consent is best described as: | A process that continues until surgery, with the right to withdraw | Best: understanding is checked and choice remains open until surgery. One signature, permanence, and family consent all misdescribe it. |  |

## Module 9: Ethics Committee Navigation and Safeguarding

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What should a coordinator do with missing ethics evidence? | Label it missing and obtain the required review or document | Best: An honest status supports a valid decision. Why not the others: “Mark it complete to secure a slot”: This misrepresents readiness. “Borrow another donor’s report”: Evidence must be person-specific. “Backdate the missing report”: Backdating falsifies the record. |  |
| 2 | Should donor answers be coached to match the recipient? | No; arrange independent honest assessment | Best: Coaching undermines voluntariness review. Why not the others: “Yes, to reduce delays”: Speed cannot justify misrepresentation. “Yes, if relatives agree”: Agreement does not remove coercion risk. “Only for an insured case”: Insurance does not change ethics standards. |  |
| 3 | Who resolves an ethics approval condition? | The responsible service and authorized committee process | Best: Closure must satisfy the actual condition. Why not the others: “The coordinator by deleting it”: Deletion does not resolve it. “The operating-room scheduler”: Scheduling staff do not approve ethics conditions. “An online vote”: Committee governance cannot be replaced by public opinion. |  |
| 4 | A credible reward concern arises after approval. What next? | Escalate and seek reassessment before elective progression | Best: Changed circumstances may invalidate prior assumptions. Why not the others: “Ignore it because approval exists”: Earlier review does not cover undisclosed changes automatically. “Ask the family to keep quiet”: Concealment compounds risk. “Collect a private fee”: This creates further conflict. |  |
| 5 | Does an expiring surgery slot override ethics review? | No | Best: Time pressure does not remove donor protections. Why not the others: “Yes, if the recipient is distressed”: Distress requires support, not bypass. “Yes, after insurance authorization”: Payment approval is separate. “Yes, after a family waiver”: A waiver cannot replace the required review. |  |
| 6 | Under Philippine law, recruiting or obtaining a person by coercion or deceit for the removal or sale of organs is: | Trafficking in persons under RA 9208 as amended | Best: removal or sale of organs is an exploitative purpose under the anti-trafficking law. Consent obtained by coercion or deceit is not a defense. |  |
| 7 | You suspect a donor is being paid. Your first action is to: | Record facts in the restricted record and escalate through the safeguarding pathway and the ethics committee | Best: document and escalate. Confronting, investigating alone, or canceling exceed your role and may put the donor at risk. |  |
| 8 | A complete ethics committee submission should include: | The question for decision, the relationship evidence, advocate and psychosocial reports, and open concerns | Best: the committee needs the question and the evidence, including concerns. A lone form, the recipient’s history alone, or a push to approve does not support a real decision. |  |
| 9 | The committee approves with a condition: a second psychiatric review. The case may proceed to surgery when: | The condition is completed, documented, and accepted by the committee or its delegate | Best: a conditional approval is open until the condition closes. A date, family agreement, or payer approval do not close it. |  |
| 10 | The Declaration of Istanbul (2018 edition) is best described as: | An international professional statement against organ trafficking and transplant tourism | Best: it guides professional ethics. It is not Philippine law, a payer rule, or a US policy, though Philippine law reaches many of the same acts. |  |

## Module 10: PhilHealth and Other Payers

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Does medical approval guarantee insurance approval? | No; the criteria and decision makers differ | Best: Both gates must be tracked. Why not the others: “Yes, in every case”: Clinical and payer decisions are separate. “Yes, after HTEC approval”: Ethics review does not determine coverage. “Yes, for living donors”: Donor services also have defined pathways. |  |
| 2 | How should a form be identified? | By package, title, policy version and annex designation | Best: Annex letters can change between versions. Why not the others: “By annex letter alone”: The same letter may mean a different form. “By file color”: Appearance is not version control. “By the family’s recollection”: Use the verified source document. |  |
| 3 | A procedure date changes across a policy transition. What next? | Obtain a payer review of the applicable transition rules | Best: Dates can affect the governing process. Why not the others: “Assume every old rule remains”: This may be incorrect. “Assume every new rule applies retroactively”: Legacy-case provisions may apply. “Discard the prior authorization”: Preserve evidence until an authorized decision is made. |  |
| 4 | Which is the safest coverage statement? | These services are confirmed; these items await payer verification | Best: It separates evidence from uncertainty. Why not the others: “Everything will be free forever”: This is an unsupported guarantee. “Donor costs are always the recipient’s private problem”: DOH protections require review. “Insurance will decide medical suitability”: Medical selection remains clinical. |  |
| 5 | Where should changing benefit amounts live in the website? | A dated verified policy table with authoritative links | Best: Centralization reduces inconsistent updates. Why not the others: “Hard-coded in every case”: Duplication makes updates error-prone. “In an unreferenced calculator”: Users cannot verify the rule. “Only in a hero image”: Images are difficult to maintain and access. |  |
| 6 | Under PhilHealth’s kidney transplant package, an approved pre-authorization is valid for: | 180 calendar days | Best: 180 calendar days. Track the expiry; surgery after it needs a new or extended authorization as the circular allows. |  |
| 7 | Pre-authorization approved March 1. Planned surgery September 15. What should you do? | Flag that surgery falls after the 180-day validity and plan the renewal step now | Best: March 1 plus 180 days is August 28, before September 15. Flag early. Rescheduling is not your decision, and the benefit is not automatically lost. |  |
| 8 | For a deceased-donor transplant, the pre-authorization request is submitted: | Within 2 working days after the procedure | Best: the circular sets two working days after the procedure for deceased donors, because the timing cannot be planned. |  |
| 9 | The facility estimate is PHP 1,200,000 for a living-donor transplant with laparoscopic donor surgery and basiliximab induction (package Z025A1, PHP 993,000). Before other assistance, the estimated gap is: | PHP 207,000 | Best: 1,200,000 minus 993,000 equals 207,000. Then add confirmed assistance and check what the package actually covers for this case. |  |
| 10 | Which statement about the post-transplant packages is correct? | They cover immunosuppressants, tests, and living donor monitoring after transplant | Best: post-KT packages (adult and pediatric circulars) cover continuing care, including donor monitoring. The operation is the separate kidney transplant package. |  |

## Module 11: Claims Evidence, Denials, and Financial Protection

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How should a date mismatch be corrected? | Verify source evidence and use an auditable correction process | Best: The original record and correction history must remain traceable. Why not the others: “Rewrite the operative record to fit the claim”: This risks falsification. “Submit both dates without explanation”: The discrepancy remains unresolved. “Ask the patient to choose a date”: Care facts are not a preference. |  |
| 2 | A payer notice is unclear. What next? | Clarify its category, reason and required action with the liaison | Best: The notice determines the response pathway. Why not the others: “Assume it is permanent denial”: A technical return may be remediable. “Ignore it until the patient complains”: Deadlines may be missed. “Alter the diagnosis”: Coding must reflect actual care. |  |
| 3 | Medicine will run out while a claim is pending. What takes priority? | Urgent clinical/pharmacy/social-work continuity planning | Best: Administrative resolution and clinical safety proceed together. Why not the others: “Wait for reimbursement before informing anyone”: This hides a foreseeable risk. “Advise dose rationing independently”: The coordinator must not alter treatment. “Tell the patient to stop attending”: This undermines continuity. |  |
| 4 | What makes a claim auditable? | Traceable authorization, services, records and submission history | Best: The claim must be supported by actual care. Why not the others: “A complete-looking form without sources”: Appearance is not evidence. “Copied signatures”: Signatures require proper authorization. “A deleted prior submission”: Removing history weakens traceability. |  |
| 5 | How should donor bills be handled? | Review against donor protections and confirmed funding responsibilities | Best: Payer limits alone do not settle all institutional obligations. Why not the others: “Charge automatically if a claim is delayed”: Delay does not remove protections. “Hide the bill”: The issue needs accountable resolution. “Ask the donor to sell another asset immediately”: This bypasses financial review and may worsen harm. |  |
| 6 | A recipient is discharged on July 1. The facility’s claim filing deadline under the package is: | August 30 (60 days after discharge) | Best: July 1 plus 60 days is August 30. Late filing is a stated ground for denial. |  |
| 7 | Which is a stated ground for denial of the kidney transplant claim? | Missing KT registry registration or form | Best: registry noncompliance is listed with late filing, missing mandatory services, and inconsistent data. The others are not denial grounds. |  |
| 8 | A claim comes back asking for a corrected form. This is: | A return to be corrected and resubmitted within the allowed time | Best: a return is fixable; a denial is a decision with an appeal route. Neither is ever a reason to bill the donor. |  |
| 9 | Under DOH AO 2021-0059, the transplant facility may charge the donor for donation-related medical care: | No | Best: donation-related medical expenses, donor care, and follow-up must not be charged to the donor by the facility. A signature does not change that. |  |
| 10 | In a Canadian prospective cohort, what share of donors had total costs above CAD 5,500? | About 25% | Best: 205 of 821 (25%). Costs were concentrated in a minority, which is why screening each donor’s situation matters. |  |

## Module 12: The Waiting List and Deceased Donation

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Does payer registry enrollment establish national waiting-list status? | No; verify each system separately | Best: Their purposes and entry processes differ. Why not the others: “Yes, automatically”: This conflates systems. “Yes, if the claim is paid”: Payment does not determine national listing. “Only for adults”: Age does not make the systems identical. |  |
| 2 | Who certifies death for donation? | Appropriately authorized physicians under current law and protocol | Best: The coordinator facilitates but does not certify. Why not the others: “Any coordinator after this course”: Self-study does not confer that authority. “The recipient’s family”: A family cannot diagnose death. “The payer”: Insurance has no such role. |  |
| 3 | A waiting candidate develops a new infection. What next? | Prompt clinical review and authorized status update if indicated | Best: Health changes may affect readiness. Why not the others: “Keep it off the record”: Concealment threatens safety. “Remove the patient permanently alone”: The coordinator cannot make that decision. “Assume the previous clearance remains enough”: New information requires review. |  |
| 4 | What should be promised about allocation? | An explanation of the approved process, without guaranteed priority | Best: Allocation is governed by authorized rules. Why not the others: “Priority for whoever pays fastest”: Ability to pay is not an ethical personal allocation rule. “A fixed transplant date”: Organ availability is uncertain. “An organ from a named stranger online”: Unverified donor promises are inappropriate. |  |
| 5 | What closes a listing transfer? | Accepted handoff and reconciled status in the relevant systems | Best: A sent request alone does not finish transfer. Why not the others: “The patient leaving the city”: Travel is not registry reconciliation. “A new clinic appointment only”: Listing status still needs checking. “Deleting the old record”: Records require an authorized traceable process. |  |
| 6 | Being registered in the PhilHealth KT Data Registry means: | A payer registry requirement is met; it is not the national waiting list | Best: the payer registry and the national waiting list are separate. Neither guarantees an offer, and registry entry is not pre-authorization. |  |
| 7 | From May 1, 2026, PhilHealth Advisory 2026-0026 requires KT registry registration for: | All patients pre-authorized for the kidney transplant package | Best: all pre-authorized patients, through the electronic system. Manual forms were accepted until April 30, 2026. |  |
| 8 | A wait-listed candidate moves to Cebu and changes phone numbers. Why does it matter? | An offer can be missed if the program cannot reach the candidate quickly | Best: offers are time-critical. Contact details do not change biology, listing status, or the package. |  |
| 9 | Who declares death before deceased organ donation? | Physicians authorized under the law and hospital protocol | Best: death determination is a medical act by authorized physicians, separate from the transplant team. Coordinators never do it. |  |
| 10 | The Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI) and Estimated Post-Transplant Survival (EPTS) scores on this site are: | US allocation tools shown for comparison, not Philippine allocation rules | Best: they come from US policy. Philippine allocation follows its own rules; coordinators do not accept offers on a score. |  |

## Module 13: Organ Offer Calls and Retrieval Logistics

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Who accepts an organ offer clinically? | The authorized transplant clinician or team | Best: The coordinator relays and documents the decision. Why not the others: “The courier”: Transport staff do not decide clinical acceptance. “The patient’s employer”: Employment is irrelevant to clinical acceptance. “The coordinator solely because the OR is ready”: Readiness does not confer decision authority. |  |
| 2 | An identifier differs by one digit. What next? | Hold and reconcile through the authorized OPO/team process | Best: Small discrepancies can represent different donors. Why not the others: “Correct it by guessing”: Guessing risks wrong-organ events. “Trust the courier’s memory”: Independent verified evidence is needed. “Remove the label”: This destroys traceability. |  |
| 3 | Why use read-back? | To confirm critical information was heard correctly | Best: Closed-loop communication reduces transcription errors. Why not the others: “To replace the original record”: The original evidence remains necessary. “To delay every offer”: Its purpose is accuracy, not delay. “To establish payment eligibility”: That is a separate process. |  |
| 4 | Weather delays retrieval transport. What should happen? | Activate the agreed contingency and inform the decision-making team | Best: Clinical decisions may depend on updated timing. Why not the others: “Hide the delay”: The team needs accurate information. “Invent a shorter transport time”: False records undermine safety. “Guarantee the organ will remain suitable”: Suitability requires specialist assessment. |  |
| 5 | What should a canceled offer trigger? | Clear patient communication, continuing care and a documented debrief | Best: Cancellation still needs coordinated support. Why not the others: “Automatic permanent delisting”: Cancellation does not imply permanent ineligibility. “Blame directed at the donor family”: This is harmful and inappropriate. “Deletion of the offer log”: The record is needed for care and quality review. |  |
| 6 | During an offer call the caller says blood group “A.” Your form says the candidate is group O. You: | Stop, read back, and escalate the discrepancy to the transplant physician at once | Best: a blood-group discrepancy is a safety event. Assuming, editing, or deferring the check can lead to a wrong-organ transplant. |  |
| 7 | The core of a safe offer call is: | A structured script with read-back of identifiers, blood group, and times | Best: structure and read-back catch errors. Memory and loose notes fail at night, and the coordinator’s role is to capture and route. |  |
| 8 | Who decides whether to accept an organ offer for a candidate? | The transplant physician or surgeon on call, under program protocol | Best: acceptance is a clinical decision. The coordinator prepares the information and convenes the people. |  |
| 9 | Time matters on an offer because: | The kidney’s storage time affects how it works, so delays should be avoided | Best: longer storage is associated with poorer early function. Payment, shifts, and waiting families are not the reason. |  |
| 10 | After a call, you log the times. This matters because: | An accurate timeline supports safety review, transport coordination, and claims evidence | Best: the log feeds review, logistics, and documentation. It is not optional, does not replace the record, and decides nothing. |  |

## Module 14: Final Readiness and Perioperative Handoff

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which approval alone clears surgery? | None; the required gates must converge | Best: Each approval answers a different question. Why not the others: “PhilHealth authorization alone”: Payment approval is not medical clearance. “HTEC approval alone”: Ethics approval is not current clinical readiness. “An available operating slot”: Scheduling is not clearance. |  |
| 2 | A donor reports fever on admission. What next? | Immediate clinical review before elective progression | Best: New symptoms may change safety. Why not the others: “Ignore it if prior clearance exists”: Prior clearance does not cover new illness. “Offer an unsupervised antibiotic”: Treatment requires the authorized clinician. “Ask the donor not to mention it”: Concealment risks harm. |  |
| 3 | What releases a documented hold? | An authorized decision with verified supporting evidence | Best: The release must be attributable and traceable. Why not the others: “The coordinator becoming tired of waiting”: Fatigue does not resolve risk. “An operating-room deadline”: A deadline cannot establish safety. “A family waiver alone”: A waiver does not replace required review. |  |
| 4 | Why separate donor and recipient handoffs? | Each has different risks, rights and care needs | Best: Linked surgery does not merge the people. Why not the others: “To avoid communicating at all”: Relevant coordination remains essential. “Because the donor needs no assessment”: The donor needs dedicated assessment and care. “To duplicate every private finding”: Sharing must remain necessary and lawful. |  |
| 5 | After postponement what needs review? | Continuing care and any time-sensitive approvals or tests | Best: A delay can create new clinical and administrative needs. Why not the others: “Only the surgery calendar”: Dialysis, medicine and support needs remain. “Nothing if the family agrees”: Agreement does not maintain care. “Automatic discharge without a plan”: Both people need an appropriate plan. |  |
| 6 | Readiness for a living-donor transplant means: | All four gates are closed for both people by the people who own them | Best: eight gates, two people, closed by their owners. A slot, a payment, or a signature closes only one part. |  |
| 7 | A hold says “Repeat crossmatch within 7 days of surgery.” Surgery is in 3 days and the crossmatch was 9 days ago. You: | Flag the hold as open and route to the team now | Best: the hold is open and the team decides. Releasing or postponing are not coordination decisions, and an old result does not satisfy a time-bound hold. |  |
| 8 | Handoff for donor and recipient should be: | Separate, each to its own receiving team, with read-back | Best: separate handoffs protect privacy and accuracy. A combined update risks disclosure; families are not handoff channels. |  |
| 9 | Which counts as evidence that the ethics gate is closed? | The ethics committee’s written decision with any conditions documented as met | Best: the committee’s decision and closed conditions. Family agreement, schedules, and consent are different gates. |  |
| 10 | A pre-surgery huddle should end with: | A clear go, hold, or stop decision by the authorized lead, recorded | Best: the authorized lead decides and it is written down. Assumptions and unrecorded huddles cause errors. |  |

## Module 15: Medicines, Discharge, and Self-Management

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A prescription is written but medicine is unavailable. Is discharge navigation complete? | No; escalate and establish a feasible supply plan | Best: Access is essential to treatment continuity. Why not the others: “Yes, the form is complete”: A form does not provide medicine. “Yes, if insurance is pending”: Pending coverage does not solve supply. “Yes, if the patient promises to try”: The barrier needs an actionable plan. |  |
| 2 | Who resolves a formulation substitution? | The authorized prescriber and pharmacist | Best: Formulations can differ and need clinical oversight. Why not the others: “The coordinator alone”: Coordination does not confer prescribing authority. “A neighbor with a spare pack”: Unverified medicines are unsafe. “An online price comparison alone”: Price is not clinical equivalence. |  |
| 3 | What demonstrates teach-back? | The person explains and applies the plan in their own words | Best: Recall of names alone does not establish usable understanding. Why not the others: “A signature without discussion”: A signature does not prove comprehension. “The coordinator reading louder”: Loudness does not confirm understanding. “A leaflet handed to a relative”: The person’s own needs still require assessment. |  |
| 4 | Drug-level sampling instructions should come from where? | The prescribed medicine-specific clinical/laboratory plan | Best: Timing depends on the treatment and protocol. Why not the others: “A universal rule for all drugs”: The timing is not identical for all medicines. “The insurance form”: Payment forms do not define sampling. “The patient’s guess”: Clarify uncertain instructions. |  |
| 5 | The donor has the recipient’s discharge sheet. What next? | Correct the error, assess exposure and provide the donor’s verified plan | Best: Wrong instructions can create both safety and privacy harm. Why not the others: “Ignore it because surgery was linked”: Care plans are person-specific. “Ask the donor to copy the recipient’s medicines”: The prescriptions are not interchangeable. “Delete all records of the mistake”: The correction and incident trail must remain. |  |
| 6 | A recipient has 40 tablets left and takes 4 a day. The pharmacy needs 5 working days to restock. The runway is: | 10 days; request the refill now | Best: 40 divided by 4 is 10 days of supply; with a 5-day lead time the refill must start now. 40 and 4 confuse tablets with days. |  |
| 7 | In a meta-analysis by Dew and colleagues, immunosuppressant nonadherence in kidney recipients was about: | 36 cases per 100 patient-years | Best: 36 per 100 patient-years, the highest of the organs studied. Nonadherence is common, so plan support for everyone. |  |
| 8 | Teach-back means: | Asking the person to explain or show in their own words what they will do | Best: the person demonstrates the action. A yes, a reading, or name recall do not show they can act. |  |
| 9 | A recipient will run out of tacrolimus during a holiday week because the pharmacy is closed. You: | Arrange supply before the closure and confirm it was received | Best: protect continuity in advance. Skipping, switching brands without the team, or waiting all risk rejection. |  |
| 10 | A systematic review by Butler and colleagues associated immunosuppressant nonadherence with: | About a sevenfold higher odds of graft failure | Best: odds of graft failure about seven times higher in observational studies. The design shows association, not proof of cause, but the signal is strong. |  |

## Module 16: Symptoms, Graft Dysfunction, and Urgent Escalation

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Does fever after transplant prove rejection? | No; it requires clinical assessment for multiple causes | Best: A symptom is not a definitive diagnosis. Why not the others: “Yes, always”: Infection and other causes are possible. “No, so it can be ignored”: Uncertainty is a reason to assess. “Only if insurance covers biopsy”: Coverage does not determine diagnosis. |  |
| 2 | Severe breathlessness in a donor should trigger what? | Emergency assessment through the local pathway | Best: Potential serious complications need prompt care. Why not the others: “A routine appointment next month”: Delay may be dangerous. “An insurance appeal first”: Administration must not delay emergency response. “A web quiz”: Education cannot assess an acute emergency. |  |
| 3 | What information is immediately useful on a call? | Identity, location, callback number and symptoms | Best: These enable safe contact and response. Why not the others: “Social-media password”: It is irrelevant and inappropriate. “Only the insurance number”: It does not establish current clinical need. “The recipient’s employer details first”: This delays relevant assessment. |  |
| 4 | The first on-call clinician is unreachable. What next? | Use the approved escalation hierarchy and document attempts | Best: A reliable backup route is essential. Why not the others: “Wait indefinitely”: The concern remains unaddressed. “Make the prescribing decision alone”: Scope limits still apply. “Tell the patient to stop calling”: This abandons the handoff. |  |
| 5 | What completes an urgent handoff? | The receiving clinical service acknowledges and a next action is confirmed | Best: Sending a message alone does not close the loop. Why not the others: “A voicemail only”: Receipt and action are uncertain. “A draft note”: It has not reached the service. “A message to an unrelated department”: The responsible team must receive it. |  |
| 6 | A recipient two weeks after transplant calls with fever and less urine. A support-path coordinator should: | Route the call at once to the on-call transplant clinician under protocol and confirm the handoff | Best: urgent symptoms go to a clinician now, and the loop is closed. Advice and delays are outside scope and unsafe. |  |
| 7 | Why does delay matter for a possible rejection? | Earlier treatment is associated with better recovery of graft function | Best: rejection is treatable, and timing matters. It does not reliably resolve without treatment. |  |
| 8 | A recipient has vomiting and cannot keep tablets down. This matters because: | Missed doses and low levels can trigger rejection; it needs same-day clinician review | Best: inability to take immunosuppressants is urgent. The other answers misunderstand the risk. |  |
| 9 | Closing the loop on an urgent call means: | Confirming the clinician received it, acted, and the patient knows the plan, then documenting | Best: receipt, action, and the patient’s understanding, documented. A text or voicemail is dispatch, not closure. |  |
| 10 | A donor one week after nephrectomy reports increasing abdominal pain and fever. You: | Route to the donor’s surgical team urgently under protocol | Best: the donor has their own team and needs urgent review. The recipient’s team is not the donor’s channel; waiting and reassurance are unsafe. |  |

## Module 17: Lifelong Follow-Up for Donor and Recipient

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | When does donor follow-up end? | It follows the lifelong monitoring system required by the applicable DOH framework | Best: Initial recovery is only one phase. Why not the others: “At recipient discharge”: The donor’s needs are separate. “When the first claim is paid”: Payment does not define follow-up duration. “After the donor moves”: A move requires an accepted continuity plan. |  |
| 2 | A recipient returns to dialysis. What next? | Coordinate an integrated renal and transplant care plan | Best: Medicines, symptoms and future options still need review. Why not the others: “Stop immunosuppression independently”: The clinical team determines treatment. “Delete the transplant record”: Past care remains relevant. “Assume no more psychological support is needed”: This transition can be distressing. |  |
| 3 | What should precede a nonadherence label? | Assessment of the actual event and barriers | Best: Evidence and support are more useful than assumptions. Why not the others: “A single unanswered call”: This is insufficient to infer motive. “A travel delay”: Travel failure may be outside the person’s control. “A low income estimate”: Income does not establish willingness. |  |
| 4 | Which source should define a current vaccine plan? | The current specialist and institutional guidance | Best: Historical pandemic documents may be outdated. Why not the others: “A 2020 interim document alone”: Interim advice may no longer apply. “A generic social-media schedule”: It may not account for transplantation. “The donor’s preferences alone”: Preferences need informed clinical discussion. |  |
| 5 | What confirms long-distance follow-up transfer? | A receiving service accepts the plan and result communication route | Best: Responsibility must be explicit. Why not the others: “Giving the patient a phone number only”: Acceptance remains unconfirmed. “Closing the old file immediately”: This can create a gap. “Assuming any local clinic will know the regimen”: The plan needs a documented handoff. |  |
| 6 | KDIGO’s living donor guideline and the DOH order both support: | Lifelong follow-up of the donor, at least yearly in practice | Best: donor care continues for life. Short or conditional follow-up does not meet the framework. |  |
| 7 | A donor misses two yearly check-ups. The respectful recall step is: | Contact through the donor’s preferred channel, explain why it matters, and offer practical help | Best: respectful, private, practical. Pressure through the recipient breaches separation; closing the file abandons the duty. |  |
| 8 | Which items are typically checked at a donor’s yearly visit? | Blood pressure, weight, kidney function, and urine albumin | Best: the donor framework centers on blood pressure, body mass, kidney function, and albuminuria. Donors take no immunosuppressants. |  |
| 9 | A recipient’s graft is failing. Navigation should include: | Early planning for dialysis access, retransplant evaluation, and support, by the team | Best: plan the transition early with the team. Waiting forces urgent dialysis; the donor’s information is separate. |  |
| 10 | Which PhilHealth package includes living donor monitoring? | The post-kidney transplantation services packages | Best: the post-KT circulars list living donor monitoring among their services. |  |

## Module 18: Psychosocial Navigation and Special Situations

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A donor nods while a family member answers everything. What next? | Arrange private supported communication and assess understanding | Best: Nodding alone does not establish a free informed choice. Why not the others: “Treat the family’s answers as consent”: The donor’s own choice must be heard. “Speed up before the slot expires”: Time pressure increases risk. “Assume agreement because they are related”: Relatedness does not prove consent. |  |
| 2 | Low literacy should lead to what? | Accessible education and teach-back | Best: Communication support enables informed participation. Why not the others: “Automatic exclusion”: Literacy alone is not a blanket exclusion criterion. “A longer form without explanation”: More text may not help. “Consent by the coordinator”: The coordinator cannot consent for the person. |  |
| 3 | Who performs specialist psychiatric assessment? | A qualified psychiatrist or clinical psychologist as required | Best: The coordinator arranges the referral. Why not the others: “Any staff member with a checklist”: A checklist does not confer specialist competence. “The recipient”: This creates conflict and lacks qualifications. “A payer clerk”: Insurance work is not psychiatric assessment. |  |
| 4 | A foreign insurance letter is presented. What next? | Verify legal, clinical and payer requirements separately | Best: One document does not satisfy every system. Why not the others: “Assume local transplant approval”: Jurisdiction and authorization still matter. “Guarantee full reimbursement”: Coverage is unverified. “Skip ethics review”: Ethics protections still apply. |  |
| 5 | How should donor guilt be handled? | Offer confidential support without pressuring donation | Best: Support should protect free choice. Why not the others: “Remind the donor they owe the recipient”: This is coercive. “Reveal private fears publicly”: This violates confidentiality. “Promise that surgery has no risk”: This is false reassurance. |  |
| 6 | In a Canadian cohort, donors with higher expenses had: | Worse mental health-related quality of life at 3 months | Best: higher expenses were associated with worse mental health-related quality of life. The design cannot prove cause. |  |
| 7 | A potential donor is an overseas Filipino worker who must return abroad in four weeks. You: | Plan the evaluation and recovery timeline honestly with the team, including follow-up abroad, without pressuring a faster decision | Best: honest planning, no pressure. Rushing undermines safety and choice, exclusion is unfair, and the recipient cannot decide for the donor. |  |
| 8 | A recipient says, “I stopped one medicine because it is expensive.” Your best response is: | Thank them for telling you, route to the team today, and explore cost help | Best: safety and trust together. Scolding hides future problems; choosing medicines is not your role. |  |
| 9 | A young woman asks about pregnancy after donating a kidney. You: | Arrange a discussion with the donor’s nephrologist and obstetric team | Best: this is a clinical counseling question for her team. Absolute statements either way are inaccurate. |  |
| 10 | For a pediatric recipient, which PhilHealth circular covers post-transplant services? | PC 2025-0011 (children) | Best: the children’s post-KT package is PC 2025-0011; the adult one is PC 2025-0012. |  |

## Module 19: Registries, Privacy, and Quality

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Should donor psychiatric findings appear on a family dashboard? | Only if a specific lawful authorized need permits disclosure; normally keep them restricted | Best: Shared milestones do not require private details. Why not the others: “Yes, because the family is involved”: Family involvement does not waive privacy. “Yes, if names are shortened”: Indirect identification may remain possible. “Yes, if the spreadsheet is convenient”: Convenience is not a lawful basis. |  |
| 2 | What is needed for an interpretable follow-up rate? | A defined denominator, time window and missing-data rule | Best: Without definitions rates can mislead. Why not the others: “A percentage alone”: The population and period are unclear. “Only the best-performing month”: Selective reporting distorts performance. “Excluding all unreachable donors silently”: This hides follow-up gaps. |  |
| 3 | What should a misdirected record trigger? | Institutional privacy incident response and data-protection review | Best: The responsible team assesses containment and notification. Why not the others: “Deletion of all evidence”: Evidence may be needed for investigation. “Posting the incident publicly with names”: This compounds the disclosure. “Ignoring it if accidental”: Accidental breaches can still cause harm. |  |
| 4 | Which metric alone risks volume pressure? | Number of completed transplants | Best: It needs safety, ethics and access balancing measures. Why not the others: “Donor understanding alongside safety review”: This helps assess quality. “Medicine-gap tracking”: This identifies continuity risks. “Barrier-resolution time with equity review”: This assesses navigation performance. |  |
| 5 | Can the training website submit real national-registry records? | No; use official authorized systems and designated users | Best: The Academy is an educational site. Why not the others: “Yes, through a guessed endpoint”: Unverified integration is unsafe and unauthorized. “Yes, using shared passwords”: Credentials must remain controlled. “Yes, through quiz answers”: Training inputs must never become clinical submissions. |  |
| 6 | Where should a donor’s private reason for withdrawing be recorded? | In the restricted donor record with access limited to those who need it | Best: record facts in a restricted record. Shared views and the recipient’s chart breach privacy; not recording loses accuracy. |  |
| 7 | A quality measure reads “Donor follow-up completeness at 1 year.” Before counting, you must define: | The numerator, the denominator, the time window, and exclusions | Best: without a defined denominator and window, the rate means nothing. Targets and blame come after a valid measure. |  |
| 8 | Of 20 donors due for a 1-year visit, 15 attended. Of 60 due in a larger program, 45 attended. Both are 75%. Which is more precise? | The program with 60, because the larger sample gives a narrower confidence interval | Best: same rate, more observations, narrower uncertainty. Report the interval with the rate. |  |
| 9 | Equity review means: | Comparing access and outcome measures across groups such as sex, income, region, and distance | Best: a fair average can hide unfair gaps. Compare groups and act on the differences. |  |
| 10 | Under the Data Privacy Act, health information is treated as: | Sensitive personal information | Best: health information is sensitive personal information with stricter processing rules. |  |

## Module 20: Integrated Capstone and International Practice

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What is the capstone’s central standard? | Safe accountable navigation for both people through all four systems | Best: Timeliness must coexist with rights, safety and accurate approvals. Why not the others: “Completing surgery at any cost”: This can reward coercion or unsafe shortcuts. “Maximizing claims alone”: Financial completion is only one domain. “Avoiding all escalation”: Escalation is essential when authority or risk requires it. |  |
| 2 | Does this course confer CCTC certification? | No; ABTC has separate experience and examination requirements | Best: Educational study is not a credential. Why not the others: “Yes, after all quizzes”: Quizzes cannot award an external credential. “Yes, after 60 study hours”: That is not the ABTC process. “Yes, after a hospital prints a badge”: A badge does not establish certification. |  |
| 3 | Can US donor advocate rules be labeled Philippine law? | No; compare the principles and apply Philippine requirements | Best: Legal duties remain jurisdiction-specific. Why not the others: “Yes, because they protect donors”: A useful principle does not transfer jurisdiction. “Yes, if translated”: Translation does not enact law. “Yes, if a coordinator prefers them”: Preference does not override local requirements. |  |
| 4 | A donor freely withdraws after support. Is navigation necessarily unsuccessful? | No; protecting voluntary choice is a successful ethical outcome | Best: Performance must not pressure donation. Why not the others: “Yes, because no transplant occurred”: Volume alone is an unsafe measure. “Yes, so the reason should be disclosed”: Confidentiality remains important. “Yes, so the donor should be billed as punishment”: Punitive pressure undermines free choice. |  |
| 5 | What permits independent workplace responsibilities? | Appropriate credentials, institutional authority and demonstrated supervised competence | Best: The facility must assess actual practice and scope. Why not the others: “The website progress bar”: A progress bar measures study only. “A downloaded completion certificate”: This course does not issue a credential. “A high quiz score alone”: Knowledge is only one element of competence. |  |
| 6 | In the United States, the independent living donor advocate (ILDA) is a useful idea for the Philippines because: | It separates the donor’s interests from the recipient’s team; local law decides who the advocate is | Best: borrow the principle, follow the Philippine definition. The US role is not local law, not automatic for coordinators, and not a replacement for the committee. |  |
| 7 | Which foreign rule should not be applied in the Philippines without legal review? | A US reporting deadline for donor follow-up | Best: deadlines are jurisdiction-specific law. The other three are principles already consistent with Philippine safeguards and safety practice. |  |
| 8 | In the capstone, which action is a critical failure? | Telling the recipient the donor’s private reason for withdrawing | Best: disclosure of the donor’s reason is a critical failure. The other three are correct actions. |  |
| 9 | A recipient had a transfusion on Tuesday; an offer comes Thursday. The coordinator’s key step is to: | Make sure the transplant team and HLA laboratory know about the transfusion before decisions | Best: a sensitizing event must reach the team and laboratory. Hiding, interpreting, or canceling are wrong. |  |
| 10 | The UK Human Tissue Authority independent assessment is best used in this course as: | A comparison showing the value of an independent check on consent and reward | Best: it is a comparison. The Philippine safeguards are the DOH order and the hospital ethics committee. |  |

# Occupational and Physical Therapist

## Module 1: The Renal Therapist Role and the First Referral

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A PT is asked to reduce ultrafiltration so exercise can continue. What is appropriate? | Refer the dialysis decision to the authorized nurse and physician | Best answer: The rehabilitation referral does not authorize dialysis prescription changes. |  |
| 2 | Which task most directly calls for renal OT input? | Analyzing how fatigue disrupts cooking and adapting the task | Best answer: Occupational analysis connects abilities and environment to a valued daily activity. |  |
| 3 | Before Philippine PT treatment, what must be checked alongside registration? | A prescription from a duly registered physician | Best answer: RA5680 section 12 addresses registration and physician prescription. |  |
| 4 | A learner completes both OT and PT lessons. What may be claimed? | Course completion within the learner’s existing professional role | Best answer: Educational exposure does not confer a second professional qualification. |  |
| 5 | Who should choose which daily activity matters most? | The patient through shared goal setting | Best answer: Participation goals should reflect the person’s priorities as well as safety needs. |  |
| 6 | In a cohort of adults with CKD stages 2 to 4, each 0.1 m/s slower gait speed was associated with about 26 percent higher risk of death. What is the most accurate way to use this finding? | Treat gait speed as an important prognostic signal worth measuring and tracking | The study was observational: gait speed predicted death better than eGFR or common biomarkers, but it does not show that raising gait speed changes survival. Measure it and track it; do not promise more than the evidence shows. |  |
| 7 | A referral says “OT and PT: improve function.” Who decides which profession leads which goal? | The two therapists agree it with the patient, tell the team and record it | Overlap is normal. Agree a lead for each goal, tell the patient and team, and write it in the plan so care is not duplicated or dropped. |  |
| 8 | Which statement about authority for renal OT and PT practice in the Philippines is correct? | Authority comes from your PRC license, the referral or prescription, and employer privileges; this course adds knowledge only | No PSN therapist certificate or national dialysis therapist ratio was found. RA 5680 still requires a physician’s prescription for PT treatment, and an Academy record never substitutes for it. |  |
| 9 | Mr. Villanueva gets dizzy while bathing on dialysis afternoons. What is the best first routing? | OT analyzes the bathing task; the dizziness is reported to the nurse and nephrologist | The task is an OT problem, but dizziness after dialysis may be low blood pressure after fluid removal, which is a medical question. Route both parts to their owners before changing the routine. |  |
| 10 | Which element is missing most often from first-contact notes and matters most to the next clinician? | The decision (proceed, adapt or defer) and the reason for it | A note that records the decision and its reason shows the checks were done and lets the next person continue safely. |  |

## Module 2: Kidney Disease Through a Functional Lens

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A previously independent patient is newly breathless at rest. What comes first? | Medical review before exertional testing | Best answer: An acute change must be assessed before a conditioning program proceeds. |  |
| 2 | Two patients have the same CKD stage. How should their plans be selected? | From individual function, symptoms, goals and restrictions | Best answer: Stage does not capture task demands, comorbidity or participation needs. |  |
| 3 | What should be recorded when comparing function around HD? | Timing relative to dialysis and current symptoms | Best answer: Treatment timing can influence performance and interpretation of change. |  |
| 4 | Which decision belongs to the renal medical team? | Selecting the kidney replacement therapy prescription | Best answer: Therapists contribute function but do not prescribe kidney replacement therapy. |  |
| 5 | A new referral says deconditioning but the patient is acutely confused. What should guide the visit? | The current change and need for prompt medical assessment | Best answer: A referral is not proof of current stability. |  |
| 6 | Which test is most likely to reveal the weakness that limits a person with CKD rising from a low chair? | Five-times sit-to-stand | Lower-limb performance falls first in CKD while grip is relatively preserved; a chair-rise test targets the problem. |  |
| 7 | A patient on hemodialysis feels dizzy on standing after sessions and takes metoprolol. What is the best explanation to plan around? | Fluid removal, weak reflexes and beta-blockade can drop pressure on standing | Ultrafiltration lowers plasma volume, autonomic neuropathy slows the reflex, and beta-blockers blunt heart rate; all favor orthostatic falls. |  |
| 8 | A meta-analysis pooled frailty prevalence in hemodialysis at 34.3 percent with a range of 6 to 82 percent. What explains the wide range? | Different frailty tools and populations | Prevalence depends on how frailty is measured and who is studied; use one tool consistently in your service. |  |
| 9 | Which statement about the KDIGO 2024 physical activity recommendation is accurate? | It advises at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity or to tolerance, graded 1D | A strong recommendation (1) with very low-certainty evidence (D): low risk, broad benefit, little CKD-specific outcome data. |  |
| 10 | Why should you record which dialysis day and how long after a session you tested a patient? | Function varies across the dialysis week, so comparisons need the same timing | Fluid load and post-dialysis fatigue change performance; without consistent timing, changes may be artifacts. |  |

## Module 3: Screen Before Movement and Respond to Deterioration

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A patient develops chest pressure during a task. What should happen first? | Stop and obtain immediate nursing and medical assistance | Best answer: Concerning symptoms take priority over a training target. |  |
| 2 | A heart rate appears normal despite severe new breathlessness. What is safest? | Stop and assess the concerning symptoms with the team | Best answer: A single observation cannot clear a symptomatic patient. |  |
| 3 | Which SBAR detail is most useful in an urgent handoff? | Onset, activity, observations, actions and help required | Best answer: Specific context supports rapid clinical decisions without guessing the diagnosis. |  |
| 4 | After an acute event, what is needed before restarting therapy? | A documented clinical review and revised parameters when indicated | Best answer: A meaningful change can invalidate the old activity plan. |  |
| 5 | What does an adapt decision mean? | A stable patient receives a modified task within the agreed plan | Best answer: Adaptation is a reasoned adjustment for an otherwise appropriate activity. |  |
| 6 | Mrs. Reyes reports chest heaviness with a pulse of 74 while on metoprolol. What is the correct interpretation? | The pulse does not exclude a serious problem; stop and get help | Beta-blockers blunt heart rate; a red-flag symptom overrides a normal-looking number. |  |
| 7 | Who sets the numeric limits on a unit’s therapy parameter sheet? | The physician, agreed with the unit, for the patient or service | This track sets no universal clearance numbers; limits come from the physician and the unit’s protocol. |  |
| 8 | A stable patient is mildly dizzy on standing but settles within a minute. What is the most suitable decision? | Adapt: seated work or more help, recheck, inform the nurse | Adapting keeps the person active while respecting the warning; the nurse should know the pattern. |  |
| 9 | In the early ICU mobility trial, how many serious adverse events occurred in 498 therapy sessions? | One | One serious event (a desaturation) in 498 sessions: supervised activity with screening is generally safe. |  |
| 10 | After a session is stopped for chest pain, when may exercise resume? | After clinical review and a documented restart authorization | A restart is a clinical decision; record who authorized it and any new parameters. |  |

## Module 4: Protect Vascular Access and Prevent Infection

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A transfer would pull on dialysis tubing. What is appropriate? | Stop and redesign with the dialysis nurse | Best answer: Line routing and assigned observation must be safe before movement. |  |
| 2 | What should a therapist do when a dialysis alarm occurs during exercise? | Stop movement and request nursing assessment | Best answer: Dialysis operations remain with appropriately authorized staff. |  |
| 3 | How should shared pedal equipment be prepared for the next patient? | Clean and disinfect using compatible approved products and contact time | Best answer: Safe turnover includes hand hygiene and equipment-specific disinfection. |  |
| 4 | Which is an appropriate approach to a healed fistula arm? | Use individualized access and medical guidance for activity | Best answer: Avoid blanket restrictions while protecting access from pressure and injury. |  |
| 5 | A patient reports a cold painful access-side hand. What should happen? | Prompt clinical review rather than continuing the task | Best answer: New distal symptoms require evaluation and should not be treated as routine exercise discomfort. |  |
| 6 | Why does compression of a fistula arm risk losing the fistula? | It slows high-flow blood in an injured vein, which can clot | A fistula depends on fast flow; still blood clots, and clotting can end the access. |  |
| 7 | In the PHYSICALFAV trial, what did eight weeks of preoperative isometric exercise change? | Vein caliber and the rate of distal fistula creation, not primary failure | Vein diameter and distal site rose (surrogate and process outcomes); primary failure was low and not significantly different. |  |
| 8 | After creation of a wrist fistula, what did a randomized trial of more intense handgrip programs find? | No better maturation than a basic program | More frequent or banded programs did not increase diameter, flow or clinical use over three months. |  |
| 9 | Which activity is acceptable for a patient during the session with needles in a forearm fistula? | Leg cycling with the access arm still and visible, with the nurse’s agreement | The needled arm stays still and uncovered; the legs do the work. |  |
| 10 | What makes shared rehabilitation equipment safe between dialysis patients? | Cleaning with the approved disinfectant kept wet for the label contact time | Disinfectants work only with the right contact time; dialysis units are high-risk settings for transmission. |  |

## Module 5: Assess Function and Agree Measurable Goals

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A repeat test uses a taller chair and arm support. How should it be interpreted? | Record changed conditions and avoid direct strength comparison | Best answer: Method changes can alter a result independently of true functional change. |  |
| 2 | Which goal is measurable and meaningful? | Use the agreed aid to reach the toilet with supervision within two weeks | Best answer: The goal specifies activity, assistance, context and time. |  |
| 3 | Which pair best captures rehabilitation outcome? | A repeatable capacity measure and a patient participation measure | Best answer: Capacity and real-life participation describe different aspects of benefit. |  |
| 4 | Before using a copyrighted assessment, what should be checked? | Administration guidance and permission requirements | Best answer: Availability online does not establish permission or proper administration. |  |
| 5 | A patient performs well in the clinic but cannot enter the home. What is the issue? | Clinic capacity has not established home performance | Best answer: Environment and support affect what the person can actually do. |  |
| 6 | A patient walks 4 meters in 5.0 seconds. What is the gait speed? | 0.80 m/s | Gait speed is distance divided by time: 4 ÷ 5.0 = 0.80 m/s. |  |
| 7 | Mr. Villanueva’s predicted six-minute walk distance is about 499 meters and he walked 290. What is the percent predicted? | About 58 percent | 290 ÷ 499 ≈ 0.58. The reference equation came from healthy adults; the person’s own trend matters most. |  |
| 8 | What is the main reason to standardize chair height, course length and instructions? | So that changes reflect the person, not the test conditions | Without standard conditions, a change in the number may be an artifact. |  |
| 9 | Which goal best meets the standard of a shared, measurable goal? | “Walk to the barangay court (250 m) with one rest, by the league finals” | It states the task, distance, conditions and time, in words the patient chose. |  |
| 10 | In the SPPB study, what did performance tests add beyond self-report? | They separated risk even among people reporting almost no disability | Performance measures carried prognostic information that self-report missed; they complement each other. |  |

## Module 6: Manage Fatigue and Rebuild Daily Routines

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fatigue suddenly worsens with new breathlessness. What comes first? | Medical assessment of the new change | Best answer: Pacing is not a substitute for assessment of deterioration. |  |
| 2 | What is the purpose of pacing? | Sustain valued participation with manageable demands and recovery | Best answer: Pacing supports activity rather than imposing permanent inactivity. |  |
| 3 | A patient overworks on non-dialysis days and then cannot function. What helps? | Redistribute tasks and trial manageable activity with planned recovery | Best answer: Task redesign and scheduling can reduce repeated overload. |  |
| 4 | Which is an OT task analysis intervention? | Move frequently used cooking supplies within reach and trial seated preparation | Best answer: Environmental and task adaptations directly address occupational demands. |  |
| 5 | What should be reviewed after a new activity routine? | Immediate response, next-day fatigue and participation | Best answer: A feasible plan must be judged by recovery and its effect on daily life. |  |
| 6 | In DOPPS, about what share of patients needed more than 12 hours to recover after a session? | About one in ten | Roughly 10 percent; longer recovery was associated with greater fluid removal, hospitalization and death (observational). |  |
| 7 | Which approach best breaks the deconditioning spiral? | Paced, planned activity plus graded capacity building | Lowering task cost (OT) and raising capacity (PT) together interrupts the spiral. |  |
| 8 | Where should a valued evening activity go in a patient’s week who recovers slowly after morning sessions? | On a non-dialysis day, when energy is highest | Energy budgeting protects valued roles by timing them when the battery is fullest. |  |
| 9 | Which fatigue source is primarily the renal team’s to treat? | Anemia | Report anemia and other medical causes; rehabilitation addresses routines and capacity. |  |
| 10 | In the EXCITE trial, a home walking program managed by dialysis staff improved which outcome? | Six-minute walk distance and five-times sit-to-stand | Walk distance rose from 328 to 367 meters and chair-stand time improved, with gains in some quality-of-life domains. |  |

## Module 7: Support Self-Care, Cognition and Treatment Routines

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
