| 1 | A patient is suddenly drowsy and cannot follow familiar instructions. What is needed? | Prompt medical assessment of an acute change | Best answer: New cognitive changes require assessment before routine training. |  |
| 2 | What does a cognitive screen establish? | Findings that may guide further assessment and supports | Best answer: Screening results need context and do not replace diagnosis or treatment competency assessment. |  |
| 3 | Which method best verifies understanding of a routine? | Ask the person to demonstrate it using teach-back | Best answer: Demonstration reveals specific support needs better than agreement alone. |  |
| 4 | An OT helps organize medication reminders. Who changes the dose? | The authorized prescriber | Best answer: Routine supports do not confer prescribing authority. |  |
| 5 | What should guide an accessible task checklist? | Demonstrated language, vision, literacy and sequencing needs | Best answer: Adaptations must fit the person who will use them. |  |
| 6 | In the Minnesota study of hemodialysis patients aged 55 and older, about what share had normal cognition? | About 13 percent | Only 12.7 percent had normal cognition, and only 2.9 percent had documented impairment: it is common and often missed. |  |
| 7 | A patient explains his treatment perfectly but misses doses. What is the best next step? | Observe the routine in its real setting | Preserved verbal knowledge can coexist with impaired executive function; observation finds where the routine breaks. |  |
| 8 | Limited health literacy in a cohort of people starting hemodialysis was associated with what? | Higher mortality (hazard ratio 1.54) | An association in an observational cohort: it identifies who needs clearer communication and support. |  |
| 9 | Which scaffold best supports a patient who forgets whether he took his morning dose? | A day-and-time pillbox with a tick sheet | Visible cues reduce the memory load of checking. |  |
| 10 | What is outside the OT’s role in a medicine routine? | Changing a dose or timing | Doses and timing belong to the physician and pharmacist; the OT designs how the routine is carried out. |  |

## Module 8: Transfers, Gait and Falls Prevention

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A patient nearly faints after dialysis. What should precede harder gait training? | Medical review and a safe assistance plan | Best answer: Unexplained near-syncope needs assessment rather than increased exertion. |  |
| 2 | What should be decided before a transfer? | Assistance, equipment, line roles and environmental setup | Best answer: Planning prevents avoidable patient, access and staff injury. |  |
| 3 | Which finding supports a multifactorial falls assessment? | Falls cluster at night and after dialysis | Best answer: Timing and context can reveal medical, environmental and activity contributors. |  |
| 4 | How should caregiver transfer training be verified? | Observe the caregiver demonstrate safe assistance | Best answer: The plan must fit the caregiver’s actual skills and physical ability. |  |
| 5 | After a fall with possible serious injury, what is appropriate? | Follow post-fall assessment and escalation before moving or resuming | Best answer: Possible injury changes the priority to assessment and safety. |  |
| 6 | In a prospective study of older hemodialysis patients, what was the fall rate? | 1.60 falls per person-year | About twice community rates; 19 percent of falls caused injury. |  |
| 7 | Why do falls in dialysis patients more often cause fractures? | Bone is weakened by CKD-mineral and bone disorder | Relative risk of hip fracture was about 4.4 times the general population in a large US analysis. |  |
| 8 | What is the correct handhold for guarding a sit-to-stand in a patient with a left forearm fistula? | A gait belt, guarding from the side, never pulling the arm | A gait belt gives control without loading the access. |  |
| 9 | A cane is correctly fitted when the handle is at what level? | The wrist crease with arms relaxed | Wrist-crease height gives about 15 to 30 degrees of elbow bend. |  |
| 10 | A patient becomes pale and dizzy while standing up. What do you do? | Sit them down or lower them with control, protect the head, call the nurse | Controlled lowering prevents injury; never try to hold up a falling adult. |  |

## Module 9: Design and Progress an Individualized Exercise Plan

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What does FITT describe? | Frequency, intensity, time and type | Best answer: FITT makes an exercise prescription explicit and reviewable. |  |
| 2 | How should the adult 150-minute activity target be used? | Adapt toward it according to cardiovascular and physical tolerance | Best answer: The guideline target does not override individual tolerance or clinical restrictions. |  |
| 3 | A beta-blocked patient has symptoms below a heart-rate target. What is appropriate? | Use symptoms and broader assessment rather than force the target | Best answer: Heart rate alone may misrepresent effort or risk. |  |
| 4 | Which progression is easiest to interpret? | Change one dose variable and document the response | Best answer: A controlled change allows the therapist to assess tolerance. |  |
| 5 | What should a home exercise plan include? | Dose, effort method, stop instructions and review plan | Best answer: A safe plan explains how to perform, monitor and revise the activity. |  |
| 6 | Why are early strength gains in the first weeks of training fragile? | They come mostly from nervous-system adaptation; muscle growth follows later | Neural recruitment improves first; fiber growth needs weeks to months. |  |
| 7 | What did the 2011 Cochrane review of exercise in CKD find? | Improved aerobic and walking capacity and quality of life, with many high-bias trials | Benefits in fitness and function were consistent; mortality was not shown, and trial quality varied. |  |
| 8 | For a patient on carvedilol, how should aerobic intensity be set? | By RPE 12 to 14 and the talk test | Beta-blockers blunt heart rate; effort-based measures remain valid. |  |
| 9 | What is the correct progression order for resistance training? | Repetitions first, then load | Increasing repetitions before load reduces injury risk. |  |
| 10 | A patient returns after a 3-day admission. How do you restart? | Get authorization, then drop back to an earlier level before progressing | Illness and inactivity reduce capacity; a drop-back rule prevents setbacks. |  |

## Module 10: Rehabilitation During Hemodialysis

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What is required before intradialytic exercise? | Current nurse handoff and an approved patient-specific activity plan | Best answer: The current dialysis session and access status affect readiness. |  |
| 2 | A pedal unit blocks emergency access. What should happen? | Correct the setup before using it | Best answer: Equipment cannot compromise treatment or emergency access. |  |
| 3 | Who controls dialysis machine settings during therapy? | The appropriately authorized dialysis team | Best answer: A therapy session does not transfer dialysis operational responsibility. |  |
| 4 | Is being in the first part of HD sufficient clearance for activity? | No, current status and the individual protocol still govern | Best answer: A time window cannot replace a current safety screen. |  |
| 5 | What belongs in an intradialytic handback? | Activity dose, symptoms, response and unresolved concerns | Best answer: The nurse needs clinically relevant information about the session response. |  |
| 6 | In DiaTT, what was the between-group difference in STS60 after 12 months? | 3.85 repetitions favoring exercise | STS60 rose from 16.2 to 19.2 with exercise and fell from 16.2 to 14.7 with usual care. |  |
| 7 | Which feature most likely contributed to PEDAL’s null result? | Low adherence (18 percent) to a 6-month cycling-only program | Short duration, aerobic-only design and poor adherence differ from DiaTT. |  |
| 8 | CYCLE-HD reduced left ventricular mass. How should you describe this outcome? | A surrogate marker; it does not show fewer heart attacks or deaths | Heart mass is a plausible marker of risk; function and quality of life did not change in that trial. |  |
| 9 | When is intradialytic exercise usually scheduled, and why? | In the first half of the session, before much fluid is removed | Hypotension is more likely later in the session as fluid is removed. |  |
| 10 | A machine alarm sounds while a patient is cycling. What do you do? | Stop the exercise and call the nurse; never touch the machine | The nurse controls the machine and the session. |  |

## Module 13: Transplant Prehabilitation and Recovery

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |

| 3 | Which claim about rehabilitation after transplantation is justified? | It can address function and participation goals | Best answer: Functional improvement cannot establish graft status or replace medical care. |  |
| 4 | A new fever and wound problem occur before therapy. What comes first? | Contact the transplant team and obtain appropriate clinical review | Best answer: Possible postoperative or infectious complications need evaluation. |  |
| 5 | What should return-to-work planning include? | Actual task demands, restrictions, supports and review timing | Best answer: Demand analysis helps align role return with current capacity and medical instructions. |  |
| 6 | In the prehabilitation pilot, which result is best described as preliminary? | Shorter length of stay in five transplanted participants | Five patients cannot establish an effect; the pilot suggests feasibility and a possible benefit. |  |
| 7 | Does a better frailty score move a candidate up the transplant list? | No; allocation and eligibility are decided by the transplant team and rules | Prehabilitation prepares for surgery; it does not buy priority. |  |

## Module 14: Frailty, Bone Disease, Neuropathy and Limb Loss

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A numb foot is newly hot and swollen. What is safest? | Defer loading and obtain prompt clinical assessment | Best answer: Reduced sensation can hide serious tissue or bone problems. |  |
| 2 | What should determine goals for a frail older adult? | The person’s priorities, assessed capacity and risks | Best answer: Frailty care remains individualized and person centered. |  |
| 3 | Before gait training after limb loss, what is essential? | Healing and weight-bearing instructions with appropriate specialist input | Best answer: Loading and equipment must match surgical and tissue status. |  |
| 4 | Why check skin after equipment use in neuropathy? | Pressure injury may occur without reliable pain warning | Best answer: Sensory loss changes how tissue risk must be monitored. |  |
| 5 | What should poor intake and functional decline prompt? | Coordination with the renal dietitian and medical team | Best answer: Rehabilitation should connect to relevant contributors beyond movement. |  |
| 6 | Why does a below-knee prosthesis fit differently across the dialysis week in a patient on hemodialysis? | Residual-limb volume changes with fluid gain and removal | Fluid between sessions swells the limb; removal shrinks it. Sock management helps. |  |
| 7 | In the cohort comparing diabetic dialysis patients with an ulcer-history group, amputation rates were: | 58.0 versus 13.3 per 1,000 person-years | Dialysis with diabetes carries a much higher amputation risk; feet need checking at every session. |  |
| 8 | Which exercise should be avoided with a history of vertebral fracture? | Loaded spinal flexion such as toe touches with weight | Loaded bending stresses fragile vertebrae; balance and leg strength are preferred. |  |
| 9 | What does a Clinical Frailty Scale score of 6 mean for planning? | Lower starting point and slower progression, not exclusion | Frailty sets the pace; frail people still benefit. |  |
| 10 | A callus over a pressure point in a numb foot is best treated as: | A pre-ulcer needing prompt review and offloading | Insensate pressure points ulcerate; early referral protects the limb. |  |

| 8 | What does a shared OT/PT plan need most? | One patient-chosen goal with named leads for each part | Patients follow one plan; leads prevent gaps and duplication. |  |
| 9 | Which stations does a PT learner take? | OS01, OS02, OS03, OS06, OS07, OS08 | PT learners take the shared stations plus mobility assessment and exercise prescription. |  |
| 10 | How should the team handle a 9 of 10 station score with one critical failure? | Fail the station, debrief, retrain and reassess on a different case | Critical failures are never averaged away. |  |

# Dialysis Unit Owner

## Module 1: The Owner Role and the Governance Charter

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A biomedical technician has held a machine after a failed alarm test. Who may return it to service? | The designated technical lead, with the required test evidence | Technical release belongs to the qualified technical lead under the unit’s procedure. Ownership and commercial pressure confer no technical competence. |  |
| 2 | Which delegation will still work on a holiday? | A named role, a scope, a spending limit, a backup, and an escalation trigger | Without a limit, a backup, and a trigger for escalation, the delegation fails exactly when the delegate is absent or the decision is too big. |  |
| 3 | Which is the strongest evidence that a corrective action worked? | A re-audit showing the problem stayed fixed | Payment, optimism, and silence are low on the assurance ladder. A re-audit against the closure criterion shows the control works. |  |
| 4 | Which of these is a protected decision? | Deciding whether a patient is fit to start dialysis today | Fitness to dialyze is a clinical judgment. The others are reserved owner decisions. |  |
| 5 | A shareholder orders a held water loop back into use. What should the board record and do? | Keep the hold, fund the fix, and record the attempted override factually | The hold stands, the owner’s role is to fund the recovery, and the attempt is recorded so the charter can be corrected. |  |
| 6 | In the national survey of hospital board chairs by Jha and Epstein, what did the data show? | Few boards examined quality data broken down by patient group | The survey described attitudes and practices, including that fewer than one in ten chairs examined stratified quality data. It did not measure patient outcomes. |  |

## Module 2: Kidney Care and the Patient Journey

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why does the weekend gap matter more than the midweek gaps? | It is the longest gap, so fluid and potassium build up the most | With three sessions a week, one gap is about two and a half days. The longer the gap, the higher the fluid and potassium peak. |  |
| 2 | In the study by Foley and colleagues, when were deaths highest? | On the day after the long weekend gap | Deaths, especially cardiac deaths, were higher on the day after the long gap. The study was observational. |  |
| 3 | A schedule has no free chairs. What is the main safety problem? | A missed session cannot be made up, so the gap lengthens | Make-up slots are a safety control. Without them, a missed session turns into a much longer gap. |  |
| 4 | The randomized HEMO Study tested a higher dose within the usual three-times-weekly schedule. What did it find? | No survival benefit from the higher dose | The higher dose did not improve survival. Faster or more intense sessions are not a free substitute for time and frequency. |  |
| 5 | A patient on your census receives a kidney transplant. How should the board record this? | As a successful referral and part of the quality report | Referral for transplant is good care. Reporting it as a quality measure keeps incentives pointed at patients. |  |
| 6 | What did Garg and colleagues report about for-profit ownership in their United States cohort? | Higher mortality and lower placement on the transplant waiting list, as associations | Adjusted hazard ratios were 1.20 for death and 0.74 for waitlisting. The study was observational and from another health system. |  |

| 3 | Four stations are installed but not yet on the license. Patients are waiting. What is correct? | Wait until the license covers them and the technical lead releases them | Treating on unlicensed stations exceeds the approved scope, however urgent the waiting list. |  |
| 4 | What must every line in a compliance register have? | Evidence, a named owner, an expiry or next check, and an alert | Without an owner and an alert, a requirement quietly expires. |  |
| 5 | Which change should always trigger a review of the register before it takes effect? | A change in station count or address | Station count, address, named appointees, and new regulations all touch licensing and accreditation. |  |

| 1 | A letter names a nephrologist clinical head of “the company’s dialysis units” without listing sites. What is the main problem? | The scope can grow without the clinician’s agreement or the time to cover it | A role with no listed sites can silently expand beyond what one person can oversee. |  |
| 2 | Which clause protects patients from commercial pressure most directly? | Protected clinical judgment with authority to stop unsafe care | These clauses keep clinical decisions on clinical grounds. |  |
| 3 | Which is an owner decision rather than a protected one? | Funding a second nurse | Funding is an owner decision. The other three need clinical or technical judgment. |  |
| 4 | What does the PSN guideline say about a separate unit manager? | Expected above 15 stations; exactly 15 is unstated | The guideline separates the role above 15 stations. It is a society provision, not law. |  |

# Renal Social Worker

## Module 1: The Renal Social Worker: Role, Ethics, and Boundaries

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Who should sign a professional social work assessment such as a social case study? | The registered social worker who did the assessment | Best: a signature states that the signer did the assessment, and professional reports belong to the responsible registered social worker. Why not the others: course completion confers no authority; chart access is not professional authority; a later countersignature would make the report false. |  |
| 2 | Before inviting a relative into an adult patient’s interview, what should you do first? | Ask the patient privately whom they want involved and what may be shared | Best: an adult who can decide chooses who joins. Why not the others: paying for care is not permission; sharing the chart breaches privacy; waiting for the whole family delays help and still skips the patient’s choice. |  |
| 3 | A pharmacy offers you a “token” for each patient you refer. What is the best response? | Decline, document it, and tell your supervisor | Best: a referral benefit creates a conflict of interest that must be declined and managed through supervision. Why not the others: a good price does not remove the conflict; secrecy compounds it; the patient cannot waive your professional duty. |  |
| 4 | Which of these decisions belongs to the attending nephrologist, not the social worker? | The dialysis prescription and whether a session can be moved | Best: treatment decisions are medical. Why not the others: transport, formulation, and assistance coordination are social work tasks. |  |
| 5 | What should you say before asking a new patient any personal question? | Your role, the purpose of the meeting, who may see the information, and the limits of confidentiality | Best: people share more safely when they know why you ask and who will see it. Why not the others: silence or a name alone leaves them uninformed; promising total secrecy is false because confidentiality has limits, such as immediate risk. |  |
| 6 | A navigator is asked to sign a social case study because the social worker is on leave. What should the navigator do? | Prepare the documents and call the covering registered social worker | Best: the navigator can prepare everything and route the professional task to the covering social worker. Why not the others: signing is outside the navigator’s authority; sending the family away abandons them; a nurse cannot sign a social work assessment either. |  |
| 7 | Which statement best describes the purpose of the renal social worker? | Helping people with kidney disease and their families address psychosocial and social barriers to the care they choose, starting from their goals | Best: the role starts from the person’s goal and covers assessment, support, and access. Why not the others: assistance paperwork is one tool, not the profession; persuasion on the team’s behalf is not the role; transplant eligibility is the transplant team’s decision. |  |
| 8 | A patient’s family asks you not to tell him his kidneys will not recover. What is the best first step? | Explore the family’s fear, involve the nephrologist, and ask the patient how much he wants to know | Best: respect the family’s concern while protecting the adult patient’s right to information, with the clinician who gives the news. Why not the others: agreeing sets aside the patient’s rights; rushing ahead ignores the family and the nephrologist’s role; ending the meeting solves nothing. |  |
| 9 | Why should a unit have a written role map with absence cover? | So that every recurring task has an owner, a backup, and an urgent route before anyone goes on leave | Best: written roles stop work from flowing to whoever is nearest. Why not the others: the reviewed DOH order sets no social worker ratio; the map is about tasks, not importance; it keeps professional tasks with professionals. |  |
| 10 | During a routine benefit request, the charge nurse reports that the patient said she “cannot keep doing this” and cried. What comes first? | Tell the attending physician and the covering social worker today, before the paperwork | Best: a possible safety or stop-treatment statement comes before forms and goes to the clinician and social worker the same day. Why not the others: delay risks missing danger; assuming the meaning skips the question; the daughter cannot answer for her. |  |

## Module 2: Kidney Care Literacy for Social Workers

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why is the two-day weekend gap the riskiest part of a three-times-a-week dialysis schedule? | Fluid and potassium keep building up between sessions, and the long gap lets them build longest | Best: without kidney function, water and potassium accumulate between sessions, most over the longest gap; a large cohort found more deaths on the day after it. Why not the others: the machines do not change; weekend eating usually adds, not reduces, load; staffing is not the mechanism. |  |
| 2 | A patient wants to skip Friday dialysis for a family trip. What is your role? | Bring the question to the nephrologist today and work on the travel arrangements | Best: the schedule is a medical decision; your work is the social part (temporary dialysis elsewhere, papers, cost). Why not the others: approval is not yours to give; one missed session is not harmless; forbidding travel is neither your decision nor the goal. |  |
| 3 | Severe breathlessness appears during a social work interview. What should happen? | Immediate clinical escalation to the nurse or physician | Best: breathlessness can mean fluid in the lungs and needs clinical assessment now. Why not the others: finishing first delays care; skipping would worsen fluid overload; a routine booking ignores the urgency. |  |
| 4 | A patient asks which dialysis type is medically best for her. What should you do? | Arrange a clinical conversation with the nephrologist and explore her practical preferences | Best: medical suitability is the clinician’s; you bring her life and preferences to the decision. Why not the others: cost alone is not the decision; promises outrun clinical assessment; choosing for her removes her voice. |  |
| 5 | Which statement about conservative kidney management is accurate? | It is active care focused on symptoms and the person’s goals, without dialysis | Best: conservative management is planned, active care. Why not the others: the team continues to care; it is not a cure; it is a clinical pathway, not a billing label. |  |
| 6 | Which kidney job explains why many people on dialysis also need injections for anemia? | Making the hormone that tells the bone marrow to produce red cells | Best: failing kidneys make too little of this hormone, which dialysis cannot replace. Why not the others: water, potassium, and urea removal are partly done by dialysis and do not cause anemia this way. |  |
| 7 | In the DOPPS cohort, how was skipping one or more sessions a month related to mortality? | It was associated with higher mortality (relative risk 1.30), an observational finding | Best: DOPPS is observational, so the right verb is “associated with.” Why not the others: an observational cohort cannot prove causation; the association was present; there was no protective effect. |  |
| 8 | A patient stopped her phosphate binders because they cost more than her rice. What is the best response? | Tell the nurse and nephrologist, and work on the medicine cost yourself | Best: the clinical decision goes to the clinician; the cost problem stays with you. Why not the others: judging the medicine’s importance or giving instructions is medical advice; doing nothing leaves both problems unsolved. |  |
| 9 | Why might a patient’s tiredness and poor concentration be misread as low motivation? | Uremia, anemia, and poor sleep in kidney failure cause these symptoms too | Best: kidney failure itself causes fatigue and poor focus, so describe what you see and let clinicians sort the cause. Why not the others: it is a stereotype; there is no such hormone; tiredness has many causes. |  |
| 10 | For most people who can have one, how does a transplant compare with dialysis, and how strong is the evidence? | It is associated with longer life and better quality of life, in many cohort studies; no trial has randomized the two | Best: consistent cohort evidence, but observational. Why not the others: there are no such randomized trials; cohorts consistently favor transplant; it is not right or possible for everyone. |  |

## Module 3: Philippine Requirements and a Defensible Service Model

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Does a United States rule on dialysis social worker qualifications apply in the Philippines? | No; it is a foreign rule for that setting, so check Philippine law and local requirements | Best: jurisdiction matters; foreign rules are comparisons, not local requirements. Why not the others: citation or preference does not create legal authority. |  |
| 2 | A licensing checklist could not be retrieved. How should you record it? | As evidence still needing retrieval and verification | Best: an inaccessible document is an open task. Why not the others: you cannot verify what you did not read, and absence of access is not absence of a rule. |  |
| 3 | Which of these is an Academy design choice, not a legal requirement? | The course’s 60-hour learning plan | Best: the hours are an educational plan. Why not the others: the law, the circular, and the Data Privacy Act are issued rules. |  |
| 4 | What is the most defensible basis for proposing social work staffing for a dialysis unit? | Demand and complexity in hours, compared with available hours and confirmed local rules | Best: workload in hours reflects the actual work and local rules. Why not the others: a borrowed ratio has no local authority; chairs ignore complexity; salaries are irrelevant to demand. |  |
| 5 | A clinical head says, “DOH did not require a social worker.” Which reply is most accurate? | “The DOH dialysis order we reviewed does not name a social worker post or ratio; the full current checklist should be confirmed.” | Best: a bounded finding states exactly what was reviewed. Why not the others: no such ratio was identified; nothing prohibits social work; “no rule anywhere” overstates a limited review. |  |
| 6 | When should you check a rule’s effective date? | Every time, because publication and effectivity can differ | Best: rules can be published before they take effect and may have transition provisions. Why not the others: circulars change often; waiting for complaints is too late; publication is not effectivity. |  |
| 7 | Which belongs on a one-page social work service charter? | Purpose, referral criteria, response targets, coverage, measures, and what the service does not do | Best: a charter explains the service and its limits. Why not the others: salary and patient details do not belong; an unkeepable guarantee becomes a broken promise. |  |
| 8 | A unit generates 15 hours of social work a week and 12 hours are assigned. What is the balance? | −3 hours a week | Best: balance = available − demand = 12 − 15 = −3. Why not the others: the sign or arithmetic is wrong. |  |
| 9 | You inherit 40 unseen referrals. How should you start? | Sort by risk: safety concerns today, threats to the next session this week, then the rest; report the backlog in writing | Best: triage by risk and make the shortfall visible. Why not the others: order of arrival or loudness ignores risk; closing without contact abandons people. |  |
| 10 | Which body issues the rules on who may practice social work in the Philippines? | Congress, through the social work law, with registration by the PRC | Best: Republic Act No. 4373 as amended, administered with the PRC. Why not the others: the DOH licenses facilities; PhilHealth sets benefits; employers set job descriptions. |  |

## Module 4: Engagement, Language Access, and Cultural Safety

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A patient stays silent while a relative answers every question. What does the silence prove? | Neither agreement nor incapacity; explore her communication and preferences privately | Best: silence has many meanings, including hiya or fear. Why not the others: each conclusion assumes what you have not assessed. |  |
| 2 | For a sensitive interview in the patient’s regional language, whom should you prefer as interpreter? | A trained interpreter or uninvolved bilingual staff member with confidentiality arrangements | Best: a neutral interpreter protects accuracy and privacy. Why not the others: children and interested relatives may filter answers; bystanders breach privacy; avoiding interpretation leaves her unheard. |  |
| 3 | Which is the safest opening question about family involvement? | “Who would you like involved in this conversation?” | Best: it gives the choice to the patient. Why not the others: the others impose, presume payment equals authority, or accuse. |  |
| 4 | What should a culturally safe assessment do? | Ask what beliefs, practices, and supports matter to this person | Best: culture is learned from the person, not assumed. Why not the others: inference stereotypes; avoidance misses strengths; consensus cannot be assumed. |  |
| 5 | Which question uses teach-back? | “So I know I explained it well, can you tell me in your own words what happens next Monday?” | Best: it checks understanding and puts the burden on the explanation. Why not the others: yes-no questions invite polite agreement; blame and pressure do not check understanding. |  |
| 6 | An older patient answers “Opo” to every explanation. What is the best interpretation? | It may mean respect or that she heard you, not that she understood; check with teach-back | Best: politeness and hiya can make it hard to admit confusion. Why not the others: each draws a conclusion you have not checked. |  |
| 7 | In the systematic review of health literacy in chronic kidney disease, about how common was limited health literacy among people on dialysis? | About 27%, mostly from United States studies of low to moderate quality | Best: pooled prevalence was 27% on dialysis (25% overall), with caveats about study quality and setting. Why not the others: the figures are wrong or the claim is false. |  |
| 8 | How should you use the concept of utang na loob in an assessment? | As a prompt to ask whom the person feels able, or unable, to ask for help | Best: cultural concepts are questions to explore. Why not the others: they become stereotypes or excuses for pressure; ignoring them may miss real dynamics. |  |
| 9 | How do you see a patient alone without offending a relative who insists on staying? | Explain a rule that applies to everyone: you start every interview alone, then invite family | Best: a universal rule protects privacy without accusing. Why not the others: accusation or force damages trust; skipping privacy loses safety and money questions. |  |
| 10 | What should you record after asking about family involvement? | Whom the patient wants involved, what may be shared, who speaks if they cannot, and the date | Best: a dated record lets the team follow the patient’s choices. Why not the others: they miss the patient’s choices or the record entirely. |  |

## Module 5: A Comprehensive Psychosocial Assessment

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which statement is a formulation? | “Work and travel costs are blocking attendance, despite his stated wish to continue dialysis.” | Best: a formulation explains why. Why not the others: a label, a fact without explanation, and a task are not formulations. |  |
| 2 | Family and patient accounts conflict. What should you do? | Record each with its source and explore the difference respectfully | Best: sourced accounts let the team weigh them. Why not the others: hiding, favoring payers, or penalizing the person are unfair and unsafe. |  |
| 3 | An assessment names a caregiver. What should you establish next? | Their actual availability, tasks, willingness, and limits | Best: a named caregiver may have little capacity. Why not the others: relationship alone says nothing about capacity; social media is irrelevant; caregivers do not replace nurses. |  |
| 4 | What is a distress-screen result? | Information to combine with the interview and clinical referral | Best: a screen points where to look. Why not the others: it does not diagnose, replace consent, or decide transplant. |  |
| 5 | Which written note uses descriptive language? | “Missed 4 of 13 sessions in October; reports work conflicts.” | Best: it states what happened and the stated reason. Why not the others: labels explain nothing and blame the person. |  |
| 6 | In the four Ps, which factor keeps a problem going? | Perpetuating | Best: perpetuating factors maintain the problem. Why not the others: predisposing makes vulnerable, precipitating triggers, protective helps. |  |
| 7 | Midway through an assessment the patient says, “Sometimes I think it would be better if I were gone.” What do you do? | Stop the assessment, ask directly about thoughts of ending his life, and follow the safety pathway | Best: a possible suicide signal comes before every domain. Why not the others: delay, avoidance, or asking someone else risks missing danger. |  |
| 8 | Why record a strength beside each barrier? | Because plans that use what a person already does well are more likely to be carried out | Best: strengths carry the plan. Why not the others: length and agency rules are not the reason; barriers still matter. |  |
| 9 | What does writing an “Unknown” line at the end of an assessment do? | Keeps the assessment honest and shows what to ask next | Best: listing unknowns directs follow-up. Why not the others: unknowns are normal; assumptions must not fill them; a complete form can still hide unknowns. |  |
| 10 | Why should you check a formulation with the person? | It is a hypothesis; their correction is valuable information | Best: the person knows their life best. Why not the others: signatures, legal claims, and persuasion are not the purpose. |  |

## Module 6: Care Plans, Referrals, and Case Management

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What does a sent referral mean? | Only that the request left; the outcome is not yet confirmed | Best: sent is the first of five stations. Why not the others: each assumes an outcome that has not been confirmed. |  |
| 2 | Which care plan action is strongest? | “Social worker confirms an affordable ride before the next appointment, by Friday.” | Best: it has an owner, a specific action, and a date. Why not the others: they are vague, untimed, or blaming. |  |
| 3 | An assistance agency declines a referral. What is the best next step? | Record the reason, tell the patient, and agree a feasible alternative | Best: a decline with a reason closes the loop and guides the next step. Why not the others: silence, falsification, and oversharing harm the person. |  |
| 4 | Demand exceeds safe service capacity. What should you do? | Escalate the capacity and risk in writing with a prioritized coverage proposal | Best: a visible, prioritized shortfall can be managed. Why not the others: hiding or abandoning work is unsafe; an invented ratio is false. |  |
| 5 | Which goal is written in the person’s own terms? | “Stop borrowing from the lender to pay for transport by January.” | Best: it is specific, timed, and meaningful to the person. Why not the others: vague, blaming, or an action rather than a goal. |  |
| 6 | A referral was sent March 3, due March 13, and today is March 20. What does the aging tool show? | 17 days open, 7 days overdue: overdue | Best: open = 20 − 3 = 17 days; overdue = 20 − 13 = 7 days, which is the overdue tier (escalate starts beyond 7). Why not the others: the arithmetic or tier is wrong. |  |
| 7 | At which station does a referral loop close? | When the person confirms the outcome reached them | Best: help is what reached the household. Why not the others: each earlier station is necessary but not sufficient. |  |
| 8 | What did the navigation trial in 23 hemodialysis units show? | Navigated patients completed more steps toward transplant (3.5 against 1.6), a process outcome | Best: the trial measured steps completed. Why not the others: it did not show more transplants or lower mortality, and it did show an effect on steps. |  |
| 9 | Which event should bring a care plan review forward? | A hospital admission or new missed sessions | Best: admissions and missed sessions signal change. Why not the others: routine or unrelated events are not triggers. |  |
| 10 | When you step a case down, what must the person know? | How and why to come back, and whom to contact | Best: a clear way back is part of closure. Why not the others: closure is not abandonment and should be explained. |  |

## Module 7: PhilHealth Navigation and Financial Protection

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What is a published annual hemodialysis benefit ceiling? | A policy-limited provider benefit, subject to its conditions | Best: benefits are paid under conditions, usually to providers. Why not the others: they misdescribe what a benefit is. |  |
| 2 | Who determines the final payer outcome of a claim? | The payer, through its process | Best: PhilHealth decides claims. Why not the others: none of these has that authority. |  |
| 3 | A new transplant circular has just been published. For an existing case, what should you do first? | Check its effectivity, the case dates, and the transition provisions with the contracted provider | Best: publication is not effectivity, and older cases may follow older rules. Why not the others: each skips the checks or makes a promise. |  |
| 4 | A family disputes a dialysis charge. What should it trigger? | An itemized review against the relevant benefit rule, through the authorized route | Best: check the charge against the rule with the claims officer. Why not the others: falsification, unsafe advice, and promises are wrong. |  |
| 5 | Under PC 2024-0023 as officially explained, how many hemodialysis sessions are covered a year? | Up to 156 | Best: up to 156 sessions a year, per the circular and Tamang Sagot. Why not the others: the numbers are wrong; the benefit is not unlimited. |  |
| 6 | A social media post says dialysis is “100% free, all year, no limits.” What is accurate? | There is no copayment for package-covered services, but the benefit is limited to 156 sessions a year and some services may cost money | Best: the official explanation covers no copayment for package services in public and private facilities, within a session limit. Why not the others: they overstate, understate, or misstate the rule. |  |
| 7 | A patient has used 120 sessions by September 30 on three sessions a week. About when will the 156 run out? | In about 12 weeks, around December 23 | Best: 156 − 120 = 36 sessions; 36 ÷ 3 = 12 weeks. Why not the others: the arithmetic is wrong. |  |
| 8 | The peritoneal dialysis circular could not be fully retrieved. How should you discuss package amounts? | Do not quote amounts; check the current circular and the contracted provider | Best: unverified amounts must not be quoted. Why not the others: estimates and rumors become false promises. |  |
| 9 | Which line best documents a benefit explanation? | “Explained per PC 2024-0023 and its Tamang Sagot, checked on [date].” | Best: naming the version and date makes the advice checkable and correctable. Why not the others: they do not say which rule was used. |  |
| 10 | A daughter asks how much PhilHealth will pay for her father’s transplant. What is the best answer? | Show the circular and the facility’s written estimate; do not promise an amount | Best: point to the official source and the provider, without promising. Why not the others: promises and refusals both fail her. |  |

## Module 8: Assistance Pathways and Resource Mobilization

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How should a guarantee letter be treated? | As a commitment whose scope and the provider’s acceptance need confirming | Best: a guarantee letter covers a stated amount for a stated provider. Why not the others: it is not total coverage, cash, or a privacy waiver. |  |
| 2 | What should an assistance directory contain? | Eligibility, access route, requirements, what it pays for, and the date it was verified | Best: dated, specific information sends families to the right place. Why not the others: names alone, promises, or credentials are useless or harmful. |  |
| 3 | Which assistance summary is strongest? | A factual account of assessed need, resources, verified expenses, and the remaining gap | Best: honest, specific reports are credible. Why not the others: invention and copying are false documentation. |  |
| 4 | A request is denied. What should you do? | Explore alternatives and immediate access risks, and explain what remains unresolved | Best: keep treatment safe and look for another route. Why not the others: promises, falsification, and unassessed loans harm the person. |  |
| 5 | An office asks for a letter saying the patient “is dying” when that is not true. What do you do? | Decline to write anything untrue and offer a factual social case study | Best: false documentation harms the person and every future applicant. Why not the others: it remains false whoever writes it; sending them away abandons them. |  |
| 6 | Total cost this month is PHP 12,000, confirmed support PHP 6,000, and a local request is pending. What is the gap? | PHP 6,000 until the local decision arrives | Best: subtract only confirmed support. Why not the others: they count pending support, ignore confirmed support, or add instead of subtract. |  |
| 7 | Which source is usually not available in a private freestanding dialysis unit? | A Malasakit Center desk | Best: Malasakit Centers are in DOH hospitals and designated hospitals. Why not the others: those programs are reached through their own offices. |  |
| 8 | A politician’s staff offer to pay a balance if the family appears in a photo. What do you do? | Ask the family privately, make refusal safe, and help them set limits if they agree | Best: the choice is theirs, made freely. Why not the others: deciding for them removes their choice. |  |
| 9 | Why track applications to their decisions instead of counting submissions? | Because only decided and received support helps the household | Best: help is what arrives. Why not the others: they misstate the purpose or the facts. |  |
| 10 | What should you list before choosing assistance sources? | The household’s costs for the next three months | Best: start from the costs, then match sources. Why not the others: they are unfocused, excessive, or private. |  |

## Module 9: Transport, Work, Housing, Food, and Disability Access

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | When is a transport plan incomplete? | When it covers only the outward trip although the return is the problem | Best: the return after dialysis, when people are weak, is often the hardest part. Why not the others: those are parts of a good plan. |  |
| 2 | How should an employer letter be handled? | With the patient’s consent, disclosing only what the employer needs | Best: consent and minimum disclosure. Why not the others: they overshare, overpromise, or exceed your role. |  |
| 3 | A patient shortens sessions to catch a cheap ride. What is the best response? | Tell the clinical team and work on the travel barrier together | Best: shortened sessions are clinical; the ride is your problem to solve. Why not the others: praise or advice is unsafe; a label solves nothing. |  |
| 4 | What does an access cost worksheet establish? | A transparent estimate with stated assumptions | Best: it is planning arithmetic. Why not the others: it creates no bill, entitlement, or eligibility. |  |
| 5 | Six visits at PHP 120 out, 120 back, 0 escort, and 30 other, plus PHP 300 one-time, with PHP 1,000 confirmed support. What is the gap? | PHP 920 | Best: 6 × 270 + 300 = 1,920; 1,920 − 1,000 = 920. Why not the others: they ignore support or miscalculate. |  |
| 6 | Household health spending is PHP 4,000 of PHP 25,000 total spending. What is the share, and what does it mean? | 16%, above the 10% SDG 3.8.2 mark, a population hardship indicator, not an eligibility rule | Best: 4,000 ÷ 25,000 = 16%; the marks describe hardship, not program eligibility. Why not the others: wrong arithmetic or wrong meaning. |  |
| 7 | What did the DOPPS travel time study find? | Longer travel time was associated with higher mortality and lower quality of life, in an observational analysis | Best: an association from observational data with a single unvalidated question. Why not the others: they contradict or overstate the finding. |  |
| 8 | A patient says the family eats rice and instant noodles “to save for the fare.” What should you do? | Tell the dietitian and nephrologist this week and work on the access cost | Best: food insecurity is a clinical risk (salt, weight loss) with a social cause. Why not the others: advice is unsafe; waiting lets harm happen. |  |
| 9 | What should you ask every patient on dialysis about the PWD ID? | Whether they have one, and help them apply if they may qualify | Best: people on dialysis may qualify as persons with disability (PWD), and the ID carries a legal discount. Why not the others: they miss or misdescribe the benefit. |  |
| 10 | A patient lost his driving job after starting dialysis. Which step could recover income? | Check his SSS contributions for sickness or disability benefits | Best: benefits from past contributions may apply. Why not the others: unsafe, defeatist, or impossible. |  |

## Module 10: Distress, Depression, Anxiety, and Stepped Support

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What does a screening score establish by itself? | Neither a diagnosis nor all of the urgency; it points where to look | Best: a screen such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) is the start of assessment. Why not the others: they overstate what a score can do. |  |
| 2 | Sudden confusion appears during a session. What should happen? | Clinical assessment for an acute cause, now | Best: acute confusion can signal a medical emergency. Why not the others: they delay or misattribute it. |  |
| 3 | You lack training in a specialized psychotherapy. What should you do? | Work within your competence and refer, or seek qualified supervision | Best: supportive work is yours; specialized therapy needs training. Why not the others: overreach, falsification, or withdrawal. |  |
| 4 | The PHQ-9 total is low, but the patient discloses immediate intent to harm himself. What is the priority? | Immediate safety response and clinical escalation | Best: a disclosure overrides any total. Why not the others: they let the number hide the danger. |  |
| 5 | Items scored: interest 2, mood 2, sleep 3, energy 3, appetite 2, failure 2, concentration 1, slowness 1, item 9 = 0. What is the total and its meaning? | 16; depression likely enough to report and refer; not a diagnosis | Best: the sum is 16, above the dialysis cutoff of 10; item 9 is 0. Why not the others: a score is not a diagnosis; 14 is wrong; the safety pathway follows item 9, not the total. |  |
| 6 | By clinical interview, about how common was depression among people on dialysis in the Palmer meta-analysis? | About 23%; rating scales gave higher figures (about 39%) | Best: 22.8% by interview, 39.3% by scales, with scales likely overestimating. Why not the others: wrong figures or method. |  |
| 7 | Which PHQ-9 items overlap most with symptoms of kidney failure? | Sleep, energy, and appetite | Best: uremia, anemia, and itch affect sleep, energy, and appetite. Why not the others: those are core mood items the kidneys do not explain. |  |
| 8 | What did the Cochrane review find about cognitive behavioral therapy for depression in dialysis? | It probably improves depressive symptoms, with moderate-certainty evidence | Best: moderate-certainty improvement in symptom scores. Why not the others: survival was not shown; benefit was found; no harm was reported as the finding. |  |
| 9 | What did ASCEND compare and find? | Sertraline versus chairside CBT; clinician-rated scores were modestly lower with sertraline, with more side effects, and no placebo group | Best: an open-label comparison of two active treatments. Why not the others: they misdescribe the trial. |  |
| 10 | A patient declines a mental health referral. What should you do? | Respect the decision, record it, keep the door open, and rescreen later | Best: patients decide for their own reasons; your role is to offer and stay available. Why not the others: they override or abandon him. |  |

## Module 11: Immediate Safety, Safeguarding, Violence, and Exploitation

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A person reports that they intend to harm themselves today. What is the first priority? | Immediate safety: stay with them and activate the clinical emergency response | Best: immediate risk comes before everything. Why not the others: paperwork and delay leave the person in danger; secrecy cannot be promised when life is at risk. |  |
| 2 | A suspected abuser controls the patient’s phone. How should you plan contact? | Agree a safe, private communication route with the patient | Best: contact must not alert the abuser. Why not the others: each risks exposure to the person causing harm. |  |
| 3 | Which response to immediate danger is inadequate? | Sending only a routine referral email | Best: a routine email may not be read in time. Why not the others: those are parts of an adequate response. |  |
| 4 | What should a safeguarding note distinguish? | Facts, the person’s own report, actions taken, and who received responsibility | Best: a clear note lets others act and stands up to review. Why not the others: each leaves out what the next person needs. |  |
| 5 | Does asking someone directly about suicidal thoughts increase their risk? | No; reviewed studies found no significant increase, and talking about it may reduce such thoughts | Best: the review found no evidence that asking induces ideation. Why not the others: they repeat a myth or use uncertainty as a reason to stay silent. |  |
| 6 | A patient says, “My family would be better off without me.” What is the best next question? | “Are you having thoughts of ending your life?” | Best: ask directly and calmly. Why not the others: reassurance, changing the subject, or deflecting all avoid the question. |  |
| 7 | In the meta-analysis of elder abuse in community settings, about what share of adults aged 60 or over experienced abuse in the past year? | About one in six (15.7%), most often psychological and financial | Best: pooled prevalence 15.7%, with few studies from low- and middle-income countries. Why not the others: wrong figures. |  |
| 8 | An older patient’s nephew holds her ATM card and there is often no food at home. She asks you not to make trouble. What is the best approach? | Talk privately, describe what you see, offer harm-reducing options that keep dialysis going, and involve your supervisor | Best: respect her autonomy while reducing harm and following the safeguarding procedure. Why not the others: confrontation can endanger her; inaction abandons her; capacity is not judged from a request for privacy. |  |
| 9 | A woman discloses partner violence, and her partner brings her to dialysis. What should the safety plan address first? | Another way to get to dialysis, before any confrontation | Best: in kidney care, safety plans must keep treatment going. Why not the others: forcing action, disclosing, or stopping treatment endanger her. |  |
| 10 | A patient asks to stop dialysis and also says he has thought of ending his life. What should happen? | Follow the safety pathway first, and involve the nephrologist in both questions | Best: the two can overlap; safety comes first, and both go to the nephrologist. Why not the others: they miss the risk or dismiss the request. |  |

## Module 12: Motivational Conversations and Treatment Barriers

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which is a motivational opening? | “What is hardest about treatment days for you?” | Best: an open question invites the person’s story. Why not the others: blame and threats provoke resistance. |  |
| 2 | A patient disagrees with his treatment. What does that alone prove? | Neither incapacity nor bad character; his understanding and concerns need exploring | Best: disagreement is information. Why not the others: each draws an unsupported conclusion. |  |
| 3 | What makes a plan ethical in motivational work? | It is negotiated and consistent with the person’s goals and safety | Best: partnership and respect for autonomy. Why not the others: coercion, guarantees, or bypassing consent are not ethical. |  |
| 4 | Before exploring motivation after a missed session, what should you check? | Immediate medical risk, with the clinical team | Best: a missed session can be a clinical emergency. Why not the others: they are irrelevant or judgmental. |  |
| 5 | What are the four core skills of motivational interviewing (OARS)? | Open questions, affirmations, reflections, and summaries | Best: OARS are the conversational skills. Why not the others: they are not the motivational interviewing skills. |  |
| 6 | A patient says, “I lose customers if I am late.” Which reply is motivational? | “Your shop is how you support your family; you need both the shop and dialysis to work.” | Best: a reflection that honors his reasons without arguing. Why not the others: arguing or dismissing triggers resistance. |  |
| 7 | A patient leaves at hour two because of severe leg cramps. Whose problem is the cramp? | The nurse and nephrologist’s, the same day; you work on any practical barriers | Best: a physical symptom during dialysis needs clinical review. Why not the others: counseling or willpower will not treat a cramp. |  |
| 8 | What is the righting reflex? | The helper’s urge to correct and advise, which usually provokes resistance | Best: resisting it is central to motivational work. Why not the others: they misdefine it. |  |
| 9 | What did the randomized trial of motivational interviewing in 60 hemodialysis patients show? | Better measured adherence, but no difference in quality of life, in a small single-center trial | Best: adherence improved; quality of life did not differ; small trial. Why not the others: they misstate the outcomes. |  |
| 10 | An informed adult chooses an option you disagree with. What do you do? | Confirm understanding, inform the nephrologist, record the decision, and keep the relationship open | Best: respect, record, and remain available. Why not the others: pressure or withdrawal damages trust and autonomy. |  |

## Module 13: Families, Caregivers, Children, and Changing Life Roles

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What does a relative’s presence at the unit establish? | Neither their caregiving capacity nor their authority, until you check | Best: presence is not capacity or authority. Why not the others: each assumes what must be assessed. |  |
| 2 | What should a family meeting have? | An agreed purpose and participation authorized by the patient | Best: the patient decides who joins and why. Why not the others: they sideline the patient or the team. |  |
| 3 | A child regularly misses school to interpret at kidney appointments. What is the best response? | Arrange language support and assess the family’s and child’s needs | Best: protect the child’s schooling and use proper interpreters. Why not the others: they entrench harm. |  |
| 4 | What should a useful caregiver plan record? | Tasks, willingness, actual capacity, strain, and backup | Best: these show whether the plan can hold. Why not the others: they miss capacity, strain, or backup. |  |
| 5 | What did the systematic review of caregivers for adults on maintenance dialysis find? | Caregivers’ quality of life was poorer than the general population’s and similar to other chronic-disease caregivers | Best: 61 mostly cross-sectional studies, generally poor quality. Why not the others: they contradict the findings. |  |
| 6 | How should you assess a caregiver? | In a separate, private conversation, with the patient’s knowledge | Best: caregivers rarely speak freely in front of the person they care for. Why not the others: they miss the caregiver’s own view. |  |
| 7 | An exhausted caregiver screens positive for low mood. What applies? | The same screening and safety steps as for any patient, including asking about self-harm | Best: caregivers can be at risk too. Why not the others: they ignore a person in distress. |  |
| 8 | What did the 2026 review of caregiver interventions in chronic kidney disease conclude? | Education and skills programs may reduce burden, with low-certainty evidence | Best: 13 studies; meta-analysis of five education programs showed reduction; certainty low. Why not the others: they misstate it. |  |
| 9 | A former provider on dialysis says he feels useless. What may help? | Finding roles he can still hold, such as managing the budget, and watching for depression | Best: role loss is normal grief; meaningful roles help. Why not the others: inactivity, overdiagnosis, or dismissal. |  |
| 10 | What protects a household from collapse when the main caregiver falls ill? | A named backup for every essential task | Best: backup keeps treatment going. Why not the others: they do not cover the missing person’s tasks. |  |

## Module 14: Modality Decisions, Home Therapy, and Practical Feasibility

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Who decides clinical suitability for home therapy? | The qualified clinical home-therapy team, through its process | Best: suitability is a clinical decision. Why not the others: they lack that authority. |  |
| 2 | What should low literacy prompt when home dialysis is considered? | Accessible education and individual assessment | Best: many people with low literacy learn home dialysis with suitable teaching. Why not the others: they exclude or deceive. |  |
| 3 | What is the social worker’s role in home therapy? | Mapping housing and support barriers and coordinating solutions | Best: feasibility barriers are social work. Why not the others: clinical tasks and guarantees are outside your role. |  |
| 4 | A trained caregiver withdraws support. What should happen? | Prompt reassessment of support with the home-therapy team | Best: a changed household changes safety. Why not the others: they ignore risk or act outside your authority. |  |
| 5 | A home visit finds no storage for peritoneal dialysis boxes. What should come first? | Look for solutions, such as smaller deliveries or storage at a nearby relative’s house | Best: solvable problems should be tried first. Why not the others: they rule out, impose, or ignore. |  |
| 6 | What did the 2024 Cochrane review of peritoneal dialysis versus hemodialysis conclude? | For most outcomes, benefits and harms of one over the other remain uncertain | Best: two small trials and 82 observational studies. Why not the others: they overstate the evidence. |  |
| 7 | When the evidence does not favor one modality for a medically suitable person, what should carry more weight? | The person’s values and circumstances | Best: that is shared decision making. Why not the others: they sideline the person. |  |
| 8 | In the regional survey, how did peritoneal dialysis use compare between lower- and higher-income countries in South and Southeast Asia? | About 3.4% against 10.1%, with policy, awareness, training, and affordability named as deterrents | Best: underuse in lower-income settings, with named barriers. Why not the others: they misstate the survey. |  |
| 9 | A farmer refuses peritoneal dialysis because he thinks he must stop working. What could help? | Asking the nurse to explain overnight automated peritoneal dialysis | Best: the barrier may be missing information. Why not the others: they skip information or decide for him. |  |
| 10 | After a modality decision, what should you record? | What was chosen, why, and when it will be revisited | Best: decisions can be revisited when circumstances change. Why not the others: they lose the reasons or the review. |  |

## Module 15: Transplant Access, Psychosocial Preparation, and Donor Protection

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What should a transplant psychosocial assessment do? | Describe specific barriers, strengths, and support needs | Best: assessment is for preparation. Why not the others: they exclude unfairly, overpromise, or exceed authority. |  |
| 2 | A donor privately reports pressure involving payment. What is the first response? | Use the authorized donor-protection and ethics pathway | Best: route through the protected pathway to the ethics committee. Why not the others: they are illegal, deceptive, or dangerous. |  |
| 3 | How should a donor’s wish to withdraw be handled? | Through a private, protected route, without sharing their reasons | Best: a safe exit is part of free consent. Why not the others: they coerce or expose the donor. |  |
| 4 | What should long-term transplant planning include? | Medicines, follow-up, travel, work disruption, and changing support | Best: transplant is lifelong care. Why not the others: they are incomplete or false. |  |
| 5 | What did the SIPAT prospective study find? | Higher scores were associated with rejection, admissions, infection, and support failure, but not with organ failure or death | Best: the Stanford Integrated Psychosocial Assessment for Transplantation (SIPAT) showed associations with some outcomes in 217 recipients. Why not the others: they overstate or misstate the findings. |  |
| 6 | What did the meta-analysis of living donor health risks find? | Higher relative risk of kidney failure but low absolute risk, and no higher risk of death or adverse psychosocial outcomes | Best: relative risk 8.83, absolute about 0.5 per 1,000 person-years. Why not the others: they contradict the findings. |  |
| 7 | A stated cousin knows little about the recipient’s family and was promised help with a business. What do these signals prove? | Nothing yet, but they must be routed through the protected pathway before evaluation continues | Best: signals are routed, not judged by you. Why not the others: they overreach or underreact. |  |
| 8 | The recipient’s wife asks how the donor’s interview went. What do you say? | “The donor’s evaluation is private; I can tell you about your husband’s own next steps.” | Best: a rule that applies to everyone protects the donor. Why not the others: any comment discloses. |  |
| 9 | Under Philippine law, how is recruiting a person for the removal or sale of an organ treated? | As trafficking in persons | Best: anti-trafficking law covers removal or sale of organs. Why not the others: they misstate the law. |  |
| 10 | How should donor interviews be conducted? | Alone, in private, more than once, with records kept separate | Best: privacy and repetition protect freedom. Why not the others: they undermine independence. |  |

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2 | How should a request to stop dialysis be handled? | Explored and referred for timely clinical and safety assessment | Best: it is the patient’s decision with the nephrologist, after depression and safety are assessed. Why not the others: they dismiss, overreach, or pathologize. |  |

| 5 | What did the SPIRIT trial of advance care planning in dialysis find? | Better patient-surrogate agreement on goals and less decisional conflict; surrogate confidence did not differ | Best: odds ratio 1.61 for agreement, less conflict. Why not the others: they misstate the outcomes. |  |
| 6 | About how common was prolonged grief disorder after non-violent bereavement in the meta-analysis? | About 10% (9.8%), higher in older people | Best: 9.8% pooled, with heterogeneous studies. Why not the others: wrong figures. |  |
| 7 | Which three questions does advance care planning cover? | What matters most, who speaks for the person, and what they want if they get sicker | Best: values, surrogate, and what-if. Why not the others: they miss the purpose. |  |
| 8 | A daughter says, “We cannot let him die; tell him he must continue.” What is your role? | Acknowledge her fear and explain that the decision is his, made with his doctor | Best: support her while protecting his decision. Why not the others: they override him or abandon her. |  |
| 9 | How should conservative kidney management be explained to a family who fears abandonment? | As active care with a team that keeps managing symptoms and supporting the family | Best: it is planned, active care. Why not the others: they misdescribe it. |  |
| 10 | After a patient dies, what is good bereavement follow-up? | A call or card in the first weeks and a check-in at three to six months, with referral if grief does not ease | Best: planned contact tells families they mattered and catches prolonged grief. Why not the others: they leave families alone. |  |

## Module 17: Transfers, Disasters, and Continuity of Care

| Q | Stem | Keyed answer | Explanation | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | When is a transfer adequately arranged? | When the receiving service accepts and practical access and follow-up are confirmed | Best: a transfer closes on confirmed arrival and treatment. Why not the others: they stop short of the outcome. |  |
| 2 | During a unit closure, what should social work do? | Coordinate access and support around clinically confirmed arrangements | Best: social work supports the clinical plan. Why not the others: they exceed your role or breach privacy. |  |
| 3 | A public spreadsheet exposes patient details during a disaster. What is the best response? | Use the privacy incident process and move coordination to protected routes | Best: contain and report. Why not the others: they worsen or ignore the breach. |  |
| 4 | What should a continuity handoff include? | Receiving acceptance, practical barriers, safe contact, owner, and follow-up | Best: what the receiving side needs for safe care. Why not the others: too little, too much, or improper. |  |
| 5 | What is the most common reason a receiving unit refuses a traveling patient on arrival? | Serology results that are missing or too old | Best: check serology dates against the receiving unit’s requirement before travel. Why not the others: they are not the usual reason. |  |
| 6 | In interviews after Hurricane Katrina, what was associated with missing three or more sessions? | Not knowing the unit’s emergency plan | Best: patients unaware of the plan were more likely to miss. Why not the others: they misstate the finding. |  |
| 7 | Before a typhoon, whom do you call first? | The patients who live alone, on islands, in flood zones, or without transport | Best: risk sets the order. Why not the others: they ignore risk. |  |
| 8 | A hemodialysis patient cannot be reached two days after a disaster. What do you do? | Alert the nephrologist and trace through relatives, neighbors, and the barangay | Best: missed sessions are dangerous; trace actively. Why not the others: they wait or assume. |  |
| 9 | What belongs in a personal emergency plan? | Two alternative units, contacts, documents to bring, emergency diet advice, and medicines | Best: what a person needs if the unit closes. Why not the others: incomplete or excessive. |  |
| 10 | When does a transfer close? | When the receiving unit confirms the first session took place | Best: arrival and treatment confirmed. Why not the others: earlier steps are not the outcome. |  |

| 5 | A spouse asks for an adult patient’s records. Why not the others: they disclose without authority or hide a safety-relevant request. |  |
| 6 | Under the Data Privacy Act, how is health information classified? | As sensitive personal information that needs a lawful basis and safeguards | Best: health data is sensitive personal information. Why not the others: they misstate the law. |  |
